#6190. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit. Ford and his team are happy to help with these requests, and can be reached at [email protected].

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

Client dinners, catered lunches and team celebrations can add up quickly. The right business credit card can turn those restaurant bills into a meaningful haul of points, miles or cash back.

From high category bonuses to uncapped flat-rate rewards, the best credit cards for dining can make every business meal work harder.

Here's how our top picks compare based on their dining returns, annual fees and reward flexibility.

The information for the U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus Visa Signature Card and the U.S. Bank Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

To determine the best business cards for dining, I looked for cards with an estimated return of at least 3% on restaurant purchases, based on TPG's valuations. I focused on ongoing earnings rather than welcome offers or dining credits, then selected cards serving distinct use cases, including high category bonuses, uncapped transferable rewards and no-annual-fee options.

Other cards that don't earn at least 3% back in value based on our valuations may still be good fits for your business within a broader rewards strategy, but are less competitive when restaurant earnings are the primary goal.

The American Express Business Gold earns valuable Membership Rewards points. Cardmembers earn 4 points per dollar spent in their top two spending categories each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in bonus category spending per year, then 1 point per dollar), with dining and restaurants falling under an available category.

That means businesses that max out their cap could earn 600,000 points each year. Even if you don't come close to that cap, 4 points per dollar is still a significant return on spend, especially when they come with all the potential of Membership Rewards.

Just be careful: Since Amex rewards extra bonus points on your top spending categories each billing cycle, if other eligible expenses overtake dining, restaurant purchases may earn only 1 point per dollar. You can use that to your advantage when your restaurant spending is low one month, but it could also catch you off guard.

To learn more, read our full review of the Business Gold.

Apply here: American Express Business Gold

The U.S. Bank Business Essentials Plus earns 5% cash back in the cardholder's top eligible spending category each month on up to $200,000 in annual eligible purchases, automatically. Dining is one of the qualifying categories, and the cap is high enough that most businesses won't have to worry about it. All purchases outside the top category earn at least 2% cash back, which is also a generous return.

The $295 annual fee makes this card best for businesses with substantial, consistent restaurant spending. Otherwise, a no-annual-fee option may provide better value overall.

If you're looking for a card with no annual fee, The Blue Business Plus earns 2 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on all purchases (for the first $50,000 in spending each year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The simplicity of this card means you don't need to keep track of spending categories; it's just as great for your dining purchases as it is for shipping, advertising and other business expenses. For businesses that can stay below the cap and earn 2 points per dollar spent on all their spending, the combination of transferable points and no annual fee is difficult to beat.

To learn more, read our full review of the Blue Business Plus.

Apply here: The Blue Business Plus Credit Card from American Express

Like the Blue Business Plus, the Capital One Venture Business earns 2 miles per dollar spent on dining and other purchases. Unlike the Amex card, however, that earning rate is unlimited. This makes Venture Business a stronger fit for businesses that expect to spend more than $50,000 each year and can take advantage of double miles well above that spending threshold, despite the $95 annual fee.

Capital One miles are highly versatile, with options to transfer to 15-plus airline or hotel partners, book travel without blackout dates through Capital One Travel and more. In fact, a different set of transfer partners could make the Venture Business a more compelling solution than an Amex, depending on your business's redemption preferences.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Business Credit Card

The Triple Cash Rewards Visa Business Card earns 3% cash back on eligible restaurant purchases with no annual fee, and there's no cap on total rewards.

It can't match the Business Essentials Plus card's 5% return, but there's no annual fee to recoup. A business would need to spend about $14,750 annually on dining for the 5% rate to make up for the $295 fee versus the Triple Cash card's no-annual-fee 3% return. Therefore, if you're looking for simple cash back but have more moderate restaurant spending, the Triple Cash is a stronger fit.

To learn more, read our full review of the U.S. Bank Triple Cash.

The Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex is a good fit for businesses that frequently entertain clients, host events at Marriott properties or incur dining expenses while traveling. It earns 4 points per dollar spent on eligible restaurant purchases worldwide, which represents a 3% return at TPG's November 2026 valuations. Since it doesn't impose a spending cap on its restaurant rewards, businesses can earn consistently throughout the year.

The card becomes especially valuable for businesses that regularly stay with Marriott and can put both its hotel benefits and Bonvoy rewards to use.

Of course, loyalty to one hotel brand won't work for everyone. Businesses that prioritize more flexible redemptions may prefer a card that includes Marriott as a transfer partner rather than choosing a cobranded card specifically.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bonvoy Business Amex.

Apply now: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

The right business card option depends on more than earning rates. You'll also need to account for how much your business spends, whether you prefer cash back or travel rewards and whether you're willing to pay an annual fee.

Start with the net value, not the largest number in the table. The Amex Business Gold and Business Essentials Plus only deliver their highest dining returns when restaurant purchases rank among the business's top eligible categories. But cards that earn lower rates of return on dining might be a better value once you factor in annual fees and spending caps.

In addition to considering the type of rewards best for your business, think about what else these cards offer. Secondary benefits like travel protections, cellphone insurance, lounge access or elite status might make up for a lower earning rate on meals when you consider the whole package.

A large welcome offer can improve a card's first-year value, but it shouldn't outweigh its long-term fit. Compare ongoing rewards after the annual fee, along with the protections, credits and other benefits your business will realistically use. That said, when two or more cards are equally strong long-term fits, a welcome bonus can be a useful tiebreaker. Especially since some credit cards currently offer welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more.

Lastly, confirm your spending will count toward elevated earning rates if the bonus rate affects which card you pay with. Dining bonuses depend on how the merchant categorizes the purchase, and not all food vendors are considered a restaurant. For example, a hotel cafe may code as travel, while a bar might code as nightlife or entertainment.

The Amex Business Gold offers the highest potential dining return based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, but its earning rate alone likely doesn't settle the decision. Spending caps, annual fees, redemption flexibility and other card benefits will also factor into which card delivers the most value for your business.

Businesses with large, predictable restaurant expenses will come out ahead by choosing premium cards, even after budgeting for an annual fee. When your dining spending is more moderate or inconsistent, though, a no-annual-fee card may produce the same net value with less monitoring. Don't pay for an earnings rate your business won't regularly trigger.

#6188. Booked! SAS Business Class To Germany, Because My Wife Chose Horses Over The Caribbean

One beauty of sitting on all these SAS EuroBonus miles is that spur-of-the-moment trips are possible…like a trip to Germany for a few days.

My wife works very hard and rather unexpectedly was given five days, though without a lot of notice. Life is busy for all of us and of course the kids are in school, but as they quickly grow up Heidi and I have elected to take advantage of opportunities like this…for we will regret not doing so later.

Heidi initially suggested a “trip to the Caribbean…somewhere warm” and I thought it would be a good opportunity  to visit Saint Kitts and Nevis and check out the Park Hyatt there. I also suggested we could fly to Iceland with no set plan, get in the car, and drive. Wouldn’t that be fun? I’ve never done a trip around Iceland’s Ring Road.

Ultimately, though, Heidi spoke to her best friend in Germany and decided it would be a prefect opportunity to see her parents (remember, she did not join us on the summer trip) and ride horses with her friend in the Black Forest. I loved the idea and got to work on the flights.

There wasn’t business class from Los Angeles, but there was from Chicago exactly on our dates…five days, with four nights on the ground. Hardly long enough, but better than nothing? We’ll fly into Zurich, but I bought a separate ticket (on Norwegian!) to return from Basel to Copenhagen to catch the SAS connection to ORD…with a very tight connection.

So as I conclude my India Trip Report and move on to our summer trip to Europe, I’ll be sharing updates from this trip. We’ll be traveling in business class on the SAS A330, a product I’ve reviewed many times, though I may do so again if the situation warrants.

There’s never an ideal time to get away, but I really hope this will be a refreshing time for Heidi and indeed for all of us. And yes, even though it’s hardly something new or different, I get really excited ahead of an intercontinental trip, especially in a premium cabin.

#6187. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6186. Ask a Local: Where to Go in Nairobi According to Runner Emily Chepkor

"Nairobi is a city best understood in motion," says Emily Chepkor, founder of We Run Nairobi, the city's biggest and most popular run club. She's from a small town in Kenya, Kapsabet, that has produced more world-class runners per square mile than anywhere else on earth. While the country is known worldwide for its running heritage, Nairobi hadn't quite caught up to the hype until Chepkor came along.

She runs as a hobby, and is a 12-time marathoner (and two-time Boston qualifier) who felt that, though Kenya's running reputation was unmatched internationally, the runner lifestyle itself wasn't accessible to everyday Kenyans—elite athletes only. She set out to change that and bring running closer to all Nairobians, starting with a weekly run club that began with just her and three friends. It slowly grew through word of mouth and especially TikTok, into something bigger, built on a simple idea: no registration, no fees, you just show up and run alongside Emily.

That run has become a defining weekly ritual for Nairobians, drawing over 1,200 people every Saturday morning. It's now etched into the city's identity. The same way New York is known for its bagels, Nairobi is known for the We Run Nairobi neighborhood runs, a cultural landmark for locals and tourists alike.

Below, Emily tells us about some of her favorite things to do in the city she calls home.

Karura Forest is “without a doubt” the best place to run in Nairobi, if you ask Emily.

"Karura Forest, without a doubt, is the most scenic route in the city”, she says. “I run the Sigiria side, through Gate F; it's quieter, more canopied. My dog Biscuit and I do the 10-kilometer loop most Sundays, crossing little rivers every kilometer. If you want something gentler, the 5-kilometer route is just as lovely." Her Saturday club runs the same way: "We're completely pace-agnostic. First-timers run next to marathoners".

Karura is the second largest urban forest in the world after the Tijuca Forest in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and provides the perfect place for an outdoor run.

“Kengele's is always a safe bet whatever's on, whether it's World Cup, rugby, athletics, you'll find a good crowd," says Chepkor. "What I love is how the embassies get involved: around big sporting events, they'll partner with venues across the city to host public watch parties. I'll never forget the British High Commission's watch party in Karura Forest, the day Sebastian Sawe broke the two-hour marathon barrier. The whole country was locked in, and experiencing that moment surrounded by hundreds of people felt incredibly special.”

The McMillan Memorial Library is one of her favorite places for some peace and quiet, and some history.

“The McMillan Memorial Library is a perfect little time capsule of Nairobi, architecturally and literally—it's currently being renovated by Book Bunk, founded by two Kenyan women committed to restoring our public libraries," she says. "I also love the Nairobi Gallery, home to Point Zero, the spot from which all distances in Kenya are measured.”

“Tigoni is a small town only 30 to 40 minutes from Nairobi, but it feels much farther away. The city gives way to rolling tea plantations and narrow country roads. I start at Brackenhurst with coffee from Muna Tree Cafe on the terrace, then rent a bicycle and ride through the plantations, stopping wherever the view is too good to pass.” Back at Brackenhurst, she'll spread a blanket on the lawn to read, maybe doze off, then finish with tennis or a walk through the Indigenous forest. "It's the itinerary I'm proudest to take an out-of-towner on," Chepkor says.

"Sigiria Coffee House is my default—small, intimate, and full of dogs on Sunday mornings. On tennis mornings it's Waitabit, same easy vibe." For souvenirs, she sends visitors to two spots near each other: "Spinners Web has beautiful rugs, a café, and a used-books library. Just up the road, Tribal Gallery has grander pieces—restored Swahili doors, oversized mirrors—alongside smaller suitcase-friendly finds like ceramics and jewelry."

"Fig & Olive in Tigoni is part bodega, part restaurant, with a lawn where no one blinks if you swap your chair for the grass. In the city, it's the Tin Roof Café in Karen—moving from table to grass and back, especially post-run, and the salad bar is iconic. For something dressier that still softens outdoors, Matteo's: white tablecloths, al fresco seating, and little intimate corners I'm still discovering."

The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart.

Scoring a place by the fireplace is a coup.

"The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart. Scoring a corner table by the fireplace on a chilly evening is a date-night dream. For something more stylish, Inti has skyline views in every direction—some Friday nights it turns into an intimate DJ set." For the rest of the evening, she splits the city in two: “If you're after energy, Geco, alive with Nairobi's music scene, especially on Wednesdays. For actual conversation, Cave-à-Manger has an expansive wine list and keeps the music in the background.”

"Toi Market, with one caveat: Nairobi isn't really a vintage city in the curated, boutique sense— we're much more of an open-air, flea market vibe, with thousands of stalls. Toi is sprawling, busy, and a little chaotic. You'll need patience and a willingness to dig, but if you put in the time, you'll almost always come away with something great for a fraction of what you'd pay elsewhere."

“Nai Nami is properly off the beaten track; it's a walking tour of Nairobi's CBD led by former street children. You see downtown Nairobi through the eyes of people who know it intimately, and leave with a completely different understanding of the city. The Alliance Française is an unexpected answer, but it's one of Nairobi's great cultural hubs—plays, concerts, exhibitions, most of which are free, and the original stomping ground of Sauti Sol, our biggest boy band.”

A view of the city from Nairobi National Park

"Nairobi is the only city in the world with a national park so if you’ve only got one day, make it a wildlife day. I’d go for a game drive through Nairobi National Park at sunrise, then the elephant feeding at Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, and the Giraffe Centre to finish. Afterwards, a slow lunch nearby at either Cultiva, Talisman, or Matteo's. "

"I'd highly recommend coming to a We Run Nairobi Saturday. One of my favorite traditions is that we 'brand' every first-timer with a little sticker, so everyone knows it's your first Saturday. I'll encourage people to say hello, ask where you're visiting from, and recommend a coffee spot. You're moving together with actual Nairobians, in neighborhoods where we actually live. You're not being shown the city, you get to experience it alongside the people who call it home.”

#6184. The Parking Spot Promo Code: Save 10%

As a New Yorker without a car, I don’t often put much thought into airport parking. However, a few years ago, my mom texted me raving about The Parking Spot, a service available near Connecticut's Bradley International Airport that allows you to park your car near (but not directly at) the airport in a secure lot, then shuttle over to the terminal. She effusively recommended the process for its ease and convenience, and has continued to rave about it since. Its reach extends far beyond Bradley—with more than 70 locations at 45+ airports, it’s a service that’s available across the US for fliers looking to reduce some of the hassle that comes with travel.

Here’s how it works: You can reserve a spot ahead of time on the company’s website or app, securing your place to park and sorting out the cost up front. Once you arrive at the airport and park your car (avoiding the dreaded terminal traffic), you’ll hop in the bright yellow, polka dot-covered shuttle (whimsical!) and head over. While you’re traveling, you can get your car washed or detailed if you so wish, a nice added value. Then, when you return, you can track the shuttle in real-time using the app to get back to your car quickly.

If all of that sounds appealing—or you’re a regular to the service and are just looking for the latest promo codes—read on for ways to save on your next booking.

(Looking to rent a car instead? Take a look at active promo codes for Budget, Avis, and Hertz first.)

Fall is a great time to squeeze in a long weekend getaway—or even a full week to yourself, if you've got the PTO days to spare—ahead of the holiday busyness. If you're headed off on a trip, know that for reservations that begin by November 15, you can save 10% or more on your airport parking with promo code FALL10.

An easy way to score The Parking Spot discounts: Sign up for the company's mailing list. New users will automatically receive 10% off their first reservation. You’ll also gain access to 10–20% off promo codes on parking reservations for select cities—right now, that includes Austin, Denver, Columbus, Houston, and Salt Lake City.

Like many brands, The Parking Spot offers a military discount for active duty military and veterans. A less common, though fitting, discount is available for airline crew members. Both groups can get 25% off a reservation with a Spot Club account. As for the fine print, discounts don’t apply to Basic parking reservations and can’t be combined with other offers. Airline crew will need to submit a photo of their work badge; similarly, proof of military affiliation must be submitted to receive the discount.

If a Parking Spot promo code isn’t working at checkout, there are a few things you can do to troubleshoot. First double-check the basics—typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization can all prevent a code from working correctly. You'll also want to confirm that the code is still valid, as expiration dates and location exclusions may apply.

#6183. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

If you have yet to take a solo trip, there are many reasons why you really should. Solo travel helps you build confidence and new skills. It also provides time to reflect, recharge and reconnect with yourself — so you can return home the best version of yourself for the people who rely on you day-to-day.

I know it can be daunting to embark on your first big trip alone. But never fear, intrepid soloist. I've rounded up the top solo travel mistakes so that you can avoid them to ensure your trip goes smoothly.

Related: Travel mistakes that could ruin your next trip

One of the perks of solo travel is that you get to decide where to stay and what to do, so put some thought into it. This will ensure you have the best trip possible.

A good starting point is to check the State Department travel advisory for your destination, which will help you understand any safety concerns and identify neighborhoods you may want to avoid. It's also a good idea to enroll your trip in STEP, so you'll be alerted to things like natural disasters and security threats.

Safety isn't the only thing to consider. Are you looking for a quiet, relaxing getaway or a bustling neighborhood with endless things to do? Would you rather stay close to the action or save money by staying in a less popular area? Choose your accommodations accordingly.

Don't make the mistake I made on my first solo trip and not plan any activities. Spontaneity sounded fun, but I found making decisions on my own much harder than expected. You don't need to have your entire itinerary planned out to the minute, but doing some planning before you travel will reduce your stress during the trip.

Plus, many popular tourist attractions and trendy restaurants fill up quickly — and waiting in long lines is even less fun with no one to talk to. Do your research, and if needed, make a reservation or book a timed-entry ticket ahead of time.

Sometimes, the difference between traveling solo and with others really shines through in the little things...like using an airport bathroom.

You can't simply ask a companion to hold your luggage while you run to the restroom or figure out how to operate a metro ticket machine; you must keep track of it at all times. So think twice about packing that extra-large checked bag or hauling a not-so-ergonomic shoulder duffel on an international trip, as you will have to take it with you literally everywhere.

I personally prefer a backpack and small rolling carryon, which I can easily maneuver through crowded airports and over cobblestoned streets — without reaching my destination with a backache. Plus, it's big enough to accommodate sufficient clothing for a week (or more). My carryon is expandable, so if I buy too many souvenirs, I can unzip the extender and check it on the way home.

Related: How to pack your carryon right and avoid checking a bag

Connecting with new people is one of the many joys of solo travel, but that doesn't mean you should completely let your guard down. You may run into pickpockets, con artists and worse on your journey, and as a solo traveler, you're more likely to be targeted.

One simple step to reduce your risk is by not broadcasting your solo status. Err on the side of caution when chatting with new friends — and if they start getting nosy, tell them you're meeting up with friends later.

One way to prevent hotel staff from knowing your single status is opting for mobile check-in so that you can bypass the front desk completely. Or, you can ask the concierge for an extra key and allude that someone will be joining you shortly. And when catching a ride to or from your accommodation, it's a good idea to be picked up or dropped off down the street from your hotel.

Related: Solo travel safety tips every traveler should know

You only want to be incognito to the locals.

Let your actual friends and family know your travel plans: flight numbers, where you'll be staying on which dates, contact info for your tour operator, etc. You'll be glad you did if you hit a snag and need help rebooking on the fly. You can go a step further by sending them a copy of your passport or ID, in case you lose your documents while traveling.

You'll probably want to stay in contact with loved ones through text messages, phone calls or social media posts every so often. But you can also share your location continuously with apps like Find My, which can help ease their minds as well as give you an added layer of security. That way, both you and your loved ones can enjoy your trip stress-free.

Some things are must-haves no matter how many people you're traveling with, but they become even more critical when you're on your own — because if you forget something, you can't just reach into a companion's suitcase.

For instance, do you have a backup plan in case your phone dies while you're navigating a new city or road-tripping through an unfamiliar country? You can't simply borrow someone else's phone, so a charged power bank or old-fashioned map can come in clutch.

The same goes if you wind up at a store that doesn't accept your credit card. Always pack a couple of backup cards (preferably ones that don't charge foreign transaction fees) and keep some cash on hand.

Similarly, if you catch a cold on your flight or get food poisoning during a solo trip, there's no one else to run to a drugstore. And if you hurt yourself while out hiking alone, it may take a while for help to arrive. Prepare yourself for anything with a travel-ready first-aid kit.

Related: Travel essentials that can save your trip when things go wrong

One of the downsides of solo travel is that it can start to feel lonely, especially on longer trips. Making new friends is a great way to combat loneliness, as well as learn more about local culture and/or meet likeminded travelers.

If striking up a conversation with a stranger sounds more stressful than fun, you're not alone. Thankfully, there are plenty of ways for even the shyest travelers to make connections, including cruises and small-group tours designed specifically for solo travelers.

Female Travel Buddies is one of many Facebook groups ideal for those flying solo: Members post open invitations for fellow travelers in the same area to join you for brunch, sightseeing or a show. If this type of thing interests you, consider joining a handful of groups a few months ahead of your trip to get familiar with the members and learn how they work.

Related: 6 tips for meeting people when traveling solo

Just because you're traveling alone doesn't mean you can't take photos along the way — but capturing memories can be trickier by yourself.

The good news is you don't have to be limited by the length of your arm. Be sure to pack a selfie stick, mini tripod with remote shutter or selfie monitor screen. You'll find it well worth the investment, as having the right tools will make it far easier to snap the perfect selfie. (Just remember: safety first, especially when hiking, taking selfies near cliff edges, etc.!)

If, like me, you feel a little awkward or uncomfortable taking selfies alone, the best advice I can give you is to do it anyway. The more you do it, the more comfortable you'll get and the better your photos will turn out.

Solo travel doesn't have to be daunting. Follow these tips to embark on your first solo trip with confidence and ensure it goes smoothly, and before you know it, you'll be a seasoned solo traveler.

#6181. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.

#6180. The Best Airbnbs in Asheville, From a Fairy-Tale Tree House to a Victorian Cottage

As someone raised in the mountains of North Carolina, I've always loved visiting Asheville. I have made the winding two-hour drive from my hometown of Boone countless times, and the city's vibrant energy never ceases to excite me. An eclectic little gem located in the heart of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Asheville’s bustling art and restaurant culture attracts visitors from all over. It's also home to famous historic sites like Biltmore Estate, which is the largest privately owned home in the United States.

What truly makes Asheville so captivating is the city's wide range of attractions, activities, and gorgeous places to stay. Unbelievable mountain views, hiking trails, and other outdoor activities are minutes from the city center, and there are dozens of gorgeous Airbnbs to hole up in no matter what area of the city you choose. The River Arts District is a hub of creativity and expression, home to hundreds of artists, galleries, and expansive outdoor murals along the French Broad River. Downtown is my favorite neighborhood, and I like to take an afternoon to mosey around, with a non-negotiable pit stop at Tupelo Honey for lunch. Wherever you stay, there's so much to do—you can spend your days soaking in a refreshing mountain spring and evenings dining at an award-winning restaurant or craft brewery, then catch live music at one of Asheville’s charming theaters. You will never run out of activities, with something to discover around each corner. Below, find 11 Airbnbs that capture every bit of Asheville’s quirky and whimsical appeal.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unbeatable mountain views, hot tub, hammock

If you’re after a serene, nature-focused stay, this glamping dome tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains will provide just that. Relax in the private hot tub, take an afternoon nap in the spacious hammock, or simply watch the sunset from the couch in front of floor-to-ceiling windows. With on-site parking, a king-size bed, a full bathroom, and a kitchenette for whipping up light meals, a stay here will feel nothing like traditional camping. Situated about 20 minutes from downtown Asheville in Fairview, this property is an ideal hideaway to unplug while still offering access to Asheville’s unbeatable dining and activity options.

Neighborhood: FairviewThings to do nearby: Whistle Hop Brewing Company, Hickory Nut Gap Farm, Fairview Community Forest

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, panoramic views, wraparound deck

There’s a reason so many people want to stay in an elevated mountain cabin in North Carolina, and it’s a must-do for first-time visitors. This unique converted fire tower is on eight acres of private wooded land with direct access to the well-known Mountains-to-Sea Trail. Sixteen panoramic windows and a 360-degree wraparound deck offer expansive mountain views from every angle. The outdoor fireplace and backyard are a s'mores-making and stargazing wonderland. A short 10-minute drive from downtown, on-site parking, and a washer/dryer make this property an exemplary mix of seclusion and practicality.

Neighborhood: Haw CreekThings to do nearby: Haw Creek Park, Creekside Taphouse, Folk Art Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Downtown location, natural light, exposed brick

Set in a prime downtown location, this charming one-bedroom is ideal for those looking to experience Asheville’s thriving urban life. Right in the heart of downtown, you will be steps away from endless restaurants, dynamic art galleries, live music venues, and so much more. The space is warm and welcoming, with natural light pouring in from a wall of multi-pane windows. The exposed brick and natural wood tones create an ideal mix of cozy and sophisticated. There is no free on-site parking, but a parking garage across the street is available for a small fee as a convenient alternative.

Neighborhood: Downtown AshevilleThings to do nearby: Tupelo Honey, Asheville Art Museum, French Broad Chocolate Lounge

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Historic character, convenient location, on-site parking

Built in 1883, this lovely stick-style Victorian cottage was the first home in western North Carolina owned by a woman. Throughout each room, original details are blended with thoughtful updates, preserving its historic character but adding a modern twist. Both queen bedrooms are enhanced with Victorian-inspired furniture and elegant fireplaces. Located in Asheville’s Montford neighborhood, this home is just two blocks from downtown, but still has a driveway and parking for ultimate ease.

Neighborhood: MontfordThings to do nearby: Nine Mile, The Montford Park Players, historic architecture stroll

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: High ceilings, spacious backyard, firepit, multiple living areas

Embrace a little piece of Asheville’s history at this carefully restored 1870s home. Each room boasts plenty of historic charm with 13-foot ceilings, crown molding, beautifully arched double doors, and detailed windows. The furniture and decor choices are an ode to the home's past, keeping the history alive yet with a modern twist. Multiple sitting areas and exceptionally spacious bedrooms (one king and one double) make this a wonderful place to spend time with friends or family without being cramped. The shared backyard has an adorable garden, and the back porch is a glorious spot to watch the sunset over the mountains. Free on-site parking is available, and if you have a particularly large group, you can inquire about renting the unit next door to accommodate four more guests.

Neighborhood: West AshevilleThings to do nearby: Early Girl Eatery, French Broad River Greenway, Sunny Point Café

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, updated interior, city and mountain views

An ideal mix of modern design and rustic character, this chic space still maintains Asheville’s mountain charm. This property is packed with amenities like a hot tub, a ping-pong table, a soaking tub, and plenty of outdoor furniture. It’s a great place for families or small friend groups, with space for up to five guests to sleep across two bedrooms and lounge comfortably throughout the house. The expansive deck offers views of downtown Asheville, local valleys, and mountain ridges. Keep in mind that you do have to walk up a set of steps from the driveway to the entrance, which may be difficult for guests who have limited mobility.

Neighborhood: Town MountainThings to do nearby: Hiking at Craven Gap, The Omni Grove Park Inn, sunset at the overlooks

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Artist-owned, minutes from Biltmore Estate, exquisite details

Thoughtful design and handmade art merge to create a sanctuary in the form of this cottage. Every inch of the Moroccan-influenced space has been curated to feel like a home away from home. An upstairs queen bedroom and a lofted single bed make this the perfect escape for a small family or a couple. The shared garden, firepit, and outdoor clawfoot bathtub mirror the light, airy interior. Free street parking is available, and West Asheville’s restaurants, breweries, and galleries are a short walk away. Biltmore Estate is only a five-minute drive and is a must-see attraction for any visitor.

Neighborhood: West AshevilleThings to do nearby: The Admiral, Carrier Park, Owl Bakery

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fairy-tale charm, on-site hiking trails, rainfall shower

Straight out of a children's storybook, this remarkable tree house feels fictional. If you are looking for a nostalgic getaway to unwind and reconnect, this property is unbeatable. The cozy, cabin-like interior is full of wooden details and comfy furniture. You can sip a cup of coffee at sunrise on one of the two decks, relax in the upstairs bed nook, or venture onto one of the property's hiking trails (maybe even catch a glimpse of the forest’s wild animals!). This is a particularly good spot for those with kiddos, and the downstairs sofa bed makes for easy sleeping arrangements for little ones. About 10 minutes from downtown, this little haven offers the best of both worlds.

Neighborhood: North AshevilleThings to do nearby: Salt Face Mule Brewing Co., Blue Ridge Parkway North, Stoney Knob Cafe

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, hiking trails, guest-approved mattresses

If you want to be close to the breathtaking Blue Ridge Parkway, this sleek A-frame is just a few steps away. The open-concept layout and vaulted ceilings make for an uncluttered and airy atmosphere. A two-minute walk from the Mountains-to-Sea Trail and a lovely on-site firepit make this a wonderful option for those who are looking to embrace nature. The primary king bedroom is filled with massive windows, and two separate bathrooms will give families enough space to be comfortable. There is on-site parking, but note that the parking space is said to be a bit steep for larger cars.

Neighborhood: ReynoldsThings to do nearby: Mountains-to-Sea Trail, scenic drive on the Blue Ridge Parkway

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ample space, two large decks, outdoor amenities

Situated right in the middle of the woods, this beautifully updated mountain cabin is a peaceful retreat. Multiple living areas, three bedrooms, and two-and-a-half bathrooms make for a very generous amount of space. The upstairs deck features plenty of outdoor seating, and the lower level is fitted with two hammocks and games for nights in. Sweeping mountain views are visible from almost every window in the house—fall here would be an absolute dream! Wooden steps lead down to a charming firepit area with extra seating. Modern touches shine throughout the house, like the exquisitely updated kitchen and bathrooms. The driveway has space for up to four cars.

Neighborhood: Mountain View EstatesThings to do nearby: Blue Ridge restaurant, scenic walk, 828 Family Pizzeria

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Gas grill, outdoor furniture, washer/dryer

Cozy and modern, this sweet three-bedroom bungalow is an absolute dream. Shiplap walls, plush furniture, and fun amenities like a ping-pong table give the space an undeniably inviting feel. Two full bathrooms and enough room for six guests to sleep across three bedrooms (a king and two queens) make this a great option for small reunions or group trips. Located in a serene neighborhood in West Asheville, you can easily stroll to nearby breweries or take a peaceful walk around the area. A surplus of outdoor furniture and a gas grill give ample opportunity for alfresco meals.

Neighborhood: Echo HillsThings to do nearby: Sunny Point Cafe, Biltmore Estate, Biscuit Head

#6179. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6178. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.

#6177. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

#6176. How We Pulled It Off: An East-Meets-West Wedding in Istanbul

Jasmin Karibzhanova and Sam Sutcliffe are a multicultural pair whose families and upbringings have spanned the globe. Jasmin was born and raised in the city of Almaty, Kazakhstan, and now lives in Toronto with Sam, a Canadian of Chinese-English descent (who grew up partly in Hong Kong). Friends introduced them in 2022 and the couple were engaged in Turks and Caicos in 2024. Quickly, they figured out that anywhere they married would require a long-haul flight for many if not most of their guests, so why not give everyone an excuse to go somewhere thrilling?

It was Jasmin’s father who suggested they wed in Istanbul for a few reasons: Turkey doesn’t require visas for Canadian or Kazakh citizens, there are direct flights to Istanbul from both Toronto and Almaty, and the city seemed like a more compelling place than typical European destination wedding locales like the countryside of France or Italy. Plus, given the bride and groom’s cultural backgrounds, an east-meets-west theme fit nicely with Istanbul’s location and history. Ahead, the couple shares how they planned their June 2026 wedding for 160 guests in Istanbul, a celebration that included a boat ride to a secret destination, a ceremony along the strait, and copious amounts of Turkish delight.

Living far away, the couple knew they’d need a lot of help plotting their destination celebration. After deciding on Istanbul, they first reached out to Turkish planners, but then struggled with the cultural divide. “Western wedding traditions are a bit different than what they were used to, and we had some communication issues with language,” Jasmin says.

They expanded their search to planners elsewhere in Europe with whom they could speak more clearly, and who were well-versed in producing larger-scale celebrations. They landed on Matthew Oliver Weddings, a London-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Europe and the Middle East. Coincidentally, the team there had recently connected with Aylinly Events, a Turkish planner who’d directly expressed an interest in collaborating on Turkish destination celebrations. Given the serendipity, working with both firms seemed like the best way to pull off the kind of highly-produced event Jasmin and Sam wanted.

From there, the wedding was plotted via weekly Zoom meetings with the Matthew Oliver team, particularly their lead planners Bertie and Georgia, while the Turkish team tended to be most comfortable over WhatsApp. “If you're sending a WhatsApp, they'll respond in 20 minutes at 4:00 a.m. their time,” Jasmin says. “The Turkish approach to hospitality is next level. They’re never off. They work the hardest of any creative team I’ve ever met.”

The couple visited Istanbul twice during their engagement, with the first trip to tour venues about one year out from the wedding date they eventually set. They sought a space that could handle their substantial guest list, and quickly fell for the Peninsula Istanbul, which spans four buildings set right on the Bosphorus in the historic neighborhood of Karaköy.

“It was integrated into the fabric of the city,” Jasmin says. “You could just walk out into the street and enjoy Istanbul, which we really loved, and it had fantastic views of the Golden Horn.” The brand was a special touchstone for Sam and his family too, as the Peninsula has roots in Hong Kong.

Given the hotel’s size, its staff was adept at events and offered plenty of standard packages, though they were happy to work outside of the typical framework. “There was nothing they would say no to,” Jasmin says. “They had a fantastic understanding of vendors in the city and issues to consider, with amazing recommendations. Their whole approach to hospitality and wedding planning was that there is no rejection of any idea. They would just figure it out.”

When reaching out to friends and family, the couple was pleasantly surprised to find how many wanted to fly to Turkey. “I sort of assumed that because it was so far, especially for the Canadians, that we’d have a smaller guest list than we did,” Jasmin says. “But people really wanted to go because it was a destination that a lot hadn’t been to before. It was a great excuse to make their way over there.”

So they felt a duty to properly entertain their loved ones. “My philosophy around the event was that I wanted it to be completely guest-facing. I wanted it to be easy for people to come and enjoy the weekend,” says the bride, who admits she went totally “overboard” in this respect. Aside from creating a wedding website with all the event info, they also offered travel tips and suggestions, fashioned suggested itineraries, and pre-booked a local tour of Istanbul for folks who arrived early.

Another reason they opted for the Peninsula was its location near many other hotels with varying price points and appeals. “Our friends stayed closer to bars and nightlife, and older guests stayed near museums and such,” Jasmin says, estimating that about a third of attendees checked into the Peninsula.

Both Jasmin and Sam have creative backgrounds—they work together on a film production company, Jasmin studied theater and acted, and Sam’s parents are celebrated architects—and approached the aesthetics of their wedding like an artistic pursuit. “We knew that a lot of our guests would be from the creative world, and we were particular about how we wanted things to look,” Jasmin says. They suggested high-level elements like the color scheme (dusty blue and rich mulberry), and then their planning teams, along with the creative studio Event Lab, filled in the gaps with more ideas.

One key element in ensuring the wedding’s cohesion was the furniture production, for which they worked with AND Event & Design Studio to create items like modular custom chairs and a platform drenched in a velvety maroon for the ceremony space. Another was the florals, designed and arranged by Fluida Design. For the eye-popping ceremony, the flowers were lush and architectural, almost alien-like, while for dinner the arrangements were tighter, paler, and more romantic.

“I wanted it to function like a play: There’s a rising energy, then a reveal, then a resolution,” says Jasmin of the aesthetic journey. In Fluida Design, they found a creative partner that pushed them in all the right directions, outside a typical wedding comfort zone. “The initial proposition was a lot more neutral colors, just whites and greens, and then our floral team was like, ‘Well, why don't we just do color because that's just more interesting?’” Jasmin recalls. And as much as the couple cared about the look, they were happy to let the experts be the experts. “We were like, ‘Well, we would like for you also to just have fun with it,” she says. “Do whatever you want.”

On Thursday of their wedding weekend, the couple hosted an intimate but more casual rehearsal dinner for their family and closest friends at the hotel. Friday brought the welcome party for all of their guests, who boarded boats bound for an unknown location at sunset from the Peninsula: it turned out to be the Rahmi M. Koç Museum, a funky transportation museum space along the Bosphorus.

When the couple toured venues, they found that many options were great but a little too similar in energy to the Peninsula. “The last place we went was this museum, which is a ridiculous, magical place,” Jasmin says. “It’s a private collection of vintage cars, boats, submarines, and planes, all cramped together in this hangar-like building on the Bosphorus. It was very kitschy but a great contrast to our wedding venue.”

The Silk Road-themed party packed in loads of Turkish details from the music to the food: carts offering grilled meatballs (or köfte), ⁠döner, and stuffed bulgur balls (or içli köfte) made for a bazaar energy, while a live dessert station formed traditional lokma, freshly fried dough balls drizzled with syrup. “Floral” arrangements were built around local vegetables, like tall piles of peppers strung on garlands, and evil-eye pendants were handed out as party favors.

Sam and Jasmin’s wedding day started out a bit drizzly, a rarity for early summer in Istanbul. One of the reasons they chose the Peninsula in the first place was for its large terrace set against the strait, with the hope of getting married at sunset along the water with boats streaming by in the background. The vision was so beloved that they refused to come up with a rain plan, even for the platform built across the space.

“Our team was like, ‘Maybe we look into other things?’ And I can be very impulsive,” Jasmin admits. “‘No, we're just going to commit to this. If it rains, it rains. I don't want to hide the city from our guests, even if it's wet.’” They delayed the ceremony for a few minutes but got their dream of holding it outside without soaking their families and friends.

Waiting for that area was worth it. “It was a very special space because normally that space is just a herb garden on top of the Peninsula, but we took it over for the wedding,” Sam says. “You both got spectacular views across the entire city and felt in it, while being slightly removed from the craziness.”

The Muslim call to prayer rang out amid a ceremony officiated by family friend and noted Canadian philanthropist Nancy Lockhart, and boats slowed down in interest. “It didn't feel invasive at all,” Jasmin says. “We wanted to be integrated into the city, and that's what we got.”

Following the ceremony, guests enjoyed cocktails steps away in a part of the courtyard wrapped in a romantic mauve pink that colored the curtains, custom loungers, and drink tables. In keeping with the ideas of travel and adventure, the cocktail hour had a hotel theme (an idea that came from the Peninsula’s staff), with staff dressed as bellhops and a wall of ornate golden keys with pink tassels serving as the escort cards.

The wall of keys also functioned to block off the dinner area as it was set up, “so when they were ushered into the next space,” Sam says, “it was a surprising and beautiful new twist for everyone.” Next to the ceremony and cocktails spaces, the dinner “room” was formed by walls of blue curtains and the soaring, upside-down umbrellas that sit permanently on that courtyard. The tables were arranged in long, wavy lines that provided open views to the water.

And while this could never have been planned—even by the considerable talents of the creative couple and their multiple event teams—the risk of rain was rewarded by an incredible sight. “We had a spectacular double rainbow from the Asian side to the European side of the Bosphorus," says Sam. “The rainbow is something I will never forget for the rest of my life.’

While the couple’s welcome dinner was packed with cultural touchpoints, the wedding day itself was more traditionally Western, albeit with some Turkish details. Sam took his groomsmen to a hamam during the day for spa treatments, and the wedding dinner was based around the best of the local cuisine. Canapes included mussel “dolma’’ with black-ink bread, a lemon commape, a bite of Ezine cheese with quince, and a simit bread crumble, while the main meal began with a mezze platter before a first course of duck or mushroom baklava.

After dinner and speeches from loved ones, the party took to the dance floor, where the Uninvited Jazz Band got the party going. The couple served a classic wedding cake in two flavors: one dark chocolate and one raspberry and white chocolate. A series of smaller sweet bites from the Peninsula’s famous high tea were also passed around the tables.

A local city ordinance that event noises die down after 10 p.m. inspired a move off the terrace and into the nearby ballroom for more dancing. The after-party space was blanketed in scarlet, with a black and white checkerboard floor. From there, DJ Live from Élan Artists spun into the wee hours, and the newlyweds poured out a Champagne tower. A poem Sam had written was displayed above the bar: “Silk Road’s starting point / union atop ancient roots / celebratory love.”

Good news for travelers who prefer vacation rentals over luxury hotels: Chase is giving select cardholders thousands of new ways to put their travel benefits to use.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, The Edit by Chase Travel℠ will include more than 10,000 curated vacation homes in addition to its existing collection of luxury hotels and resorts.

That means eligible Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see ), Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see ) and J.P. Morgan Reserve® cardholders will soon be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward vacation home stays — and potentially enjoy additional perks as part of their stay (minimum four-night stay required).

The information for the J.P. Morgan Reserve card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you're unfamiliar, The Edit by Chase Travel is a curated collection of luxury hotels and resorts that offers eligible cardholders additional perks when booking through the Chase Travel portal (minimum two-night stay required).

Currently featuring more than 1,500 hotels and resorts, the collection will expand to include more than 10,000 vacation homes beginning Jan. 1.

The homes will be curated by Plum Guide, a luxury vacation rental platform that evaluates properties using "more than 150 criteria related to comfort, design and location".

This builds on Chase Travel's partnership with Plum Guide, announced in April 2026, which brought luxury vacation rentals to more Chase cardholders through the travel portal.

With the latest expansion, eligible Reserve cardholders will have access to a curated collection of vacation homes through The Edit, complete with premium benefits.

Cardholders will also have the flexibility to redeem Chase Ultimate Rewards points toward these stays through Chase Travel.

Additionally, Sapphire Reserve and Reserve Business cardholders will have access to Reserve Travel Designers, who can help match travelers with vacation homes and provide personalized concierge assistance before, during and after their stays.

Related: I’ve been using the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business for a year — here’s why I’m keeping it

One of the biggest draws of booking a hotel through The Edit is the additional perks that come with a qualifying stay (minimum two-night stay required).

Depending on the property, these can include complimentary breakfast for two, a $100 property credit, room upgrades when available and early check-in and late checkout.

Vacation home bookings through The Edit will come with a different set of benefits.

There's an important catch, however: Vacation home stays must be at least four nights to qualify for these The Edit benefits. Some benefits are subject to availability and may vary by property.

Eligible cardholders will also be able to use their annual The Edit statement credits toward qualifying vacation home bookings.

As a refresher, here's how those credits break down:

Beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business will offer four statement credits of up to $250 each for The Edit stays that can be used throughout the year. That's up from two statement credits of up to $250 each available on the card in 2026.

Keep in mind that while a two-night prepaid booking may qualify for the statement credit, vacation home stays must be at least four nights to receive the additional The Edit benefits.

Also, be aware that while you can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for eligible bookings, stays paid entirely with points do not qualify for The Edit statement credits under Chase's current terms. If you want to use the statement credit, you'll need to make an eligible prepaid purchase with your card.

Related: How to stack Sapphire Reserve credits for up to $500 off

The addition of more than 10,000 vacation homes to The Edit is welcome news for eligible Chase cardholders, particularly those who prefer the space and flexibility of a vacation rental over a traditional luxury hotel.

It also gives cardholders more options for using their annual The Edit statement credits, while offering perks such as a $150 in-stay credit and early check-in and late checkout when available.

Just keep the minimum-stay requirements in mind, and compare prices before booking to make sure you're getting the best value.

#6174. Former China Eastern Chairman Jailed In $10+ Million Bribery Scandal

The former chairman of China Eastern Airlines has been sentenced to 14 years in jail, as he accepted more than $10 million in bribes in his official role. Yowzers!

A court in China’s Liaoning Province has sentenced former China Eastern chairman Liu Shaoyong to prison. The court ruled that he accepted over $10 million in bribes in his official capacity as chairman of one of China’s largest airlines.

The court found that between 2002 and 2023, Liu abused his position at the airline to provide assistance to companies and individuals in business operations, project contracts, and flight route management. Liu has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, and has been ordered to pay a fine of $600K, plus his illicit gains and related proceeds have to be recovered.

While the court ruled that his conduct constituted bribery “in an exceedingly large amount,” the sentence he got was actually lighter than it could’ve been, due to mitigating circumstances. These include his confession, voluntary disclosure of previously unknown offenses, and expression of remorse and cooperation in recovering illicit gains.

Make of this what you will, but it’s interesting to note that this is all part of China’s “anti-corruption campaign,” targeting officials at various levels, including executives of state-owned enterprises.

In June 2025, Liu had been placed under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision, for violations of party discipline and state laws. In January 2026, he was expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), after investigators found that he had abused his authority for personal gain, and he was formally charged in May 2026.

China Eastern’s former chairman has been sentenced to 14 years in prison, after he admitted to taking over $10 million in bribes in his official role. This came as part of a larger crackdown by the government, which also saw the executive expelled from the Communist Party of China.

Over the years we’ve seen a decent number of airline executives charged with corruption — after all, they control a lot of spending, and in some cases, might get influenced for the wrong reasons.

What do you make of this punishment for China Eastern’s former chairman?
