#6173. Air Serbia Flight To Moscow Diverts After Politician Reportedly Skips Security

An Air Serbia flight that was supposed to fly from Serbia to Russia ended up turning around over Lithuania, in order for additional security checks to be carried out on passengers. The circumstances surrounding this sure are unusual, given who was onboard.

This incident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and involves Air Serbia flight JU134, scheduled to fly from Belgrade (BEG) to Moscow (SVO). The 1,074-mile flight was operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration code YU-APH. The flight was scheduled to depart at 6:25PM and land at 11:40PM, with a two hour time change, so it was blocked at 3hr15min.

The plane took off at 6:48PM, basically on schedule, and it started flying north, over Hungary, Slovakia, Poland, and then Lithuania. However, around 90 minutes after takeoff, while more than halfway, the plane u-turned, and flew back toward Belgrade.

The plane ended up landing in Belgrade at 9:57PM local time, a little over three hours after it first departed. The plane ended up once again taking off in the early morning hours of November 4, departing at 1:56AM, and landing at 6:43AM, over seven hours behind schedule.

Diversions happen, though it’s definitely unusual for a flight to turn around to the origin when it’s already more than halfway to its destination, especially when maintenance wasn’t to blame. Officially, the airline has shared that the decision to divert was made “in accordance with the instructions received and all applicable security rules.” That’s obviously really vague, though… so what really happened?

Here’s where the story gets really interesting. Onboard this Air Serbia flight were a few associates of former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, who just recently lost an election. One of the people onboard was Aleksandar Vulin, who served as deputy prime minister until 2025, and is viewed as being very pro-Russia. The US had even imposed sanctions on him due to his close ties with Russia.

Media reports in Serbia suggest that the reason for the diversion was that security camera footage at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport had been reviewed, and it was determined that someone had helped him avoid security checks. Now, I understand the need to carry out security checks, though I’m also not sure the point of diverting when you’re already more than halfway to your destination.

Vulin denies that he was the reason that the plane diverted, claiming that it was instead a political showdown. After the diversion, he went on national TV in Serbia, to say the following:

“It’s all a lie, an act of violence and an attempt to prove to these new authorities how ready they are here at the airport, how much they are on the defensive of their ideology. So, of course it’s all a lie, of course it’s all utter nonsense. I’m really sorry and uncomfortable, so many people have returned, their lives are being ruined, their obligations are being ruined because of the attempt to politically deal with me.”

“I am completely calm, I know that I am in the right. And you know, I did not go to Moscow as a tourist, I went on business. I am going there to fight for the extension of the gas agreement. Not for me and you, but for all citizens of Serbia.”

He also said he was asleep at the time of the diversion, and had no clue what was going on until the plane landed back in Belgrade:

“We just woke up, to be honest, I fell asleep. I was sleeping on the plane, I wake up, they say: You are in Belgrade. How are you in Belgrade? When we went outside, I see the police, the special forces gathered. I say: ‘Colleagues, have you come for me?’ They laugh. They say: ‘We are not, Minister.’ I go down with all the other passengers. I go through the procedure with all the other passengers again. I go through another procedure by myself. And now, I am standing and waiting for them to let us get on the plane again.”

An Air Serbia flight from Belgrade to Moscow turned around while over halfway to its destination. The decision to divert was made in accordance with “applicable security rules,” and all passengers were screened when the plane landed back in Serbia.

While it’s believed that a pro-Russia Serbian politician who was onboard may have avoided security checks at the airport, the politician denies that, and claims this was a political move.

What do you make of this unusual Air Serbia diversion?

#6172. Hegseth's leadership questioned by GOP military veteran as Democrats talk impeachment

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., questioned Pete Hegseth's leadership and said more qualified officials could lead the Pentagon. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

FIRST ON FOX: Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital that the Department of War should not be led by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, criticizing his leadership and questioning his judgment.

Bacon, who questioned Hegseth's "moral compass," made his remarks after Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, raising the possibility of impeachment proceedings against members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet in the 120th Congress.

"I don't think he was a good choice to begin with," Bacon told Fox News Digital. "I wouldn't have voted to confirm him."

Bacon, a 30-year Air Force veteran, argued that Hegseth's personal conduct would have resulted in disciplinary action for other members of the military.

GOP SEN THOM TILLIS URGES TRUMP TO REPLACE PETE HEGSETH, BLASTS PENTAGON LEADERSHIP

Split image of Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. (Tom Brenner for The Washington Post via Getty Images; Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"Anybody that got caught having affairs would've gotten fired," Bacon said before pointing to the controversy surrounding the administration's use of the Signal messaging app to discuss sensitive military operations.

HEGSETH FIRES TOP PENTAGON STRATEGIST ACCUSED OF LEAKING CLASSIFIED IRAN, UKRAINE WAR INFORMATION

"He didn't take any responsibility for it, though it was his fault. And things like that bother folks who've served a lifetime in the military, have a moral compass and take responsibility," Bacon continued.

GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH

Bacon also suggested that Hegseth lacks substantial support among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, where a Democratic-controlled House could pursue impeachment proceedings against the war secretary.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell responded to Bacon's remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying Hegseth "will not back down" or "be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists."

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington on April 30, 2026. (Cliff Owen/AP Photo)

Without mentioning Bacon by name, Parnell added that Hegseth "will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America" on behalf of President Donald Trump, "despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office."

Toward the end of the 119th Congress, a group of Democrats backed legislation introduced by Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., seeking to impeach Hegseth.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

"Hegseth doesn't have a lot of friends on the Hill," Bacon said while discussing whether Trump should replace the war secretary before possible impeachment proceedings. "I do think we could have more qualified leaders."

Trump told reporters Wednesday that he intends to keep Hegseth in his Cabinet, despite speculation about the war secretary's future.

DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

The president's comments came after other Cabinet departures during his second term, including former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Attorney General Pam Bondi, who were asked to resign.

During his interview with Fox News Digital, Bacon addressed the future of the Republican Party following its midterm defeat, arguing that the GOP must distance itself from Trump to regain congressional majorities, win governorships and remain competitive in the 2028 presidential election.

Bacon did not dismiss the idea of running for president himself when asked by Fox News Digital, and has previously said in podcast interviews that he would "love" to.

MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS

"I do think we should have a big debate in our party," Bacon said, leaving open the possibility of playing a role in the party's future leadership. "I'd like to fight for the soul of our party. And I want to be a part of that discussion, that debate."

"If somebody steps up and wants to take on the little more of the Reagan mantle and the sort of things I think need to get done to the country," the retired one-star Air Force general continued. "I'm glad to support them. But somebody's got to be speaking out against illegal immigration, cost of healthcare, and national security policy, and they got to be able, we'll work across the aisle to get things done. You can't solve this from all your Democrats only."

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., arrives for a House Republican conference meeting at the U.S. Capitol on May 6, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Bacon argued that Republicans should return to the principles championed by former President Ronald Reagan, including "the basic principles of economic freedom, free markets and free trade, peace through strength, stand up to the bully, which in this case, is Russia."

He also emphasized the importance of "federalism and the pro-life movement" as priorities for the party moving forward.

The Nebraska Republican criticized Trump's approach to traditional U.S. allies, arguing that the administration has been "very bad towards our allies," including Canada and Greenland, amid disputes over tariffs and the president's threats involving Greenland.

Bacon suggested that Trump's foreign policy decisions and military involvement overseas contributed to Republican losses in down-ballot races across the country.

"They only got beat because they had an R next to their name," Bacon said, accusing congressional Republicans of having "rubber-stamped" the president's agenda since he returned to the White House for a second term.

Here’s how to make the most of South Australia

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

It took me several trips to Australia to realize I’d been skipping one of its best parts.

I’d visited the country a handful of times before, but this was my first trip to Adelaide and my first time exploring South Australia. Within a few days, I was eating my way through a 150-year-old market, walking among kangaroos and wallabies, blending my own bottle of shiraz, kayaking alongside wild dolphins, and bopping between breathtaking beaches, rolling hills, and wine country.

And getting there from the U.S. is about to become considerably easier.

United is bringing back its seasonal service between San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and Adelaide Airport (ADL) beginning Dec. 17. The route, now entering its second season, gives travelers the only nonstop connection between the U.S. and Adelaide, with schedules subject to change. Service is scheduled to run through Feb. 10, 2027.

Adelaide turned out to be an ideal home base for seeing just how much variety South Australia packs into a relatively small radius.

The state capital and largest city in the region still manages to feel surprisingly approachable. Its central business district mixes modern towers with low-slung stone cottages and other remnants of its colonial-era architecture, while the entire city center is wrapped in parklands that date back to Adelaide’s original 1837 city plan.

From the center of town, I could be among the rolling hills and small villages of the Adelaide Hills, heading toward the coast, or making my way into wine country — all in roughly half an hour.

That is, assuming you are prepared to drive on the left. My first encounter with my Australian rental car began with me confidently getting into the wrong front seat and momentarily wondering where someone had put the steering wheel.

For my stay, I checked into Hotel Indigo Adelaide Markets. My suite had a separate living area and a large balcony with sweeping views across the city and toward the hills. The hotel also has Merrymaker, a lively rooftop bar 16 floors above the surrounding market district.

Before I could start bouncing between wineries, markets, and wildlife encounters, though, I first had to cross the Pacific. United’s San Francisco-to-Adelaide service is scheduled to operate on a Boeing 787-9, and I got to make the overnight journey in United Polaris business class. After spending some time in the Polaris Lounge at SFO, I boarded and settled into my lie-flat seat for what was essentially going to be an entire night in the air.

Dinner started with tomato tartare and crostini, followed by braised short rib with risotto Milanese, garlic green beans, and fresh gremolata. It was genuinely tasty, to the point that I could almost forget I was eating dinner at 35,000 feet.

Even more memorably, I got my first experience with United’s Polaris sundae service. My extremely attentive flight attendant recommended I simply go for all the fixings, and I took her advice. She was right.

From there, I put the lie-flat seat to good use and got a substantial stretch of sleep before waking for breakfast closer to Adelaide. I went with a mushroom omelet and chicken sausage, which provided a convenient marker that it was time to stop thinking in San Francisco time and get onto my new schedule.

That rhythm ended up being one of the biggest benefits of flying the route in Polaris. Dinner, a real block of sleep, and breakfast before landing gave the flight something resembling a normal overnight routine. By the time I arrived in Adelaide, I felt far more functional than I normally do after crossing that many time zones and was ready to start exploring almost immediately.

Over the next few days, I got to see several very different sides of the region. Looking back, most of what I loved about South Australia fell pretty neatly into one of three camps: adventure, indulgence, and culture.

I managed to sample a little of all three, but depending on how you like to travel, any one could easily become the backbone of a trip here.

My adventure itinerary began less than half a block from my hotel at Adelaide Central Market.

The market has been operating since 1869 and today packs more than 70 artisans under one roof. What struck me more than its age, though, was how much it still felt like a place Adelaide actually uses.

At lunchtime, workers from the surrounding central business district mixed with families, visitors, and people picking up groceries. Around them were rows of fresh produce, flowers, bakeries, bookstores, sweet shops, and food stalls representing cuisines from around the world.

I had some of the best paella I’ve had in a long time, worked my way through a few of the savory pies and rolls Australia does especially well, and found my favorite at Smiley’s: a hot chicken roll that I would have happily eaten again the next day.

Dessert sent me down another very Australian rabbit hole. Honeycomb is a flavor I encounter constantly here and almost never back home, and I found a honeycomb cornflake slice that was essentially the Australian cousin of a Rice Krispies treat.

The food scene spills beyond the market, too. Elsewhere in the central business district, streets like Peel and Leigh narrow into pedestrian-friendly laneways packed with wine bars, restaurants, cocktail spots, and cafes.

And if there is one thing I’m reminded of every time I return to Australia, it is that Australians take coffee very seriously. My favorite stop was Exchange Coffee, where the menu seemed capable of accommodating essentially any permutation of coffee I could come up with.

From there, I headed into the Adelaide Hills for Cleland Wildlife Park.

I have been to enough petting zoos in the U.S. to approach almost any animal experience with a little skepticism. Cleland was nothing like that.

The park centers on conservation and education, and many of its kangaroos and wallabies move freely through large natural areas where visitors can walk among them. Adult admission costs AU$35.80.

I spent much of my visit wandering between animals that seemed largely unconcerned by my presence. At one point, I spotted a baby wallaby riding in its mother’s pouch with just its little head poking out, which may have been the single cutest thing I saw on the entire trip.

I also paid extra for a koala encounter and met Tek, a 10-year-old male whose fur was far softer than I expected. A keeper remained beside him throughout the experience, supplying eucalyptus and making sure the interaction stayed very much on his terms.

The keeper also informed me that Tek might have better labor protections than most humans. After a 30-minute stretch of close-up visitor encounters, he gets two complete days off from that kind of work entirely, which made me both laugh and feel a little jealous.

For the final stop on my adventure itinerary, I traded ground-level bush walks for the roof of Adelaide Oval.

The stadium manages to feel both thoroughly modern and distinctly historic, with its grassy northern mound, enormous fig trees, and century-old scoreboard still intact amid the contemporary grandstands. Those trees also have a wonderfully petty backstory: They were planted, at least in part, to stop people on nearby Montefiore Hill from watching games inside the Oval for free.

For an even better view, I signed up for Adelaide Oval’s RoofClimb. After changing into a jumpsuit and clipping into a harness, I followed my guide onto a track running across the stadium roof. From the top, Adelaide suddenly made much more sense geographically. I could trace the river through the city, see the Adelaide Hills rising in one direction, and look toward the coastline in another.

At the turnaround point came the obligatory opportunity to lean backward over the edge, arms out, with my harness very much attached.

A standard daytime RoofClimb takes about two hours and starts at AU$125 for adults and AU$95 for children ages 8 to 15. By the time I unclipped, it had landed in a very specific sweet spot: scenic, informative, and just adrenaline-inducing enough to make me feel like I had earned the view.

My indulgence itinerary began with one of the most elaborate meals I have ever experienced.

Restaurant Aptos sits inside a converted church in Stirling, in the Adelaide Hills, and serves just 14 diners at a time. Its 16-course tasting menu unfolds progressively across three interconnected dining rooms.

From the moment I walked in, it felt like stepping into another world.

The first course made it abundantly clear what kind of evening I was in for. I was handed what was essentially a branch dotted with five native Australian fruits and instructed to lick each flavor directly off the wood.

I tried crocodile tongue for the first time, paired with Geraldton wax flavors, and kangaroo seasoned with native Australian ingredients. The latter was considerably more tender and less gamey than I expected.

Across the 16 courses, the flavor combinations were at times so layered that my first reaction was almost sensory overload. I would take a bite, spend a few seconds trying to work out what exactly I was tasting, and then suddenly everything would settle into place.

Each course also arrived with a beautifully designed card detailing the ingredients and preparation. By dessert, I had a stack of 16 that felt less like a menu and more like a collection of art prints I wanted to take home and frame.

The following day, I stayed in the Adelaide Hills but traded a tasting menu for a pair of walking shoes at Mount Lofty Botanic Garden.

Calling it a botanical garden almost undersells it.

Spread across 97 hectares, Mount Lofty showcases cool-climate plants from around the world, with sections devoted to flora from places including South America, Africa, and Asia.

The landscape felt closer to a nature preserve than a manicured city park. I wandered past ponds, streams, flowers, and dense pockets of forest, with the scenery seeming to change every few minutes.

The birdlife also made me stop more than once. One thing I never quite get over in Australia is how exotic even an everyday bird can look compared with what I am accustomed to seeing in New York. At home, my baseline is largely pigeons and crows. Here, seemingly commonplace birds can look like something escaped from an aviary.

Admission is free, making Mount Lofty an easy way to spend a few hours in the hills.

From there, I continued to Hahndorf, Australia’s oldest surviving German settlement. Its main street is lined with heritage buildings, bakeries, pubs, boutiques, and antique stores.

I stopped at Otto’s Bakery for a vanilla slice, one of those Australian desserts whose name does very little to explain what it actually is. Rather than cake, it is a thick layer of silky vanilla custard sandwiched between crisp sheets of puff pastry.

The final stop on my indulgence itinerary took me south to McLaren Vale and d’Arenberg, where the Osborn family has been growing grapes since 1912.

The first thing I noticed, though, had nothing to do with wine.

The five-story d’Arenberg Cube rises above the vineyards in a jumble of black, white, glass, and mirrors. Against the rolling countryside, it looks a little like a Rubik’s Cube Salvador Dalí might have designed himself. Fittingly, one floor houses an exhibition of Dalí sculptures and graphic works.

My main reason for visiting was the Blending Bench, a hands-on experience that lets you create and bottle your own wine.

By sheer luck, I was the only person booked for my session. In front of me were three shiraz samples made from vines planted in 1898, 1969, and 1999, and all three tasted remarkably different.

Using pipettes, a worksheet, and plenty of trial and error, I measured different percentages into my glass, tasted the result, and adjusted from there.

I went in convinced the 1898 sample, easily my favorite on its own, would make up most of my final bottle. But tiny changes in the proportions completely altered the flavor. Eventually, I settled on something I liked even more than any of the three components separately.

Then I got to bottle, name, and label a full 750-milliliter version to take home.

The Blending Bench costs AU$120 and takes about 75 minutes. Between the architecture, art, vineyards, and leaving with a bottle I had actually created myself, it was easily one of the more memorable winery visits I have had.

For the culture itinerary, I started with a restaurant I had been excited about well before I ever landed in Adelaide.

Africola has one of the most distinct visual identities I have ever seen from a restaurant, from its website and branding to the space itself.

Once inside, though, what stood out was how much it felt like a neighborhood institution.

More than once, I watched members of the staff greet diners with the easy familiarity of people who had clearly been coming back for years. I sat at the bar, which gave me a front-row view into the open kitchen and all of the plating and preparation happening behind it.

I started with the crispy chicken tea sandwich, one of Africola’s signatures. Soft white bread encloses crisp chicken skin, with peri-peri drippings served alongside for dipping. Think of it as a tiny, rich South African cousin of a French dip.

Then came the peri-peri chicken itself, smoky, spicy, and incredibly savory, along with salt-baked Dutch cream potatoes with labneh, za’atar, and chives that landed on my palette like an elegant twice-baked potato. I also ordered the cos lettuce with buttermilk, dill, and shallot, essentially Africola’s much more interesting answer to a wedge salad.

When everything was placed in front of me, I was mildly horrified by how much food I had ordered. About an hour later, I had eaten most of it and was contemplating whether I could simply roll myself through the central business district and back to my hotel.

It ended up being one of my favorite meals of the entire trip.

The next afternoon, I headed to Adelaide Botanic Garden on the eastern edge of the city center.

The 50-hectare garden is free to enter and mixes outdoor collections with ponds, shaded paths, historic buildings, museums, and glasshouses.

One of those spaces is the Palm House, a Victorian glasshouse from the 1870s that now holds plants from Madagascar, including species threatened or endangered in the wild.

Nearby, the Museum of Economic Botany ended up being one of my favorite stops. The collection includes enormous seeds, preserved plant specimens, and historical models centered on the many ways humans have used plants for food, medicine, textiles, inks, and other parts of everyday life.

Taken together, the garden felt less like simply spending an afternoon looking at pretty plants and more like a reminder of how deeply the natural world has shaped the way people eat, build, heal, create, and live.

Another way to dig deeper is through the garden’s Aboriginal Native Plant and Social History Tour. Led by an Aboriginal guide, the 90-minute experience explores traditional uses of native plants for food, medicine, and tools, along with Aboriginal social history, cultural practices, and relationships with the land. Tickets are currently AU$42 per person, plus booking fees.

For the final stop of my trip, I traded the central business district for a morning on the water at the Adelaide Dolphin Sanctuary near Garden Island.

I joined the three-hour Dolphin Sanctuary Kayak Tour, where my guide, Kendall, first walked us through the basics before leading our group onto the water.

We paddled between mangrove-lined creeks and the partially submerged remains of old ships. The Garden Island ships’ graveyard contains 25 known vessels abandoned between 1909 and 1945 after they became obsolete, damaged, or no longer economical to maintain.

Farther into the mangroves, I started getting serious Florida Everglades energy, only without quite as many things I was concerned might kill me.

Kendall, who happens to be an American from Florida herself, was equal parts kayak instructor and naturalist, filling us in on dolphin behavior, conservation efforts, and the maritime history behind the wrecks as we paddled.

Then came the moment I had convinced myself probably would not happen.

I am an eternal pessimist when it comes to any wildlife activity involving the phrase “possible sighting,” but we ended up spending several minutes alongside a mother dolphin and her calf.

The pair moved back and forth through the water together, surfacing side by side, disappearing beneath us, and then looping around again.

The tour costs AU$79 per adult, lasts about three hours, and includes the necessary kayaking gear.

Between the shipwrecks, ancient mangroves, and a wild dolphin sighting I had fully talked myself out of expecting, it was a fitting way to finish a trip that consistently surprised me.

In only a few days, Adelaide gave me a version of Australia I had not experienced on any of my previous visits.

I could spend the morning in the center of a major city, the afternoon walking through vineyards or alongside kangaroos, and the evening eating ingredients I had never heard of before the trip. More importantly, almost none of it required spending hours getting from one place to the next.

That is ultimately what made Adelaide work so well as a home base. Whether I leaned into adventure, indulgence, or culture, there was a different once-in-a-lifetime experience within easy reach.

Beginning Dec. 17, United’s returning seasonal San Francisco-to-Adelaide service will make it easier for U.S. travelers to arrive directly in South Australia and start exploring, with schedules subject to change. So take it from me — don’t sleep on South Australia, unless it’s from the comfort of a Polaris Business Class seat on the way there.

#6170. Is World Of Hyatt Points + Cash Worth It? The Value Varies Wildly

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night redemptions, the program also has a Points + Cash option, whereby you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay.

The reality is that the value of Hyatt Points + Cash has fluctuated significantly over the years. Going back a decade, it was the primary way that I redeemed my points. Then it was devalued significantly, and then some value was brought back. So I’d like to take a look at the current state of things… is Hyatt Points + Cash worth considering nowadays?

As the name suggests, with Hyatt Points + Cash, you can redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a Hyatt stay. More specifically, you’ll redeem 50% of the points required for a stay, and will receive a 30-50% discount off the standard rate for the room type chosen.

Now, there are some important things to be aware of:

Just as a reminder, below is the standard room World of Hyatt award chart, which shows the award pricing for a free night hotel stay based on which of the five pricing tiers applies for a particular night (lowest, low, moderate, upper, or top).

When booking Points + Cash, you’d pay half of the points, plus 50-70% of the flexible revenue rate, so below is that chart.

With the basics of Hyatt Points + Cash out of the way, let’s do some number crunching. Let me state upfront that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each, though I usually get quite a bit more value out of them in comparison to what a hotel stay would cost with cash.

For the purposes of the below examples, I’ll simply be comparing the cost for a free night redemption to the cost of a Points + Cash redemption. This doesn’t consider the outright cost of a stay if paying cash, so for more on that, see my post about when you should redeem points for a hotel stay.

I picked six hotels at random, belonging to different brands and in different regions. I picked totally random dates, so let’s take a look at what I found.

For the night I picked, the Grand Hyatt Tampa Bay is charging 15,000 points per night, or 7,500 points plus $103 ($116 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 7,500 extra points to save $116, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.55 cents each.

The Park Hyatt Los Cabos is charging 55,000 points per night, or 27,500 points plus $500.50 ($680.68 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 27,500 extra points to save $680.68, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.48 cents each.

The Hyatt Studios Mobile is charging 3,000 points per night, or 1,500 points plus $61 ($71.98 including taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 1,500 extra points to save $71.98, which is like buying Hyatt points for 4.8 cents each.

The Thompson Rome is charging 35,000 points per night, or 17,500 points plus $281.20 (that includes taxes & fees). If redeeming outright, you’re spending 17,500 extra points to save $281.20, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.61 cents each.

The Hyatt Centric Dubai Jumeirah is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $115 ($145.14 including taxes & fees). You’re spending $145.14 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 1.45 cents each.

The Grand Hyatt Seoul is charging 20,000 points per night, or 10,000 points plus $221 (that includes taxes & fees). You’re spending $221 to save 10,000 points, which is like buying Hyatt points for 2.21 cents each.

As you can see, the value of Hyatt Points + Cash varies significantly. In the above six examples I randomly pulled up, you’re essentially “buying” Hyatt points for anywhere from 1.45 cents to 4.8 cents each (these aren’t actually points in your account, but rather you’re spending some amount of cash in lieu of points).

So the idea is that if the “purchase” price on points were relatively low, it could be worth booking Points + Cash, rather than just redeeming outright. On the low end of the spectrum, some people might find this to be worthwhile, though I think on the high end of the spectrum, we can all agree this represents an awful deal.

Before you make a final decision, just keep in mind:

Lastly, let me just mention that in many cases Points + Cash is a better value compared to redeeming points outright in situations where the cash rate is lower than usual, and a hotel is in low season. In those situations it might not make sense to redeem points at all. This comes down to how reimbursement for these awards works between World of Hyatt and individual hotels.

For example, the single best Points + Cash deal above is at the Hyatt Centric Dubai, but if you look at the cash rate, you’ll see that redeeming points isn’t a great deal in the first place. There’s no reason to redeem 20,000 points (or 10,000 points plus $115) when the cash rate in the first place is well under $200.

Hyatt Points + Cash lets you redeem part points and part cash toward the cost of a hotel stay. While it’s nice to have the flexibility of this redemption opportunity, more often than not it doesn’t represent a good deal, in my opinion.

The value you’re getting per point through Points + Cash does vary wildly, but one thing that’s fairly consistent is that you won’t get outsized value. In a majority of situations where Points + Cash represents a good deal compared to the outright points cost, it’s a hotel where a points redemption isn’t a good deal in the first place.

Personally, I avoid Points + Cash redemptions, though it’s always worth checking and crunching the numbers.

What’s your take on Hyatt’s Points + Cash option? Do you ever use it?

With P+C you still pay the full % taxes on the cash portion and lose the resort fee waiver, so at a resort with a big daily fee that alone can wipe out the gain. #6169. Allegiant Says MAX 7 Seat Cost ‘Loses Pace’

Allegiant prefers the economics of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 over the smaller MAX 7 as its plans for premium seating change how it evaluates the two aircraft.

The MAX 7 originally accounted for the majority of Allegiant’s Boeing commitment. In January 2022, the airline announced an order for 50 aircraft, split between 30 MAX 7s and 20 high-density MAX 8-200s, with options for another 50 jets.

The agreement, signed in December 2021, was Allegiant’s first direct Boeing order and marked a shift for a carrier that had largely built its business around buying used aircraft. At the time of the announcement, Allegiant operated 108 Airbus A319s and A320s.

Boeing said the new jets would reduce fuel consumption by about 20% compared with the older Airbus aircraft.

Speaking during the carrier’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, President and Chief Financial Officer Robert Neal said the MAX 7 initially offered an attractive balance between the cost of operating each flight and the cost per seat.

“When we did the order, we really liked the MAX 7 because we were looking at both the MAX 8 and MAX 7 at very high density,” Neal said. “And so you’ve got a really nice trip cost seat cost mix with the MAX 7.”

That calculation has changed as Allegiant expands its extra-legroom Allegiant Extra product and prepares to introduce Allegiant First.

“But over time, as you’ve seen us roll out incremental premium offerings at the moment through Allegiant Extra and eventually with Allegiant First, the seat cost just sort of loses pace with the MAX 8,” Neal said. “And so we prefer the cost economics of the MAX 8 at this point.”

Allegiant began shifting its order toward the larger variant in September 2023. An amended agreement retained the 50 firm aircraft but increased the number of MAX 8-200s, reduced the number of MAX 7s and expanded the option pool to 80 aircraft.

The MAX 7 faced years of certification delays, including work to redesign its engine anti-ice system. The FAA approved the variant on Aug. 3, after requiring changes to that system, flight-control software, and cockpit alerts.

The ultra-low-cost carrier added to its MAX 8 commitments last month, exercising six options for delivery in 2028. That brought its firm Boeing order to 56 aircraft, including 22 delivered through Oct. 23, with 74 options remaining.

#6168. Republican AGs stand ready as 'last line of defense' against leftist policies after dismal midterms for party

Bold conservative policies and crucial ballot measures helped Florida successfully mitigate the blue 'wave' during the midterm elections. Governor Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a near extinction level event for the Republican Party.

Republican attorney general candidates outperformed other midterm GOP hopefuls in several key races, according to a post-election analysis from the Republican Attorneys General Association, which urged colleagues to view their role as the "front line" against leftist policies following results that were likened to a "category-five political hurricane."

"America needs Republican Attorneys General now more than ever," RAGA Executive Director Adam Piper wrote in a late-night memo to colleagues shared with Fox News Digital. "With an emboldened Democrat Congress, Republican AGs are both America’s front line and is the last line of defense when it comes to their left-wing wish list – such as court packing, the Green New Deal, Medicare for All, Second Amendment restrictions, and abolishing ICE."

Piper, who has worked in Virginia and on the staff of South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson, noted midterm election results showed Republican attorneys general candidates holding up slightly better on ballots despite a difficult Tuesday night for the party.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Republican midterm dissatisfaction will have a lasting impact on the party, but the executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association is urging its colleagues to hold the "front line" against the Democrats' "category-five hurricane" of sweeping blue takeovers. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)

"Last night was the worst election night for the Republican Party in 50 years," Piper's memo began, acknowledging a difficult midterm "environment" that was ultimately made worse. "Last night, voters, regardless of party, preferred Democrat candidates by a mean of D +13.8 compared to D +7.9 in 2006 and D +8.4 in 2018.

"Today, we are dealing with the aftermath of a category-five political hurricane. It will take years to fully rebuild."

As Republicans are picking up the pieces and evaluating the map overcome with blue, even along wide swaths of Texas' southern border, the party is looking to the slight holds in Florida and any other silver linings.

Attorneys general might have something in the way of a pep talk for the party from Piper's memo.

GOP AG candidates ran an average of 4.62 percentage points ahead of GOP Senate candidates in comparable states and 2.12 points ahead of Republican gubernatorial candidates, according to the returns as of the late Wednesday night memo.

Republican AG candidates posted better margins than GOP Senate candidates in nine of 10 comparable states and outperformed Republican gubernatorial candidates in nine of 13 states, Piper wrote.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Still, Piper made clear that "there are no moral victories." Republicans did lose five AG seats to Democrats in these midterms, compared to a projected net loss of 51 in the House and a potential net loss of nine Senate seats.

Iowa, Ohio and Colorado were among the widest outperformers. The Republican attorney general candidates in those states ran 9.3, 7.3 and 10.3 points ahead of their party’s gubernatorial candidates, respectively. In Colorado, the GOP attorney general candidate also outpaced the Republican Senate candidate by 7.7 points.

FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS

In Florida, now the largest red state with the handing over of Texas to the Democratic Party, Republican Attorney General James Uthmeier won by 1.8 percentage points, outperforming Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, who won by 1.3 points.

Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers won re-election by 12.6 points, compared with a 6.7-point win for Republican Senate candidate Pete Ricketts and an 8.4-point victory for Republican Gov. Jim Pillen.

RAGA spent more than $40 million on these midterms, nearly twice its spending in 2022, and was on track to raise more than $50 million, according to Piper.

"No amount of outperformance can make up for the historical Republican losses," his memo concluded. "RAGA will start to candidate recruit for 2027 and 2028 now and has set the expectation that we will continue to overperform, no matter the environment."

#6167. 5 Airlines Offering Complimentary Premium Economy WiFi

Free Wifi is becoming an increasingly common feature onboard flights. As technologies like satellite connectivity become more widely available to airlines, passengers have, in turn, felt the benefit more and more. The caveat is having to fork out extra for the privilege in many cases.

But some carriers bundle complimentary WiFi into their fares, particularly for passengers who are already paying more for an upgraded experience. While not overly common, that can mean the added bonus of staying online at 30,000 feet-plus (9,144 meters-plus) at no additional cost. Here, we explore a handful of airlines where WiFi has become part and parcel with premium-class travel.

Cathay Pacific is among the clearest examples of where complimentary WiFi is a standard feature for customers flying premium economy and above. The Hong Kong-based operator now includes the service in the cost of these fares, leaving passengers little to do to get online mid-flight.

According to the carrier, high-speed inflight connectivity is offered onboard every aircraft in its fleet. Passengers can typically connect once their aircraft has climbed above 10,000 feet (3,048 meters). Beyond 35,000 feet (10,668 meters), satellite connectivity is possible in most areas of the world, excluding vast swathes of far northern and polar regions which lack coverage, and provided poor weather conditions do not cause disruptions. As to which apps passengers can use when online, Cathay Pacific notes online that messaging services are available, short-form streaming services can be accessed with a paid pass, while internet-enabled calls cannot be made.

*WiFi is available across the entire Cathay Pacific passenger fleet

Alongside first, business, and premium economy class travelers, those with diamond and gold loyalty program status are granted complimentary access to the service. The caveat is that a Cathay Pacific membership number must be attached to each ticket, either at the point of booking or at check-in. In other words, premium-class passengers must sign up as Cathay members to connect to the inflight internet. That is free to do, though, with the process of connecting to the internet for those eligible as simple as selecting the Cathay Pacific WiFi option on a given device and going through the operator’s online portal during the journey.

Fellow Asian operator Singapore Airlines is another to offer WiFi free of charge to a number of its customers. Unlike Cathay Pacific, however, Singapore extends complimentary access to passengers in any class, including those holding economy tickets on various routes.

Business class and first class fares include unlimited onboard internet as standard. Economy and premium economy passengers can also get free WiFi through membership in Singapore Airlines’ loyalty schemes. These include PPS Club — Singapore Airlines’ exclusive program for frequent premium-class passengers — as well as KrisFlyer, which is free to join.

Singapore Airlines Fleet (Planespotters.net)

Following the retirement of the Boeing 737-800 from its fleet at the back end of last year, Singapore Airlines now also offers WiFi on all of its passenger aircraft. Again, this is offered to customers once their aircraft have surpassed 10,000 feet (3,048 meters), or approximately 15 minutes into each flight, as Singapore Airlines notes on its website. Per the airline, internet calling and the use of streaming apps are not supported by its inflight WiFi.

Staying connected is becoming an increasingly important priority for modern-day air travelers.

Emirates is another that gives members of its loyalty scheme access to WiFi for free during their journeys. In the United Arab Emirates co-flag carrier’s case, this means signing up for its Skywards rewards program. However, how you can use onboard internet service varies by cabin class and loyalty status.

Emirates says WiFi is available to all Skywards members, and the scheme costs nothing to join. Those traveling in economy or premium economy will tend to be confined to a messaging-only internet package, though, unless they have achieved platinum status through Skywards. While this offering largely mirrors rivals' complimentary internet, Emirates explicitly advertises a better service for those in higher classes or with platinum status. “Free WiFi internet for the whole flight” is available in any such case, Emirates notes online, as opposed to “free unlimited chat” for blue, silver, or gold members flying economy or premium economy. Paid WiFi upgrades are offered, and start at $9.99.

*Ongoing retrofit program means connectivity speeds vary between aircraft

WiFi capabilities and speeds between Emirates’ aircraft also differ thanks to a massive, ongoing retrofit program primarily relating to its Boeing 777 and Airbus A380 fleets. As of early July, 33 of its 777s and three A380s had been retrofitted with satellite-enabled Starlink WiFi. One million connections to the system had been made via its aircraft, Emirates said at the time, with this having strengthened connectivity for streaming, internet calling, social media browsing, and gaming. All told, Emirates is set to bring Starlink to 232 of its aircraft as part of a wider $5 billion refurbishment effort.

Qatar Airways, like Emirates, is also in the process of rolling out Starlink across its portfolio of aircraft. Namely, that primarily includes its widebodies, on which the Qatari operator advertises uninterrupted, gate-to-gate connectivity. That means WiFi capabilities depend on specific aircraft and airports, as it stands.

Where Starlink is available onboard Qatar Airways jets, anyone can use the service for free. Access is granted across the board for 45 minutes per person, regardless of membership status or cabin class. To use Starlink-enabled internet for the duration of journeys, customers must be a part of Qatar Airways’ Privilege Club. As with other carriers, joining the loyalty scheme is free and lets travelers collect Avios to redeem later, as well as points to move up membership tiers and access stronger benefits. At Qatar Airways, free uninterrupted WiFi with speeds of up to 500 megabits per second — where available — is among these perks.

*Starlink currently rolling out across Qatar Airways’ widebody fleet

According to tracking website Starlink Flights, Qatar Airways had installed Starlink on 149 of its aircraft as of the time of writing in early November. This included all of the airline’s Airbus A350, Boeing 777-200LR, and Boeing 787-8 planes. The rollout was ongoing across its Boeing 777-300ER and Boeing 787-9 fleets in the meantime. WiFi was also available for purchase on other models, per the airline, where other WiFi technologies had been installed previously.

More space, better meals, and none of the business class price tag — but only if you know which airline to book.

Starlink is increasingly emerging on flights operated by Virgin Atlantic too. Where it is unavailable, Virgin Atlantic’s existing WiFi service covers many flights, per the British carrier’s website. Speeds and capabilities vary by route, and pricing also depends on the aircraft.

Through its Starlink rollout, Virgin Atlantic is progressively offering customers free internet. As is common among its rivals mentioned above, this is at least the case if one has signed up for Virgin Atlantic’s Flying Club prior to departure. If so, complimentary connectivity is available onboard for everything from messaging to streaming across much of the globe.

Virgin Atlantic Fleet (Planespotters.net)

*Virgin Atlantic A350s have Starlink, while streaming is unavailable on its A330-300s

Thus far, however, Virgin Atlantic’s A350s are the only jets in its fleet fully fitted with Starlink and so boast free WiFi. Plans are to install the technology across its wider aircraft portfolio at some point in 2027. Its other models already offer internet access, but WiFi packages cost extra depending on duration and which apps travelers wantto use.

#6166. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points Double Dip Explained

The single best way to earn American AAdvantage Loyalty Points with credit card spending often flies under the radar, so I’d like to talk a little more about that in this post, especially since this tends to cause some confusion. Furthermore, this was recently made an “official” card perk, rather than something that just unofficially applied to most cardmembers.

Link: Double dip your Loyalty Points earning with the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

With the American AAdvantage Loyalty Points program, you can typically earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on a co-branded American credit card. However, there’s one card that’s an exception, and by far the best.

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more) is the co-branded Citi and American Airlines business card. There’s a quirk to the card, though, when it comes to authorized user rewards. On the surface, the authorized user ordinarily earns the Loyalty Points for their spending, and not the primary cardmember, which is an unusual policy for a small business card.

However, through December 31, 2028 (and it’s possible this will be extended again, as it has been in the past), both the primary cardmember and the authorized user earn Loyalty Points for authorized user spending. It basically means you earn two Loyalty Points per dollar spent, just in different accounts. Just to be abundantly clear here:

So the key is for the spending to be on the authorized user’s card, so that this spending unlocks double Loyalty Points (spread across two accounts).

Either way, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers several valuable perks, and also has an excellent welcome bonus, making it a good time to apply. So if you are eligible, I’d consider applying even if the double Loyalty Points opportunity doesn’t work out (though hopefully it does).

Personally, the Citi AAdvantage Business Card Loyalty Points double dip is how I qualified for AAdvantage elite status last year. I had a hard time justifying putting spending onto co-branded American cards compared to some other cards out there, when I was only earning one Loyalty Point per dollar.

But if I can qualify for elite status for two people at once, and earn the corresponding Loyalty Point Rewards perks, the math on that spending starts to look much better:

#6165. At 26, Sean Duffy's son-in-law is headed to Congress as its youngest member

Congressman-elect Michael Alfonso, R-Wis., thanks his family, wife and newborn daughter for his election night victory, as the youngest member of the 120th Congress vows to fight for faith, family and freedom in Washington. (Credit: WSAW - Nov. 4)

Michael Alfonso is set to become the youngest member of Congress at 26 years old after winning a key Wisconsin House seat.

Alfonso, a Republican, will head to Washington this January after running a campaign focused on delivering on affordability and restoring the American Dream, two priorities he emphasized throughout his campaign.

"As the youngest member of Congress and a new dad, I have a personal stake in our future, and I’m going to Washington with one job: put Wisconsin and America first by making life affordable, restoring the American Dream, and putting the prosperity of American citizens above all else," the congressman-elect told Fox News Digital.

WATCH: DUFFY FLIPS SCRIPT ON DEM SENATORS WITH POINTED QUESTIONS ABOUT THEIR OWN CAMPAIGN CASH

Michael Alfonso, a candidate for U.S. House in Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, speaks during a campaign event Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in New Richmond, Wis. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)

Alfonso, who is married to Duffy's daughter Evita, defeated Democratic challenger Fred Clark, a former Wisconsin state lawmaker, in Tuesday's election to represent Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, a seat previously held by his father-in-law, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

Alfonso will succeed Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., who opted against seeking re-election to pursue the Wisconsin governorship.

Alfonso, who received endorsements from President Donald Trump and Duffy, has vowed to champion policies aimed at helping first-time homebuyers and reducing healthcare costs, protect individual freedoms and bring a new generation of conservative leadership to Washington.

Alfonso has also pledged to introduce legislation strengthening Title IX protections by restricting transgender women and girls from using facilities designated for women.

BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP

Duffy, who previously represented the district in Congress, publicly supported his son-in-law's campaign, highlighting his working-class background and construction experience.

Republican Michael Alfonso won the open GOP-held U.S. House seat in Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District. (Alfonso congressional campaign)

"I think it'd be great to have someone who knows how to put on a pair of jeans and a pair of boots and a hard hat and work his butt off 12 hours a day," Duffy said during an August appearance on NewsNation's "Morning in America."

Alfonso, who was born in February 2000, works as an accountant for the Diocese of Superior and lives in Hayward, Wis., with his wife and their 5-month-old daughter.

Before entering politics, Alfonso worked in the construction and concrete industry while attending the University of Wisconsin-Madison. He also spent time in Florida, where he worked as a producer for "The Dan Bongino Show."

Trump endorsed Alfonso in May, describing him as a "MAGA warrior" and a "young 'STAR.'"

LAURA INGRAHAM: RICHER, SAFER AND STRONGER: WHY THE TRUMP AGENDA DESERVES TO KEEP GOING

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy, left, speaks during a news conference at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Friday, Oct. 24, 2025. Chief Operating Officer of Turning Point Action Tyler Bowyer presents next-generation expected representatives Amanda McKinney, former Sheriff Mark Lamb, Joe Mitchell and Michael Alfonso during Turning Point USA's annual AmericaFest conference in Phoenix, Arizona, on December 21, 2025. (Left: Ryan Collerd/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Right: Olivier Touron / AFP via Getty Images)

Alfonso celebrated the president's endorsement as the "greatest honor" and pledged to support Trump's agenda in Congress.

During an Election Day interview with the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel, Alfonso pushed back against concerns about his age and lack of political experience, arguing that longtime politicians have failed to deliver results for Americans.

"What has experience gotten us at the congressional level? Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, I mean, Joe Biden was a senator for a long time ... we tried that already," Alfonso told the outlet. "It's not working."

During his primary race, Alfonso faced criticism from his Republican opponents about his family connections, as they raised questions about nepotism and his campaign donors.

#6164. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

#6163. Blue wave nearly swallowed some of America's reddest states as election data exposes GOP's close calls

Midterm election analysis reveals a wave of progressive victories as Lawrence Jones, 'Fox & Friends' co-host, breaks down key races and economic voter polls. The segment highlights James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas.

Races in traditionally staunch Republican strongholds came incredibly close to flipping amid Tuesday night's landslide Democratic victory, even in states where GOP candidates enjoyed overwhelming financial advantages.

Signs of something going horribly wrong for the GOP appeared late in the election cycle when Fox News rated the Senate races in South Carolina and Kansas, two states with decades-long loyalty streaks for the Republican Party, as competitive. As results poured in on election night, however, it became clear that even states that practically nobody thought would be competitive, such as Louisiana and Tennessee, were coming within a razor's edge of going blue.

Mississippi, seen by most political forecasters as among the safest of GOP seats, remains undecided as of publication, with just dozens of votes separating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee is running for governor in the 2026 race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Bill Lee. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

In Tennessee, for instance, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jerri Green spent just over $2 million, dwarfed by the nearly $13 million Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the GOP nominee, poured into the race. Outside groups burned through millions more to boost Blackburn’s candidacy.

The result of outspending a Democrat by nearly 6-to-1 in one of the reddest states in the country was Blackburn defeating Green by less than three points in a state that favored Republicans by almost 30 points in 2024.

Louisiana’s Senate race told a similar story.

The Republican nominee, Rep. Julia Letlow, and her allies paid out approximately $9.4 million to win the seat, compared to the roughly $3.89 million Democrats spent on the race. Letlow ultimately won by just under two points in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 22 points in 2024, underscoring the dramatic erosion of the GOP's advantage in one of its longtime strongholds.

FROM TEXAS TO KANSAS, 6 STUNNING MIDTERM RESULTS THAT UPENDED THE POLITICAL MAP

Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas, ending the state’s 94-year streak without a Democratic Senate win. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

Many Democratic strategists and observers have lamented that the party didn’t spend more money on long-shot races that could have delivered even more commanding margins to liberals when the new class of lawmakers and governors take office early next year.

Even Florida, a state that has become nearly synonymous with Republican ascendancy, saw the GOP come dangerously close to losing its grasp, an outcome that was avoided, in the telling of some, thanks to the political apparatus constructed by Gov. Ron DeSantis.

FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY

James Talarico’s victory over Ken Paxton helped make Texas one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 midterms, as Democrats flipped a Senate seat in a state Trump carried by double digits in 2024. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Republicans outspent Democrats by roughly five-to-one in their bid for the state’s governor's mansion, ultimately winning by less than two points. In 2022, DeSantis carried the state by nearly 20 points. The GOP won its Senate race in the Sunshine State by a similar margin, also outspending the opposition by millions.

Similar trends played out across the country, with multiple House and state legislative seats that Republicans won by double digits in 2024, flipping to Democratic control.

The election night bloodbath for the GOP has ignited a brutal blame game within the party that could easily bleed into the 2028 Republican presidential primary.

#6162. UPS Took A $137 Million Hit By Replacing Its McDonnell Douglas MD-11s With Smaller Widebody Freighters

Wikimedia Commons, M_Kaempfer | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

UPS Airlines' decision to retire its remaining McDonnell Douglas MD-11 freighters following the fatal 2025 flight 2976 accident marked a significant turning point for its cargo operations. The move carried substantial financial consequences and left the company facing a considerable gap in long-haul freight capacity.

Replacing the aging aircraft with Boeing 767-300Fs presents operational challenges, particularly given the difference in payload capacity between the two aircraft types. Meanwhile, the National Transportation Safety Board continues investigating the mechanical failures behind the crash, an inquiry that could have lasting implications for aircraft maintenance and cargo aviation safety.

On November 4, 2025, a UPS MD-11F aircraft was involved in a fatal crash shortly after taking off from Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) in Louisville, Kentucky. Following the incident, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered major cargo carriers, including UPS, FedEx, and Western Global Airlines, to ground their MD-11 fleets until thorough inspections and any necessary maintenance could be completed to ensure their structural integrity.

UPS, however, went one step further. Following the crash, the company decided to retire its entire fleet of 26 MD-11Fs, according to AeroTime. This decision was highly consequential, as the fleet served as a primary mover on long-haul international routes. According to its website, UPS' delivery network reaches more than 220 countries. Given the reach of its 500 company-owned and chartered aircraft, the resulting reduction in carrying capacity is significant.

Highlighting its capabilities, Boeing states that the MD-11BCF can carry up to 184,700 lb of revenue payload, with an optional engine configuration increasing that figure to 194,700 lb. In terms of cargo arrangement, the MD-11F can accommodate 26 main-deck pallets and up to 18 lower-deck LD-3 containers.

While UPS has relegated its MD-11Fs to the boneyard, it is replacing them with more fuel-efficient, twin-engine Boeing 767-300Fs. This is not an entirely new development for the company. According to its 2025 year-end aircraft fleet data (from the Selected Financial Data / Fourth Quarter financial statements), UPS already operated 99 aircraft of the type across three variants (89 Boeing 767-300Fs, six 767-300BCFs, and four 767-300BDSFs) and had 18 additional aircraft on order to help replace the retired MD-11s. Regarding the induction of the replacement aircraft, UPS plans to acquire 18 new Boeing 767s. Of these, 15 were scheduled to join its fleet this year, according to AeroTime.

The aircraft was once a long-haul workhorse.

Following the permanent retirement of its MD-11F fleet, Supply Chain Dive reports that "UPS incurred a non-cash, after-tax charge of $137 million..." Brian Dykes, the company's EVP and CFO, stated that "We believe these actions are consistent with building a more efficient global network positioned for growth, flexibility and profitability..."

In terms of compensating for the loss of capacity following the retirement of the MD-11Fs, Yahoo Finance reports that Dykes stated UPS would reposition some of its aircraft from other parts of the world to the United States, increase the volume of freight moved by truck, and lease aircraft from partner airlines. These measures were intended to ensure sufficient capacity during the fourth quarter of 2025, which is also a peak season for customer activity. However, outsourcing some operations to other freight carriers would ultimately cost the company about $50 million in additional expenses.

Nevertheless, the ability to meet demand through alternative capabilities convinced Dykes that the aging aircraft could be retired, a move the company was already in the process of making. The decision to accelerate the retirement of the MD-11Fs reflected a desire to avoid further costly repairs or prolonged regulatory scrutiny. Further, just about anyone (the author included) whose vehicle has frequently been in the shop eventually begins considering a newer model before selecting the best option for their circumstances. UPS made a similar move by expanding its already sizable fleet of Boeing 767-300Fs.

The classic Boeing 737-200, after 22 years with Indian Airlines, was then acquired by the Indian Air Force on July 29, 1993.

As noted above, when UPS made the decision to retire its remaining MD-11Fs, it had a combined fleet of 99 767-300s across three variants. The addition of 18 aircraft, most of which will enter service this year, will bring this force up to 117 airframes. The oldest three aircraft in the fleet are between 30 and 35 years old. While these aircraft provide substantial replacement capacity, their age highlights the importance of UPS' ongoing fleet modernization efforts.

Aside from the financial hit UPS has had to endure while it parceled out its workload to partner airlines, the company will not fully regain the carrying capacity of its retired MD-11Fs unless it invests in the Boeing 777F, which could be a worthwhile move. The Boeing 767-300F, which already represents a sizable portion of UPS' fleet, is equipped with 24 container positions on its main deck and 15 on its lower deck.

Fully loaded, the aircraft has a total payload capacity of 115,700 lb (52,480 kg), according to Boeing. This represents a reduction of approximately 70,000 lb in carrying capacity per flight compared with the retired MD-11Fs. While the company can offset some of this difference through increased flight frequency or greater reliance on ground transportation, the reduction could theoretically amount to around one million pounds of daily freight capacity, depending on the number of flights previously operated by the MD-11 fleet.

The Boeing 777F could therefore offer UPS an opportunity to recover some of the capacity lost through the MD-11's retirement while improving the efficiency of its long-haul operations. Although introducing another widebody freighter type would require a significant investment, the aircraft's greater payload capacity and range could help consolidate freight movements and reduce the need for additional flights. Nevertheless, UPS appears committed to expanding its existing 767 fleet, suggesting that the company currently favors fleet commonality and operational flexibility over introducing a new large freighter type.

The 747 transformed air cargo, but the Boeing 777F is reshaping the industry with greater efficiency, longer range, and a next-generation successor.

On November 4, 2025, at approximately 5:11 PM EST, UPS Flight 2976 received clearance for takeoff from runway 17R, according to the National Transportation Safety Board's (NTSB) preliminary report. Shortly after the aircraft left the ground, surveillance footage "...showed the left (No. 1) engine and pylon separating from the wing shortly after airplane rotation, with a fire igniting on the left engine while it traversed above the fuselage and subsequently impacted the ground...", the report stated.

According to the NTSB report, the aircraft climbed no higher than approximately 30 feet (9.1 meters) above ground level before clearing the blast fence at the end of runway 17R. Upon impact, the plane struck a storage yard and two additional buildings, including a petroleum recycling facility, which the ensuing blaze almost entirely consumed. The debris field extended from a UPS warehouse to approximately 3,000 feet (914.4 meters) south-southeast of the facility, centered near 38° 8’ 49.85” north, 85° 44’ 3.86” west.

Tragically, all three crewmembers aboard the aircraft and 11 people on the ground were killed. Two additional people were seriously injured, while 21 others in the immediate area of the impact sustained minor injuries.

The NTSB's examination of the wreckage identified significant damage to the left engine pylon's aft mounting assembly, which connects the engine to the wing. Investigators found evidence of fatigue cracking in both the forward and aft attachment lugs, alongside areas of overstress failure. On the aft lug, cracks were observed where the bore met its forward face, while additional fatigue cracks were identified along the bore of the forward lug's inboard fracture surface. Its outboard fracture surface, however, showed evidence of overstress failure alone, with no signs of fatigue cracking.

The investigation also examined the right pylon aft mount and wing clevis assembly, as well as two engine fan blade fragments recovered from runway 17R. Investigators found no evidence of deformation or pre-existing fractures on the forward top flange of the left aft mount assembly. Investigators also removed the spherical bearing from the wing clevis for further examination. Analysis of these components was expected to help establish how the engine separated from the aircraft, while the NTSB's investigation into the accident's precise cause remained ongoing.

From the Philippines to Northern Canada, this ATR 72 traveled the world, even after 17 years of use. Why is an aircraft like this needed?

The retirement of UPS' MD-11 fleet represents a significant operational and financial shift, reducing the company's available cargo capacity while accelerating its reliance on the Boeing 767-300F. Although additional aircraft and alternative transportation arrangements can help offset the loss, replacing the MD-11's capabilities will remain a challenge.

Meanwhile, the NTSB's investigation continues to examine the mechanical failures behind the fatal accident. Its findings could have lasting implications for aircraft maintenance and cargo aviation safety. They may also help determine whether additional inspections or maintenance measures are necessary across the remaining MD-11 fleet.
