#6144. DOJ civil rights chief Harmeet Dhillon resigns, says White House asked her to wait until after midterms

U.S.  Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division Harmeet Dhillon defends the Trump administration's voter roll initiative to CBS News' "60 Minutes."

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon is resigning as head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, telling Fox News Digital exclusively that she made the decision weeks before Republicans' midterm losses and was asked by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to delay her departure until after the election.

"I wasn't asked to resign," Dhillon told Fox News Digital. "I resigned three weeks ago, and Susie asked me to please wait until after the midterms."

Dhillon formally submitted her resignation on November 5, according to a letter obtained by Fox News Digital.

Dhillon said she informed Wiles three weeks before Election Day that she believed she had "accomplished everything" she came to Washington to do and wanted to return to private practice.

BONTA SAYS HE'LL COUNTER DOJ ELECTION MONITORS WITH OBSERVERS OF HIS OWN

Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general for Civil Rights, speaks with reporters after former Attorney General Pam Bondi sat for a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee deposition about the Jeffrey Epstein files, in Rayburn building on Friday, May 29, 2026.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Asked if she would testify before Congress if subpoenaed after leaving the administration, Dhillon said there would be limits on what she could discuss because of executive privilege but indicated she would seek legal advice and follow it.

"I would certainly take legal counsel and follow it in that regard," she said.

Dhillon was also asked whether she expected Trump to pardon her or other administration officials if congressional Democrats sought to target them.

"I have no idea. I haven't ever discussed that with him, asked for it," Dhillon said. "And I have done nothing, in my opinion, that would require that, but, you know, that's up to the president."

She revealed that the decision to leave the DOJ ultimately came down to wanting to return to the work she had done for much of her career in the private sector.

Dhillon moved to Washington following the deaths of her husband and father to "serve my country," but after roughly two years in the administration, she believed the time has come to leave.

"My decision, my choice," Dhillon said. "It's time."

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon," Attorney General Todd Blanche wrote on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

DOJ FIRES BACK AT DEM AG OVER ELECTION DAY GUIDANCE TELLING OFFICIALS WHEN TO CALL COPS ON FEDERAL AGENTS

She was nominated by President Donald Trump in December 2024 and was sworn into office in April 2025 after being confirmed by the Senate. She is leaving after Trump's Republican Party lost the House and Senate in this week's midterm elections.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Dhillon defended the Trump administration's investigation into noncitizen voters.

"There are people who feel that the point is to sow distrust about the whole election system. There are very few people who are noncitizens who end up voting — very, very few. And so, therefore, what's the purpose?" Lesley Stahl, host of CBS' "60 Minutes," had asked Dhillon.

Dhillon's departure caps a roughly 19-month tenure in which the longtime conservative attorney carried out a sweeping overhaul of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, shifting its priorities toward issues including DEI and race-conscious policies, religious discrimination, transgender participation in women's sports, Second Amendment rights and election integrity.

The transformation also brought extraordinary turnover inside the division, with roughly 300 attorneys departing during Trump's second term, according to recent reports. Dhillon has aggressively sought to rebuild its ranks, telling Fox News Digital that she recruited more than 130 lawyers during her tenure.

Harmeet K. Dhillon speaks at the IAC National Summit 2026 at The Diplomat Beach Resort on January 17, 2026 in Hollywood, Florida.  (Photo by Noam Galai/Getty Images) (Noam Galai/Getty Images)

Before joining the administration, Dhillon founded the Dhillon Law Group and the Center for American Liberty and built a national profile litigating First Amendment, election law and other civil-rights cases. A longtime Republican Party official and Trump ally, she was nominated by Trump in December 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in April 2025.

Her appointment drew fierce opposition from Democrats and some traditional civil-rights groups, while conservatives argued that she would redirect a division they believed had become ideologically tilted under previous administrations.

"We changed it, and that's what we came here to do. And it's done," Dhillon told Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital's Lindsay Kornick and Hanna Panreck contributed to this post.

#6143. 10 Classic Airliners That Needed A Third Person In The Cockpit

Swissair | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying

A third seat in an airliner’s cockpit can tell you a surprising amount about the machine itself. On some jets the person occupying it was often a flight engineer, responsible for monitoring and managing systems that modern flight crews now take for granted . On others, the job became so closely tied to the aircraft that the engineer’s station was almost as recognizable as the engines or the silhouette.

The flight engineer’s place in the cockpit did not disappear overnight, and the aircraft that carried one were far from interchangeable. Some made the role part of everyday long-haul operations; others pushed it into unusual territory. This countdown features ten classic airliners that were designed or operated with three crew members in the cockpit. The selection is based on that crew configuration, rather than requiring every aircraft to use the same title or staffing arrangement for its third crew member. The aircraft are ranked by their historical influence, fleet size, and the lasting place the third cockpit position held in their identity.

The Douglas DC-6 first flew on June 29, 1946, and entered airline service with American Airlines and United Airlines in 1947. More than 700 examples were eventually built, making it one of the most successful large piston-powered airliners of the postwar era. Its four Pratt & Whitney R-2800 radial engines, pressurized cabin, and long-range capability helped airlines expand their domestic and international networks. NASA's aviation history covers the aircraft's introduction and commercial impact.

The DC-6's cockpit required a minimum crew of three: a pilot, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer monitored the four engines and managed the aircraft's systems, taking on responsibilities that would otherwise have added to the pilots' workload. Delta initially operated the aircraft with two pilots, but federal regulations soon required a third cockpit crew member. The Delta Flight Museum documents that change, and the aircraft's operating manual specifies the minimum three-person crew.

The DC-6 ranks tenth because it represents the postwar expansion of the traditional three-person cockpit. Its combination of four complex piston engines and long-distance operations made the flight engineer an important part of airline operations, setting the stage for the larger piston airliners and early jets that followed.

The Douglas DC-8 first flew on May 30, 1958, and entered commercial service with Delta Air Lines on September 18, 1959. One of the first American jetliners designed for long-range passenger operations, it combined four underwing engines with a pressurized cabin and the speed needed to transform transcontinental and international travel. Douglas eventually built 556 examples, including the stretched Super 60 series. The FAA's historical chronology records the aircraft's development and entry into service, while Boeing's historical archive preserves its first-flight history.

The DC-8 retained a three-person flight deck, with a captain, first officer, and flight engineer. Seated behind the pilots, the engineer monitored the four engines and managed systems including fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The aircraft's type certificate specified a minimum crew of three, making the engineer an integral part of its approved operating configuration.

The DC-8 ranks ninth because it brought the traditional flight engineer's station into the first generation of successful American jetliners. Its long passenger and cargo career also showed how enduring that arrangement would be: even as jet technology advanced, the third cockpit position remained standard throughout the DC-8's production life.

The DC-8, a rival to the Boeing 707, defied the odds and continued flying cargo missions well into the 2020s, outlasting its competitor by decades.

The Lockheed Constellation first flew on January 9, 1943, initially as a military aircraft, before entering commercial service with TWA in 1946. Its pressurized cabin, long-range capability, and distinctive triple-tail design made it one of the defining airliners of the postwar period. Later versions, particularly the Super Constellation, introduced improved engines and greater operating range. The Smithsonian's Lockheed Constellation collection record documents the aircraft's development and its first flight.

The Constellation also helped establish the flight engineer as an important member of the long-distance airline crew. Operating four large piston engines while monitoring fuel distribution, electrical systems, and other aircraft functions demanded considerable technical knowledge. A dedicated engineer's station allowed these responsibilities to be separated from the pilots' flying duties, particularly during lengthy oceanic operations. The Airline History Museum's Constellation archive provides additional aircraft history and restoration information.

The Constellation ranks eighth because it helped establish the traditional three-person cockpit as a practical arrangement for long-range commercial aircraft. Its engineer's position represented a growing specialization within airline flight crews.

The Tupolev Tu-154 first flew on October 4, 1968, and entered Aeroflot service in February 1972. More than 1,000 were eventually built, making it a standard Soviet and later Russian medium-haul airliner. Its designers wanted a relatively lean flight crew of captain, first officer, and flight engineer, at a time when other Soviet airliners routinely carried four or five people up front. The Tu-154B-2 could be flown by three crew members, because Hungary's Malév judged larger crews economically unacceptable. Simple Flying notes that the Tu-154 filled nearly the same role in the Eastern Bloc that the 727 played in the West.

Navigation requirements meant that many Tu-154 operations retained a dedicated navigator in addition to the engineer. The navigator and flight engineer occupied separate workstations, illustrating how cockpit staffing differed between Soviet and Western aviation. The German Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation's report on the 2002 Überlingen collision documents the positions of the Tu-154M's navigator and engineer. Crew arrangements varied by operator and version.

The Tu-154 ranks seventh because it demonstrates that the three-person cockpit was not a universal solution. Its long production life and continued use of additional specialists highlight the different approaches to cockpit staffing that existed during the jet age.

BA Concorde first flew on March 2, 1969, and began scheduled passenger service in January 1976 with British Airways and Air France. Its flight crew consisted of a captain, first officer and flight engineer. Cruising at approximately 1,350 mph (2,170 km/h) and reaching altitudes of around 60,000 feet (18,300 m), it presented technical challenges unlike those of an ordinary subsonic airliner.

The engineer occupied a dedicated station behind the pilots, monitoring fuel, electrical, hydraulic, air-conditioning, and engine systems. Fuel management was particularly important because fuel was transferred between tanks to control the aircraft's center of gravity as it accelerated and decelerated. Warren Hazelby, a former Lockheed L-1011 flight engineer who later worked on Concorde, described the aircraft's complexity in a CNN interview about his experience operating the supersonic jet.

Concorde ranks sixth because it demonstrates how essential the flight engineer could remain even in a technologically advanced aircraft. Only 20 were built, including development aircraft, but the third crew member remained part of its commercial operation until retirement in 2003.

How the L-1011-500 pioneered long-haul thin routes, using innovative design and extended range to fill a unique aviation niche.

The Lockheed L-1011 TriStar first flew on November 16, 1970, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines in April 1972. Lockheed built 250 examples, and the aircraft became known for its advanced flight-control technology and relatively quiet operation. Despite having an advanced autopilot capable of automatic landings, the TriStar retained a three-person cockpit. Lockheed's own historical account of the L-1011 describes its advanced automatic flight-control system and the technical ambitions behind the aircraft.

The flight engineer monitored the aircraft's complex mechanical and electrical systems, including fuel, hydraulics, and engine performance. The importance of crew coordination became particularly evident during Eastern Air Lines Flight 401 in December 1972. While the crew investigated a landing-gear indicator problem, attention shifted away from monitoring the aircraft's flight path. The FAA's account of the Flight 401 accident explains how the crew became distracted while troubleshooting the indicator and failed to monitor the aircraft's flight path. The accident helped shape later thinking about crew resource management. The TriStar's engines brought their own challenges, as the Rolls-Royce RB211 program experienced major development difficulties that delayed the aircraft's introduction.

The TriStar ranks fifth because it demonstrated that sophisticated automation did not immediately make the flight engineer redundant. Even one of the most advanced airliners of its generation continued to rely on a dedicated systems specialist.

The McDonnell Douglas DC-10 first flew on August 29, 1970, and entered service with American Airlines on August 5, 1971. Its flight deck was designed for three people: a captain, copilot, and flight engineer. The engineer occupied a dedicated panel behind the pilots, monitoring systems that included fuel, electrical power, hydraulics, and engine performance. The DC-10 was developed as a widebody trijet, with two engines mounted beneath the wings and a third installed at the base of the vertical tail. This arrangement provided the capacity and range airlines wanted while meeting the long-haul regulatory environment of the period.

The flight engineer's responsibilities included monitoring fuel distribution, electrical buses, and hydraulic systems, as well as helping identify abnormal conditions. According to Boeing, the later MD-10 conversion introduced a modern glass cockpit, allowing the removal of the flight engineer's position.

The DC-10 ranks fourth because it illustrates both the importance and eventual disappearance of the flight engineer's position. The DC-10's passenger career gradually ended as more efficient widebody aircraft replaced it, although freighter operations continued for decades. Its long service history makes it one of the clearest examples of the transition from traditional three-person flight decks to modern two-pilot cockpits.

The Boeing 727 first flew on February 9, 1963, and entered service with Eastern Air Lines on February 1, 1964. It became the first commercial jetliner to pass 1,000 sales, with production eventually reaching 1,832 aircraft before ending in 1984. The type required a three-person flight deck, with the engineer seated sideways behind the pilots. Its distinctive arrangement of three rear-mounted engines allowed Boeing to deliver the performance airlines wanted without placing engines beneath the wings. The aircraft's integrated rear airstair and sophisticated high-lift system also made it attractive for operations at airports with limited ground facilities and relatively short runways.

The 727's third engine emerged from a compromise among United Airlines, American and Eastern. United wanted strong performance at hot-and-high airports such as Denver, while Eastern needed an aircraft suitable for overwater operations. Many smaller airports offered runways of just 4,500 feet (1,372 m), which the 727's triple-slotted flaps helped it handle. Its systems remained complex enough to require a dedicated engineer, who monitored engine instruments and the fuel, electrical, and hydraulic systems. Boeing's historical aircraft collection provides further information about the aircraft's development and its remarkable production run.

The 727 ranks third because its flight-engineer era stretched across decades of everyday flying. It became a familiar sight at airports around the world, and its long freighter career kept the third cockpit seat in use well after newer passenger jets had moved toward two-pilot operations. FedEx retired its final 727s in 2013, marking the end of a particularly important chapter in the company's freighter fleet. For many airline pilots and engineers, the 727 remained one of the defining aircraft of the traditional three-person cockpit.

Discover how a retired Boeing 727 became a home and how planes worldwide are finding second lives as restaurants and hotels.

The Boeing 707 opened the jet age for most travelers. Developed from the Boeing 367-80 prototype, the first production 707-120 flew on December 20, 1957, and FAA certification followed on September 18, 1958. Pan Am began regular service on October 26, 1958, with a transatlantic flight from New York to Paris. Boeing eventually delivered more than 1,000 aircraft across the 707 family, including the smaller 720. The aircraft's four turbojet engines and long-range capabilities made it one of the most influential commercial transports ever built. Its cockpit was designed around a captain, first officer, and flight engineer, establishing a layout that would become familiar throughout the first generation of jet airliners.

The engineer's workstation was particularly important during the 707's early years. The aircraft's systems required continuous monitoring, including fuel management, electrical power, hydraulics, and pressurization. The engineer also assisted the pilots during engine start and monitored the four engines throughout the flight. Pan Am's Clipper America helped establish the aircraft's international reputation, and the 707 quickly became a symbol of the new era of commercial aviation. Its military derivatives extended the design's life considerably, with aircraft such as the E-3 Sentry continuing to use flight engineers long after most passenger airlines had moved to newer designs. The Pan Am Historical Foundation's account of the airline's first 747 also provides useful context for the transition from the early jet age to the widebody era.

The 707 ranks second because it helped establish the standard for the first generation of long-range jetliners. The 727, 747, and DC-10 that followed inherited the same three-person philosophy, and the 707 proved that jet aircraft could operate profitably on major international routes. Its influence extended far beyond passenger service, with military derivatives continuing to fly for decades. The 707's engineer station became a familiar feature of the early jet age, making it one of the most historically significant aircraft on this list.

The Boeing 747 made its first flight on February 9, 1969, with Brien Wygle as copilot and Jess Wallick as flight engineer. Pan Am launched passenger service on January 22, 1970, on a New York–London flight. The Boeing 747-100 was designed to carry approximately 366 to 452 passengers, depending on configuration, and its introduction transformed the economics of long-distance air travel. Behind the pilots, the engineer faced sideways toward a large collection of panels. The aircraft's size and complexity demanded continuous attention to fuel pumps, electrical buses, pressurization, hydraulics, and air conditioning, tasks that two pilots would have struggled to manage alongside their flying responsibilities. Boeing's official 747 history documents the first flight, the aircraft's development, and the beginning of passenger service.

The flight engineer's role on the 747 was particularly recognizable because of the dedicated sideways-facing station. Boeing's early jumbo jets contained numerous switches, lights, and gauges, and the engineer monitored systems that extended throughout the aircraft. Typical duties included operating fuel pumps, managing fuel transfer, monitoring electrical systems, and coordinating the use of backup systems when required. The position remained a standard feature on the 747-100, Boeing 747-200 and Boeing 747-300, but the introduction of the Boeing 747-400 in 1989 changed the arrangement. Its Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System, together with more advanced digital displays, allowed the aircraft to operate with two pilots instead of three. The Pan Am Museum Foundation's history of the jumbo jet provides additional background on the aircraft's introduction and its impact on international travel.

The classic 747 earns the top spot because it fused scale, symbolism, and the traditional flight engineer's role. Boeing built more than 1,500 747s across the aircraft's production history, and the engineer's sideways seat became the best-known example of the third crew position. The jumbo jet represented the peak of the traditional widebody cockpit, but it also demonstrated how quickly that arrangement could become outdated. Automation, digital displays, and integrated warning and monitoring systems eventually allowed newer aircraft to receive certification for two-pilot operations. The 747-400's introduction marked one of the clearest turning points in that transition, bringing the classic three-person cockpit era closer to its end.

#6142. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

A ‘FOX News Democracy 26’ panel discusses the impact of the war in Iran on the 2026 midterm elections, the Trump administration’s messaging on the conflict and more.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is facing a bipartisan impeachment threat when Congress returns next week as Republicans seethe over their devastating losses in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Bipartisan frustration over the war in Iran, quietly simmering for months, is now openly erupting after Democrats stunned the country with historic victories in the House and Senate. That anger could all now hit Hegseth, with several House Republicans telling Fox News Digital that they believe a resolution to impeach him could pass as early as next week.

"He's screwed," one House GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a longtime critic of foreign intervention by the U.S., told Fox News Digital he intends to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth when Congress returns if the Pentagon chief does not resign first.

GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH

War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference on U.S. military action in Iran at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., on March 2, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

He'll do so by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at getting a vote on legislation despite opposition from the majority party's leaders. Once a privileged resolution is filed, lawmakers have two legislative days to hold a vote.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

But the procedure notably carries two steps. Before a vote on the measure itself, leaders can call up a vote to "table" the bill or refer it to the relevant committee, which in both instances effectively kills it.

That procedural vote is normally where most privileged resolutions die. But in this case, several House Republicans told Fox News Digital they believe the impeachment resolution could ultimately be successful.

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS'

"If he introduces it, it'll pass," a second House Republican told Fox News Digital. Two more said they expected the same.

And with just a razor-thin majority, only a handful of absences would be enough for Hegseth to get impeached if all Democrats stuck together.

The Fox News Decision Desk projected Democrats taking the House shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Projections showed that the war in Iran, along with tariff policies, were key drivers in voters turning their backs on the GOP.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

And while President Donald Trump told reporters he believes Hegseth is doing "a good job," people in his circle appear to have their knives out.

"Hegseth is on the chopping block," a former White House official told Fox News Digital.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

But the White House criticized the potential impeachment push on Thursday.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. And another White House official said, "If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Wednesday dismissed rumors that Trump could get rid of Hegseth himself.

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America," he told Fox News Digital.

It's also worth noting that the majority of House Republicans will still oppose impeaching Hegseth — and many are still skeptical.

CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

"I really doubt [it]," another House Republican told Fox News Digital. "Depends on if anyone wants to flip off the president walking out the door."

There is likely to be healthy support on the other side of the aisle for such a push as well.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker, has consistently criticized Hegseth. He posted on X Thursday morning, "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?"

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic candidate Suzan DelBene celebrate at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee midterm election night watch party in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

Even more moderate Democrats have signaled their support, given the administration did not seek the consent of Congress at any point during the ordeal.

"I've said a long, long time ago that he's not qualified for the job, and he should be removed, and I think we're going to pursue that," Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to take over leadership of the House Armed Services Committee next year, told CNN's "This Morning" last month.

If Hegseth were impeached, he would not be removed before a trial in the U.S. Senate.

Fox News Digital reached out to the committee's Republican majority and the Pentagon for comment.

#6140. Southwest Airlines Now Runs Late Nearly A Third Of The Time

Southwest Airlines was late nearly a third of the time in October, and its cancellation rate was more than twice Delta’s. It finished last for punctuality among the ten North American airlines in aviation analytics company Cirium’s new monthly report, while Delta led on both. For the past two months, I’ve pointed out that Southwest’s poor on-time rankings were offset by canceling fewer flights than anyone else. They weren’t on-time but they reliably got passengers to their destinations. In October, though, Delta, United and even Frontier cancelled a smaller share of flights than Southwest. Here are Cirium’s North American results. On-time means arriving at the gate within 15 minutes of schedule. Airline   September On-Time   October On-Time   October Canceled Delta   82.52%   86.86%   0.24% United   78.65%   84.06%   0.31% WestJet   85.31%   83.56%   0.90% JetBlue   74.64%   82.27%   0.57% Alaska   80.73%   81.06%   1.10% American   77.11%   80.10%   0.63% Allegiant   Not listed   77.89%   1.13% Frontier   75.49%   77.62%   0.38% Air Canada   73.19%   75.74%   2.80% Southwest   71.14%   68.90%   0.51% Southwest’s Fixes Extend Into January Southwest’s on-time performance fell 2.24 percentage points from September. Every other U.S. airline improved. And Southwest was nearly seven points behind even Air Canada, the next airline up the list. They’re also way down from last October when they were 75.5% on time versus 68.9% this year. Delta improved year-over-year from 84.5% to 86.9%. Southwest’s cancellation rate increased from 0.38% to 0.51%. That’s still only about five cancellations per thousand flights, but Delta was at 2.4 per thousand and United at 3.1. There was no longer a cancellation advantage in October to offset the Dallas-based carrier’s greater likelihood of arriving late. Management knows there’s a problem. On the October 22 earnings call, chief operating officer Andrew Watterson said the weakness was concentrated in delays between roughly 15 and 45 minutes. He described the airline consistently starting aircraft turnarounds well, then losing time at the end. Changes to gate checking bags and closing flights are supposed to begin in November. Southwest gate checks a lot more bags now that passengers want to carry more belongings onboard, since checked bags have a fee. Agents will finally be able to close flights using an iPad at the aircraft. And adjusted schedules begin in January. Fast turns let Southwest get more flying out of each airplane. But those savings shrink when those produces delays, and CEO Bob Jordan acknowledged that poor punctuality is adding to costs including from misconnecting passengers. Delta Leads, United Closes In, And JetBlue Recovers Delta took first place from WestJet, ending the Canadian airline’s five-month run at the top of North America. Delta also ranked third on Cirium’s global list. Their cancellation rate has fallen from 1.77% in August to 0.92% in September and 0.24% in October. That’s real improvement compared to their abysmal summer operation. United is getting improving, too. Delta’s punctuality lead over United narrowed from 3.87 percentage points to 2.80. Delta canceled less often this time, but the difference was just 0.07 percentage points or seven flights per 10,000 scheduled. I wouldn’t pay much extra for Delta over United based on that operational gap. Against Southwest, Delta was nearly 18 percentage points more likely to arrive within the on-time window. American improved, too, but fell further behind both of its major competitors. Delta’s lead over American widened from 5.41 to 6.76 points. United’s lead widened from 1.54 to 3.96 points. American’s better month left them sixth in North America. And JetBlue went from 63.85% on time in August to 74.64% in September and 82.27% in October. Their 7.63-point gain was the largest of any North American airline. JetBlue finished ahead of both Alaska and American on punctuality, and canceled less often than either. Their cancellation rate fell from 5.09% in August to 0.57% in October. Even Newark Made The On-Time Airports List The airport report measures on-time departures, rather than arrivals. Six U.S. airports made Cirium’s top 20 large airports worldwide, up from just two in September: Minneapolis–St. Paul: 87.00%, eighth Washington Dulles: 86.25%, eleventh Detroit: 86.13%, twelfth Salt Lake City: 85.69%, thirteenth Newark: 85.64%, fourteenth Atlanta: 85.17%, eighteenth Four are Delta hubs. The other two are United hubs. No American hub made the list. This is partly another view of the airlines themselves, since a hub’s results depend heavily on its dominant carrier. I never expect to see Newark doing well! And this data can be useful to some degree in choosing between otherwise similar connecting options, although can also be seasonal due to weather. #6139. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

@Lucky, "I doubt many people will avoid online check-in or book away from Lufthansa Group because of this initiative" Well, maybe not because of this, but when combined with every other shitty decision LH has made, they just might... With more than 9,000 properties across over 35 brands worldwide, Marriott Bonvoy offers plenty of ways to earn free hotel stays.

Whether you're looking for a premium travel card, a no-annual-fee option or a business card, Marriott's cobranded credit card lineup has something to offer.

Below, we break down the current offers and help you decide which Marriott card might be worth it.

Marriott Bonvoy loyalists can choose from card options issued by American Express and Chase.

There are multiple personal cards and one business card available. Make sure you’re eligible for a business card before applying. Keep in mind that TPG recommends a credit score in the good-to-excellent range to give yourself the best possible chance of approval.

*The bonus value is based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Marriott stays?

Best for: Travelers who only stay with Marriott once or twice each year

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Credit Card is one of Chase’s two mid-tier Bonvoy cards.

Welcome offer: Earn three free night awards (valued up to 50,000 points each) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. Additionally, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

Per our valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,225 (including the statement credit).

We recommend applying when at least 150,000 points are on offer, making now a great time to apply.

Why we like it: The Boundless gives you great Marriott perks without paying a high annual fee. With this card, you’ll get automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and 15 elite qualifying nights every year. You’ll also earn one elite night credit toward the next level of elite status for every $5,000 spent, and you can reach Gold Elite status by spending $35,000 on the card in a calendar year.

The card's most valuable perk is the annual free night award (worth up to 35,000 points) at each account anniversary, though Marriott’s lack of award charts could hinder your ability to use this benefit.

Fortunately, this free night award can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless card.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Credit Card

Best for: Small-business owners who can maximize the card's annual free night award (certain hotels have resort fees)

The Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card is Marriott’s only business card currently available to new applicants.

Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, this bonus is worth up to $563.

This is the standard offer, so it's worth waiting for an elevated bonus.

Why we like it: With this card, you’ll get automatic Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and a 7% discount on eligible bookings made directly with Marriott through an eligible channel at participating properties with this card’s rate.

The card also comes with 15 elite night credits annually (which can be stacked with a Marriott Bonvoy consumer card) and a free night award annually after your card renewal month (worth up to 35,000 points and can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night). In addition, you can earn a second free night (also worth up to 35,000 points) after $60,000 of purchases on your card in a calendar year. (Certain hotels have resort fees.)

Marriott’s use of dynamic pricing may make it hard to use these awards. Still, you should be able to find a participating property that can cover your annual fee (and then some), as our data indicates there’s still significant value in the program.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Business.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card

Best for: Mega Marriott fans who stay with the brand at least a few times each year

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card is Marriott’s top-tier card.

Welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $750.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: The card also has valuable perks, such as automatic Platinum Elite status, an annual free night award (worth up to 85,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees) after card renewal month, up to $300 per year (up to $25 in monthly statement credits) for eligible purchases at restaurants worldwide, Priority Pass™ lounge access and 25 elite qualifying night credits per year. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Remember that Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so you may need to work harder to find a property where you can use your free nights. But you can top up free night awards with up to 25,000 points now, which allows you to book a night worth up to 110,000 points.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card is Bonvoy’s mid-tier card from American Express. It has earnings, benefits and an annual fee that mirror the Bountiful.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

This bonus is worth $638, per TPG's valuations.

This is the standard offer we typically see on the card, so we recommend waiting for a higher offer before applying.

Why we like it: This card also offers mid-tier perks, including complimentary Gold Elite status, a solid earning rate at Marriott properties and elite night credits. However, it lacks several benefits that you might expect from a mid-tier card.

For example, you must spend $15,000 in a calendar year to earn a free night (worth up to 50,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees). Other Marriott cards with lower annual fees offer a similar perk with no spending requirement, making this card tough to justify keeping after earning the welcome offer in the first year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Bevy.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card

Best for: High-spending Marriott fans who prefer to bank with Chase

The Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful is the other mid-tier Bonvoy card from Chase.

Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG’s valuations, this offer is worth $638.

This is typically the standard welcome offer we see in the card's history. Unless you absolutely need this card now, you’re better off applying when the offer is higher.

Why we like it: While American Express issues the Bevy, the Bountiful comes from Chase. The two cards offer mostly the same benefits, making it hard to justify the Bountiful's $250 annual fee. However, the welcome bonus may interest you.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card.

Best for: Travelers who infrequently stay with Marriott, but want to enjoy perks when they do

The Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card is Chase’s entry-level card for Bonvoy enthusiasts.

Welcome offer: Earn 45,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The bonus points are worth $338, according to TPG’s valuations.

This is slightly higher than the standard welcome offer we've seen on the card, but we'd still suggest waiting for a more rewarding bonus if your timeline is flexible.

Why we like it: The card offers automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and five annual elite night credits. It also charges no foreign transaction fees. Additionally, the Bold features Chase’s Pay Yourself Back, allowing you to redeem points toward eligible travel purchases made directly with airlines or Marriott Bonvoy hotels (up to $750 in total redemptions per year).

This is a solid set of perks for a card with no annual fee. However, frequent Marriott guests may do better with a card that offers more perks during each stay.

To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bold card.

Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card

If multiple Marriott card offers intrigue you, you can indeed have more than one Marriott card open. Some TPG staffers have two or three.

It can make sense to leverage the annual anniversary award nights and stack the 5 to 25 elite nights awarded by carrying both a personal and a small-business Marriott card.

However, with six Marriott cards available to new applicants, there are several restrictions on who can earn the welcome offers across the cards, especially since Marriott cards are issued by both Amex and Chase.

Note that these restrictions are all in addition to Chase’s 5/24 rule (which applies to new applicants for the Bold, Boundless and Bountiful cards) and Amex’s one-bonus-per-lifetime rule (which applies to the Bevy, Brilliant and Business cards).

Make sure you’re eligible for these offers before applying.

Related: Here’s how to calculate your Chase 5/24 standing

Marriott credit cards regularly rank among the best hotel credit cards thanks to the long-term value they offer through perks such as elite status and annual free night awards.

The Boundless currently has a great welcome offer; we'd recommend holding off for higher bonuses on the other cards.

Before applying, consider the size of the welcome offer, whether you're eligible and if the card's ongoing benefits justify adding it to your wallet.

#6137. Boeing's Renton Factory Must Stagger The 737 MAX 10 With Smaller Jets, But Everett Can Run Nose-To-Tail

Boeing rolled the first 737 MAX 10 out of its new North Line at the Everett facility on October 26, and media attention naturally focused on the historic location shift. Destined for launch customer WestJet, this is the first time a 737 variant has been assembled outside of Boeing’s historic Renton plant since 1970. This change in build location makes sense because the longest variant in the 737 family has outgrown the layout of the factory that birthed it.

The motivation for establishing the North Line isn't simply to increase monthly hull count. The 143 feet, 8 inches (43.8 meters) fuselage of the 737 MAX 10 is not best suited to fit inside Renton’s compact assembly bays. To build the MAX 10 in Renton, Boeing had to stagger the elongated airframe between smaller variants like the MAX 8 to prevent structural overlap between adjacent stations. Now, by repurposing space in Everett’s massive widebody plant, Boeing has finally provided its largest narrowbody with an assembly line tailored to its length.

Boeing’s Renton factory has been the manufacturing heart of the 737 program for decades, but its boundaries were drawn around significantly shorter airframes. Covering roughly 1.1 million sq feet (102,000 m²) of total floor space, Renton’s three active assembly lines operate within tight architectural confines bounded by Lake Washington and local rail lines. When managing standard 737 MAX 8 aircraft, measuring 129 feet, 6 inches (39.5 meters) long, the moving assembly lines operate with minimal spatial clearance between stations.

The introduction of the 737 MAX 10 disrupted this tightly calibrated footprint. Stretched 14 feet, 2 inches (4.3 m) longer than the baseline MAX 8, the MAX 10’s nose and tail sections intrude into overhead crane pathways and the working envelopes of adjacent stations when positioned directly in sequence. To avoid costly structural collisions during station transitions, Renton line managers must manually stagger the build sequence so a longer MAX 10 is always preceded and followed by shorter MAX 7 or MAX 8 airframes.

This requirement creates scheduling friction across Renton’s 12,000-person workforce. Staggering limits production flexibility, as line operators cannot build MAX 10s based solely on order-book priority. According to Boeing, there are 1,555 firm orders for the MAX 10, about 31% of the total 737 MAX backlog, so Renton’s layout threatened to become a permanent operational bottleneck for Boeing’s most important commercial variant.

Something had to be done about Renton’s layout constraints, so Boeing began a $1 billion capital project to establish the 737 MAX North Line inside its flagship Everett facility. Occupying high-bay space in Building 40-22, vacated following the consolidation of 787 Dreamliner assembly to South Carolina, the new line provides approximately 20% more usable floor area per station compared to Renton. This means the 737 MAX 10 can move continuously in a true nose-to-tail orientation and does not need those staggered buffers.

Supported by an initial workforce of roughly 1,000 employees, about half of whom were reassigned directly from Renton to transfer specialized narrowbody assembly expertise, the North Line operates with modernized tooling, according to Barron's. The added clearance permits automated overhead crane systems and mobile scaffolding rigs to work around the MAX 10’s extended fuselage without interfering with adjacent work centers. Crucially, the dedicated layout increases total 737 manufacturing capacity by 25% across Boeing's Puget Sound industrial network, Lynwood Times reported.

However, uncoupling the MAX 10 from Renton's spatial constraints is not the end of the story for Boeing. Of course, the North Line provides the needed floor space for smooth assembly, but bringing these aircraft to market is a completely different reality for Boeing, and just adding floor space does not guarantee success in this area.

The opening of a second 737 assembly line in Everett represents more than just additional manufacturing space.

Achieving rollout on October 26 was a major milestone, but it does not mean customer deliveries are imminent. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) granted amended type certification for the 737 MAX 10 flight platform just a few days earlier on October 20, 2026. It was excellent news for Boeing, confirming that the MAX 10’s aerodynamic design, flight controls, and safety systems meet airworthiness standards, though it is only the first stage of regulatory clearance and many more stages remain.

Before WestJet or any subsequent customer can take delivery of an Everett-built MAX 10, Boeing must secure a separate amendment to its FAA Production Certificate. Everett is an entirely new production line for the 737 program, so FAA inspectors must audit every station, tool calibration log, and quality management process inside the North Line. The agency will need to independently verify that the Everett facility builds aircraft with the same structural consistency as Renton, which is a huge undertaking for Boeing.

During this initial low-rate production phase, the North Line moved the first airframes through assembly stations at a deliberately slow pace, according to Assembly Magazine. The extended flow time allows quality engineers to validate assembly steps alongside FAA observers. Consequently, initial WestJet deliveries will remain paused until the production certificate amendment is formally issued, making the short-term backlog relief more of a future expectation than an immediate result.

Everett solves Boeing's internal floor space limitations, but the pace of total 737 production remains tied to Tier-1 supplier health. As Boeing leadership confirmed, the main constraint on narrowbody output is an ongoing shortage of wing subassemblies. The complex wing structures, featuring advanced-technology winglets and dedicated trailing-edge flap mechanisms designed to handle the MAX 10’s higher takeoff weight, are arriving at assembly plants well behind schedule.

Even with a vastly improved production environment, an airframe cannot progress past early structural joining stations without its wing sets, so wing availability sets the pacing clock for both Renton and Everett. In response, Boeing revised its master production ramp. The target rate of 47 aircraft per month has been revised slightly, and Boeing now expects to reach and hold the 47-per-month milestone in 2027, before attempting a further push toward 52 jets per month later that year, according to Fortune.

The controlled ramp rate is designed to prevent traveled work, or moving unfinished airframes to downstream stations without completing preliminary assemblies. Holding the North Line at a steady, measured pace means Boeing is protecting manufacturing stability while supplier factories bring wing deliveries back into alignment.

The move will also free up capacity in Renton as Boeing looks to scale up MAX 8 and MAX 9 production.

The strategic commitment to build a $1 billion dedicated line in Everett is backed directly by market demand. At the top of the 737 MAX family, the MAX 10 carries 185 to 210 passengers in a standard two-class layout, with a maximum capacity of 230 seats. With a range of 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 km), the variant competes directly with Airbus’ dominant A321neo, offering airlines low seat-mile costs on high-density domestic and transcontinental trunk routes.

With 1,555 firm orders logged from global operators including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, WestJet, and Ryanair, the MAX 10 is seeing a wave of popularity worldwide. Even Lufthansa has opted for the type, bringing the 737 back into the fleet after 10 years of pure Airbus narrowbody focus in the mainline fleet. Airlines have structured long-term fleet renewals around the high-capacity variant to replace aging 757-200s and older 737-900ERs. Failing to deliver the MAX 10 efficiently risked pushing these key customer accounts to convert options into competing European narrowbodies.

With Everett’s North Line dedicated to the MAX 10 alongside high-density MAX 8 runs, Boeing has clearly divided industrial labor. Renton can focus its three moving lines on high-volume MAX 8 and MAX 9 builds, while Everett takes on the complex, elongated MAX 10 airframes. As a result, Boeing has the industrial headroom needed to fulfill its multi-year backlog and finally get its production lines moving at record speed once again.

The rollout of the first 737 MAX 10 from Everett is really a significant milestone for more reasons than just the beginning of a new era for the 737 family. It also ushers in a permanent structural transformation in Boeing’s manufacturing footprint. What began in 1970 as a single-factory narrowbody setup in Renton has evolved into a multi-facility production network spanning Puget Sound. Boeing recognized that floor space, rather than worker effort, was limiting MAX 10 efficiency, so it positioned its commercial airplane division to push higher manufacturing rates with greater structural precision.

Over the coming years, the co-existence of Renton and Everett will redefine Boeing’s production dynamics. Renton remains the high-volume engine of the 737 program, while Everett provides the spatial flex capacity needed for specialized, high-capacity airframes. Once the FAA approves Everett’s production certificate and supplier wing deliveries stabilize, Boeing will possess an industrial system capable of supporting its long-term target of 52 aircraft per month.

Ultimately, the Everett North Line shows that modern aircraft manufacturing is as much about factory geometry as it is about aerodynamics. Giving the 737 MAX 10 the floor space it needs to move nose-to-tail, Boeing has cleared a path to deliver its largest narrowbody variant to global customers.

#6136. Chase Adds 10,000 Vacation Homes To The Edit In 2027—Use Your Hotel Credits, But No Points Boost

Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) cardmembers will be able to use their hotel credits at more than 10,000 vacation homes starting January 1, 2027. And Chase tells me consecutive bookings at the same home can each trigger a credit, potentially letting someone use the personal card’s full $500 annual allowance on one trip. There’s a significant limitation, though: Points Boost won’t apply to these homes at launch. The Edit name also won’t bring breakfast or upgrades. The home benefits require four nights, while the statement credit only requires two. Two Night Bookings Qualify For Credits, And Back-To-Back Bookings Are Allowed Chase already added Plum Guide to Chase Travel in April. The January expansion moves a selection of those homes into The Edit, alongside more than 1,500 hotels and resorts. The annual Edit statement credits available for bookings made in 2027 is: Chase Sapphire Reserve® and J.P. Morgan Reserve: up to $500, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business: up to $1,000, with a maximum of $250 per eligible booking. The business card’s increase to $1,000 was announced in September. And Chase confirms that a prepaid two- or three-night home booking qualifies for the statement credit, even though it receives none of the vacation home benefits because those require a minimum four night stay (and individual properties can impose longer minimum stays). Bookings will be instantly confirmed, and full prepayment is required for The Edit benefits. I also asked whether you could book consecutive reservations at the same property. A Chase spokesperson tells me: Yes. Cardmembers can book back-to-back stays at the same property. Each eligible booking of two or more prepaid nights can qualify for the annual Edit statement credit, subject to the annual credit limit. For on-property benefits, however, consecutive reservations at the same property are considered a single stay, so only the first eligible stay will receive The Edit benefits. Two eligible two-night reservations could use both $250 credits from a personal Reserve card on a single four-night trip, or book a two-night and four-night reservation for a six night trip to use both credits and receive The Edit benefits on the stay. But you only get benefits on one four-night mininum stay. Back-to-back bookings aren’t entitled to benefits twice even if each reservation is for four nights. Chase commits to matching Plum Guide’s pricing. Asked about the identical home, dates and occupancy, the spokesperson replied: Yes. For the same home, dates and occupancy, the total price and cancellation policy offered through Chase Travel will match those available through Plum Guide. The credit shouldn’t get eaten up by a higher price than Plum Guide charges for the same reservation. Chase says it worked with Plum Guide to select homes based on design, guest ratings and distinctive features. Plum Guide does the vetting, not Chase. Chase isn’t sharing representative homes or pricing examples yet, so we can’t compare actual bookings. No Points Boost At Launch I’d hoped putting these homes into The Edit would create better opportunities to redeem Ultimate Rewards points. I asked and was told: No. Points Boost will not be applicable to vacation homes in The Edit at launch. Cardmembers can still redeem points, as they already can for Plum Guide through Chase Travel. But joining The Edit won’t bring better redemption value. This follows American Express adding Airbnb Luxe to its Platinum lodging credit. Eligible prepaid Luxe stays of at least two nights can use up to $300 each half-year, and a qualifying booking opens access to a separate $250 annual Airbnb Experiences credit. Amex doesn’t allow Pay with Points for those Airbnb bookings. Chase does allow points, but without Points Boost that’s not useful. It’s really just a new way to use the $250 statement credits. Four Nights Gets A $150 Credit, But No Breakfast Or Upgrades I asked Chase to confirm exactly which hotel benefits would carry over. At launch in January, the vacation-home benefits will include a $150 in-stay credit, plus early check-in and late checkout when available. Breakfast, room upgrades and welcome amenities are not part of the vacation-home benefit package. The benefits have been designed specifically around the vacation-home experience and how travelers use these properties. I’ve found The Edit credits useful on two-night hotel stays priced below $300 per night, with breakfast and a $100 property credit included. The home package adds $50 to the service credit but requires at least four nights, and drops breakfast and upgrades. Not surprising – there’s little to upgrade into when you’re booking a unit of one. And there’s nobody to make you breakfast! The $150 credit actually sounds better than just private chefs and massages highlighted in the announcement. Here’s what guests can buy and whether they’ll see prices before booking: Cardmembers will be able to see the eligible services available for a vacation home on the Chase Travel booking page before booking. Offerings vary by property and can include services such as fridge stocking, babysitting and dry cleaning. Pricing will depend on the specific service and request and will not be displayed at booking, however cardmembers can work with Reserve Travel Designers to understand available options and obtain pricing estimates for the services they are interested in. Fridge stocking and babysitting are things a family might actually buy. But the booking page won’t show how much the credit buys. After booking, guests will receive an email explaining how to use the credit. Reserve Travel Designers can help arrange services, and Chase recommends doing so at least 72 hours in advance. Early check-in and late checkout don’t actually seem like a Chase value add. A hotel has a pool of rooms. A house with guests leaving that morning needs to be cleaned before the next guests arrive. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours. Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. If another group is coming that afternoon, there isn’t much room for a late departure. So late checkout is either available or not, based on whether other reservations butt up against yours. Plum Guide already accommodates early check-in and late check-out requests subject to availability, albeit sometimes with fees. I asked whether Chase would waive those charges, require hosts to grant requests when possible, prioritize cleaning or offer earlier confirmation. Early check-in and late checkout are benefits offered to eligible vacation-home stays through The Edit, but both remain subject to availability and cannot be guaranteed in advance. We Don’t Know Yet If We Can Double Dip With Loyalty Credit Chase’s “The Edit” bookings earn hotel loyalty program points and elite stay credit, and receive elite benefits. What’s interesting is that Plum Guide properties earn 5% of eligible spending, excluding taxes, in GHA DISCOVERY Dollars. GHA Discovery is effectively the loyalty program for Plum GUide. (There’s no elite status earning bonus, all members earn the same, and these dollars expire after 12 months and can be spent at GHA hotels, but not on Plum Guide rentals). Direct bookings also earn qualifying nights, spend and brand credit toward status, with Plum Guide counting as one GHA brand. The partnership terms exclude non-Plum Guide booking channels. So it wasn’t clear to me whether Chase’s The Edit would count as a third party booking or not? They don’t for hotels. Chase responded that they “don’t have information to share on this yet.” It would be a great stack, though! For a Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardmember with unused Edit credits, the ability to apply several to one vacation home trip at Plum Guide’s pricing is the strongest part of this. I already use my hotel credits, so moving them to a home means giving up those hotel uses. Of course you can always identify a property, search for the owner or management company and book direct – often for less. Chase already added Plum Guide to Chase Travel in April. The January expansion moves a selection of those homes into The Edit, alongside more than 1,500 hotels and resorts.

The annual Edit statement credits available for bookings made in 2027 is:

The business card’s increase to $1,000 was announced in September. And Chase confirms that a prepaid two- or three-night home booking qualifies for the statement credit, even though it receives none of the vacation home benefits because those require a minimum four night stay (and individual properties can impose longer minimum stays). Bookings will be instantly confirmed, and full prepayment is required for The Edit benefits.

I also asked whether you could book consecutive reservations at the same property. A Chase spokesperson tells me:

Yes. Cardmembers can book back-to-back stays at the same property. Each eligible booking of two or more prepaid nights can qualify for the annual Edit statement credit, subject to the annual credit limit. For on-property benefits, however, consecutive reservations at the same property are considered a single stay, so only the first eligible stay will receive The Edit benefits.

Two eligible two-night reservations could use both $250 credits from a personal Reserve card on a single four-night trip, or book a two-night and four-night reservation for a six night trip to use both credits and receive The Edit benefits on the stay.

But you only get benefits on one four-night mininum stay. Back-to-back bookings aren’t entitled to benefits twice even if each reservation is for four nights.

Chase commits to matching Plum Guide’s pricing. Asked about the identical home, dates and occupancy, the spokesperson replied:

Yes. For the same home, dates and occupancy, the total price and cancellation policy offered through Chase Travel will match those available through Plum Guide.

The credit shouldn’t get eaten up by a higher price than Plum Guide charges for the same reservation. Chase says it worked with Plum Guide to select homes based on design, guest ratings and distinctive features. Plum Guide does the vetting, not Chase. Chase isn’t sharing representative homes or pricing examples yet, so we can’t compare actual bookings.

#6135. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?
