How Sophr is still CEO just shows you how the LH board and management is clueless. Its one bad decision after another and they keep the guy on...

Nah they just knew all the premium travelers were going to spend their money elsewhere. Smart. :D

......yet still there is no accountability. Now that AA seem to have finally seen the light, LH must be out on their own as the most incompetant managemnt for a major airline

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.

Lufthansa is not alone. SQ is also always playing catch-up.

The World of Hyatt personal and business credit cards can help you save money and enjoy valuable perks on your next Hyatt stay.

Right now, the personal card is offering its most lucrative bonus since February, making now a good time to apply.

The World of Hyatt program is known for offering some of the best redemption rates in the industry, along with a diverse portfolio of distinctive hotel brands.

Let's dive into these offers and help you decide whether to apply.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (see rates and fees) is currently offering new cardholders four free nights (at Category 1-4 Hyatt hotels) after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Per Hyatt's award chart, Category 1 Hyatt hotels can cost as few as 3,000 points per night, while Category 4 properties can cost as many as 25,000 points per night.

That means the value of this welcome offer depends on how you redeem the free nights. If you use all four certificates at Category 4 properties that would otherwise cost 25,000 points per night, you'd "use" 100,000 points. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that puts the bonus's potential value at up to $1,650.

While this isn't the strongest welcome offer we've seen in the card's history, it does meet our threshold for when to apply.

Why we like it: This card has valuable ongoing perks, the best of which is an annual free night certificate at a Category 1-4 Hyatt property, which you’ll receive after every account anniversary. You’ll also get a second free night after spending $15,000 in a calendar year.

Here are some ideas to maximize your World of Hyatt points.

To learn more, read our full review of the World of Hyatt card.

With the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (see ), new cardholders can currently earn 70,000 bonus points after spending $7,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on our valuations, this bonus is worth $1,155. This isn't the highest offer we've seen on the card, but it meets our criteria for applying (when at least 65,000 points are on offer).

Cardholders also earn 2 points per dollar spent in their top three spending categories each quarter with no spending cap. These categories include:

The points-earning rates will be adjusted automatically on the categories where you spend the most each quarter, so there’s no need to select your preferred categories.

Beyond the bonus categories, you'll earn 1 point per dollar spent on all purchases.

Why we like it: Hyatt loyalists who own a business can find value in the card’s up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year (spend $50 and receive a $50 statement credit, up to two times) and the ability to gift Discoverist status to up to five employees.

You’ll also earn five tier-qualifying nights for every $10,000 you spend on the card in a calendar year.

Both the World of Hyatt personal and business cards offer plenty of benefits for Hyatt loyalists. In fact, the Hyatt personal card ranks among the top picks of TPG staffers.

Having either card automatically grants you Discoverist status, which includes benefits such as late checkout, preferred rooms and a 10% points bonus on eligible purchases. Spending on either card can also earn you additional elite-qualifying nights.

You’ll also enjoy several travel protections, such as baggage delay insurance, lost luggage reimbursement and trip interruption and cancellation insurance.

Plus, the personal card comes with a free night certificate every anniversary year (valid at Category 1-4 properties), which is extremely valuable for any Hyatt enthusiast.

#6133. British Airways Kept Losing Consumer Complaints—So They Found A New Arbitrator

British Airways is dropping the independent complaints service through which passengers won £5 million in a year. Its replacement has a record of much lower passenger success rates. They appear to be shopping for a more accommodating referee, putting their thumb on the scales by choosing who hears complaints against them. On August 24, 2016, I asked this exact question: Will the Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution get to keep the British Airways contract if they rule against BA too frequently? Ten years later, British Airways isn’t renewing that contract. They’re moving to AviationADR, the other major U.K. provider. And Head for Points reports that losing its biggest airline customer means CEDR is leaving aviation altogether. British Airways confirmed the switch, describing it as a contract renewal decision and saying: British Airways has selected AviationADR as the independent alternative dispute resolution body to resolve disputes between customers and the airline. British Airways Wasn’t Winning Enough Cases The Civil Aviation Authority’s figures for April 2025 through March 2026 show: British Airways settled 4,414 complaints before a decision. CEDR ruled for passengers in 1,619 cases and for British Airways in 2,234. Settlements and decisions together produced £5,001,728 in passenger awards. That’s a 73% passenger success rate including settlements. Passengers had already gone through the airline’s complaint process, then had to escalate to an outside body before getting an offer which means that BA was improperly rejecting complaints. Most passengers just give up at that point. EasyJet Already Made This Switch easyJet made the move from CEDR to AviationADR after CEDR upheld passenger complaints 79% of the time over its final six quarters with with the airline, and just 29% in the following six quarters with AviationADR. AviationADR’s explanation was that airlines had improved their handling of claims, including using major law firms to filter cases before escalation. Valid claims were being paid earlier, leaving weaker ones for adjudication. And that just happened to coincide with the switch. Ok sure. Airlines Get Advance Access To Decisions Against Them A February 2026 review commissioned by the Civil Aviation Authority described AviationADR giving airlines decisions in passengers’ favor one week before the passengers received them, ostensibly to ‘prepare payment’. During that time, airlines could raise legal challenges, although AviationADR said its legal review panel hadn’t needed to convene for years. The reviewer warned this advance access “may create an impression of bias in favour of the aviation body” and recommended ending it, along with airline challenges to individual binding decisions. CEDR generally uses legally qualified adjudicators. AviationADR doesn’t require legal qualifications and provides more extensive initial training. The commercial pressure to retain the contract paid for by one side is huge, and the fact that BA made this switch underscores what the new adjudicator has to do to keep its revenue stream. Relatedly, Ryanair left AviationADR in 2018 after adverse decisions over staff strikes, then rejoined in 2021 after rules changes. AviationADR says its decisions are independent and based on the evidence and law. Its service is free to the consumer, and passengers who reject a decision can still go to court. Head for Points reports that CEDR will stop accepting new aviation cases on December 31. The Civil Aviation Authority says it’s working with AviationADR on the capacity needed to handle the additional caseload. While some at View from the Right Wing will clutch pearls over businesses having to pay fines to consumers when they fail, the rest of us, who actually fly, and have to deal with the inconvenience, real costs, and disruption caused by airlines that excessively delay and cancel flights under their control.

We’re overdue for meaningful air passenger rights legislation in the US, akin to UK and EU laws like 261 with a real, enforceable duty of care and compensation where appropriate, not mere partial refunds and silly games. So, no, it’s not a third party processor issue here. It’s the incentive structure; thankfully, their laws have teeth.

BA is just being cheap, like usual; operate a reliable airline, or pay up.

Exhibit A for why arbitration needs to be controlled. Looks good on the surface, fails badly when one side gets to choose whoever gives the most favorable results.

So basically BA doesn’t want customers to have fair arbitration. I’m a bit surprised that whatever body governs UK aviation is fine with this.

This is just so typical of BA and the Walsh legacy: rather than make badly needed improvements that would keep the airline from losing arbitration cases they dump the company that recognizes that BA is frequently wrong.

The credit card companies in the US set up a phony baloney arb service, the National Arbitration Forum, to resolve the problem of fair arbiters; the newly elected Senator from MN when AG uncovered the scheme.

#6132. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

And I have to say, the touchpad for operating the seat and lights was not very intuitive to me and I like to think I'm pretty savvy with those things. And apparently for some of the new planes, the wired headphone jack didn't work at my seat (taped over). The gate agent in SIN and flight attendant were very proactive in telling me the bluetooth worked (once I figured out how to pair it) and the gate agent gave me 7500 miles as compensation. Food was decent, didn't blow me away, but very good, even the chicken. The crew also locked the exterior windows to keep it dark. Overall, the seat is quite comfortable and the flight crew was excellent (though the purser seemed stretched and if you weren't GS or 1K, I wasn't on his radar). Would be nice if purser didn't exclude regular pax in biz when thanking them for flying and loyalty.

#6131. 5 Airlines Flying The Airbus A321XLR With Lie-Flat Business Class Seats

The Airbus A321XLR is an aircraft designed for thin long-haul routes. By bringing narrowbody economics to intercontinental services, the aircraft promises to open up new city pairs that couldn't be served economically by widebodies. The aircraft is small, and it sips fuel in comparison to even a modern Boeing 787 or Airbus A350, let alone an A330 or 777.

It has already proven reasonably popular for its niche, but even though the economics are great for airlines, passengers still want widebody comfort. A321XLR operators, as well as operators of the older A321LR, are now widely installing lie-flat business class seats on these planes.

While these are narrowbody-optimized models with significant differences from those used on widebodies, they still provide passengers with a lie-flat seat, while newer models offer direct aisle access by using either a herringbone or reverse herringbone layout. As the A321XLR is introduced by more airlines, these are the five carriers with the largest lie-flat business class cabins on this aircraft type.

Iberia was the global launch operator of the A321XLR, having operated the type's first commercial flight on November 6, 2024, from Madrid to Paris, as well as its first long-haul flight from Madrid to Boston on November 14. The airline now operates eight A321XLRs, with no more currently remaining on order.

Iberia uses the type to serve destinations such as Toronto, Boston, New York, Washington-Dulles, Santo Domingo, San Juan, Recife, and Fortaleza. Iberia installs 182 seats on the A321XLR, which is a relatively high number for this aircraft. 14 of these are business class seats, which are based on the Thompson VantageSOLO.

This is a herringbone seat model optimized for narrowbodies, and was first introduced by JetBlue in 2021 on the A321neo as its new Mint Suites. Unlike JetBlue, however, Iberia did not option sliding doors, nor did it opt for the front row 'business class plus' option that JetBlue did. Air Canada also operates the A321XLR with 14 business class seats, and its examples also feature 182 seats in total.

However, Iberia gets the bump over Air Canada in this list because it operates more examples, with Air Canada currently flying five A321XLRs to Iberia's eight. With that being said, Air Canada holds orders for 30 XLRs in total, which means that it will eventually operate substantially more A321XLRs. It will, in fact, be one of the larger A321XLR operators in the world.

Aer Lingus was originally set to be the worldwide launch operator for the A321XLR, but a dispute with parent company IAG over pilot pay led the holding company to allocate the first A321XLR to Iberia instead. However, Aer Lingus would soon begin receiving its own XLRs, and the Irish flag carrier now operates six examples.

These planes complement the airline's existing fleet of eight A321LRs, giving it a total fleet of 14 long-range A321neos with lie-flat seats. Aer Lingus installs 184 seats on the A321XLR, including 16 business class seats. Unlike Iberia, the carrier uses the Thompson Vantage, a staggered seat model featuring three rows configured four-abreast and two rows containing 'throne seats'.

This seat is ultimately far from cutting-edge, as it debuted in the late 2000s and it doesn't even offer direct aisle access. However, the seat remains quite space-efficient, and Aer Lingus also uses it on its A330 fleet in addition to the A321s. The A321XLR is ultimately an improved, more capable A321neo, and Aer Lingus already operates eight A321LRs.

Aer Lingus's A321LRs have the same configuration as the XLRs, while also using the same exact business class seats. The main way to tell the two apart on the inside is the fact that the XLRs feature the Airbus Airspace cabins, while also featuring newer, larger screens. In addition, Aer Lingus installs newer Recaro seats on the A321XLR, while the A321LRs are equipped with the Collins Aerospace Meridian.

Air Canada's Airbus A321XLR skips Premium Economy entirely, opting for 14 business suites and 36 extra-legroom seats on thinner transatlantic routes.

United Airlines is the newest operator on this list, having taken delivery of its first A321XLR in May 2026. The carrier now operates three examples, and it has another 47 on the way. These planes are currently only flying from Washington-Dulles to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

However, they will eventually fully replace United's Boeing 757 operation across the Atlantic, serving thin destinations in Europe with far greater efficiency than what the 757 could do, while also featuring all-new interiors. These aircraft are equipped with 20 Polaris suites, based on the Elevate Altitude. This is a herringbone seat installed at a notably high 49-degree angle.

This represents the first time that an Elevate seat has been put into service on an Airbus aircraft. United will use the A321XLR to replace its 757s on transatlantic services, but the two aircraft are configured very differently. United's 757s feature 16 business class seats and 160 economy seats.

Meanwhile, the A321XLRs have four additional Polaris suites, 42 fewer economy seats, and a Premium Plus cabin consisting of 12 seats. While the A321XLR is currently only operating domestic services for United Airlines, it will begin flying the aircraft transatlantic in December, initially deploying it from Washington-Dulles to Amsterdam and Dublin.

American Airlines was the US launch operator of the A321XLR, having taken its first XLR in July 2025. For American, the A321XLR serves a similar role as it does for United, but the airline is using its current fleet of 11 A321XLRs to serve both transatlantic and transcontinental routes. United's deployment of the A321XLR on transcontinental services is temporary until the type begins long-haul flights.

However, this is American's long-term strategy for its 40 A321XLRs. Just like United, American Airlines installs 20 Flagship suites on the A321XLR, although American gets the bump in this list as it has more examples. American selected the Collins Aerospace Aurora, a herringbone seat model very similar to the Thompson VantageSOLO and Elevate Altitude.

American Airlines Future Lie-Flat Narrowbody Fleet

United Airlines Future Lie-Flat Narrowbody Fleet

Both airlines have opted to install 20 business class seats, along with 12 premium economy seats. The main difference is that American sells five extra economy seats on its A321XLRs, as United has installed a snack bar at the rear of the cabin, which takes up a set of three seats, while it has also blocked two exit-row seats to bring the total seat count down to 150.

The next-generation narrowbody has an exciting future ahead of it.

Saudia has ordered 15 A321XLRs in total, and took delivery of its first example in May 2026. The airline now already has five A321XLRs in its fleet, and they're currently being used to serve thinner routes to the Maldives, Mauritius, and Europe out of the carrier's hubs in Jeddah and Riyadh.

Saudia was the first customer in the Middle East to take delivery of the A321XLR, and it expects to have all 15 aircraft on property by the end of 2027. The airline installs the largest business class cabin on the A321XLR of any operator, equipping these planes with 24 business class seats. It uses the Thompson VantageSOLO, similar to Iberia.

Current Narrowbody Lie-Flat Seat Models Being Used By Airlines

Reverse herringbone direct aisle access lie-flat

Saudi Arabia is looking to attract more visitors, which it hopes to accomplish in part by expanding Saudia's operations while also starting a new full-service airline named Riyadh Air. The A321XLR plays a unique but important role in connecting the country to destinations such as Barcelona, where demand from Jeddah Airport (JED) could be low. The A321XLR enables the airline to expand its reach and relevance without committing to an expensive widebody.

#6130. Lyft Launches 8% Ride Rewards—Free With Chase DashPass, But Airport Discounts And Priority Pickup Perk Go Away

Lyft’s new membership program earns 8% back in credits on eligible rides, and customers who get DoorDash DashPass through an eligible Chase card can claim it without paying. But they’re also losing benefits like a 10% discount on scheduled airport rides and free Priority Pickup upgrades. Lyft Go launched today, replacing ordinary Lyft Pink and the old DashPass ride benefits. Existing DashPass customers have to activate it even if their Lyft and DoorDash accounts are already linked. And anyone still holding Lyft Pink All Access through Chase: you can’t keep that membership and add Go alongside it. Lyft is selling two versions of Go: Benefit   Lyft Go With DashPass   Lyft Go Core Price   $9.99/month or $96/year   $4.99/month Credits earned   8% of eligible spending   5% of eligible spending Monthly earning limit   $40   $20 Where credits can be used   Eligible Lyft rides or DoorDash orders   Eligible Lyft rides DashPass membership   Included after activation   Not included Relaxed cancellations   3 per month   3 per month Lost-item return fee waiver   Unlimited   Not included Round Up & Donate matching   100%   100% The full plan works in both directions. Pay for Go and get DashPass, which waives delivery fees and reduces service fees on eligible orders, and DashPass members claim full Go at no added cost. DoorDash purchases don’t earn the new 8% rebate but you can spend credits earned with Lyft there. Chase may now get you both complimentary memberships: Make sure your Chase DashPass benefit is activated. Go to DoorDash’s Lyft benefit page, or claim Lyft Go in the DoorDash app. Complete activation, including the confirmation in Lyft. Previously linking the accounts isn’t enough. The complimentary membership lasts while you retain the qualifying membership and keep the accounts linked. And an eligible ride can now earn four layers of rewards: Lyft Go credits: 8% of eligible spending, up to $40 per month. Linked loyalty program points: for example, 2 Bilt points per eligible dollar when Bilt is your selected partner. Credit card rewards: for example, 5 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar when you pay with an eligible Sapphire card. Card-linked offers: an activated offer for Lyft on the card you use, such as a targeted Chase Offer or SimplyMiles offer when available. You choose one linked loyalty points partner such as Bilt, Alaska Airlines or United. $100 of fare eligible for all three programs, paid with an eligible Sapphire card and credited to Bilt, can earn $8 in Go credits, 200 Bilt points and 500 Chase points – plus whatever card-linked offer applies. Sapphire Reserve and J.P. Morgan Reserve also have their separate $10 monthly Lyft ride credit. Sadly though existing DashPass discounts are going away. I’ve written about combining those discounts with Lyft’s other rewards. The old arrangement gave linked DashPass members: 5% off eligible on-demand rides. 10% off scheduled airport rides. A combined limit of four discounted rides per month. Two free Priority Pickup upgrades monthly. Under DoorDash’s transition terms, those benefits end at 11:59 p.m. Pacific on November 11, or when you activate Go, whichever comes first. So a frequent ordinary ride customer can gain – 8% back instead of 5% off, with earning continuing beyond four rides. A customer using the scheduled airport discount gets a lower percentage, has to spend the savings later, and loses the pickup upgrades. Here’s how the 8% works: Base fare only. Taxes, fees, tolls, tips, donations and amounts covered by coupons, discounts or earned credits don’t earn. 60-day expiration. You have to select credits to use them; they aren’t automatically applied. A monthly cap. Full Go stops earning after $500 in eligible spending. Core stops after $400. Membership dependence. Pausing blocks redemption while expiration continues. Once your membership ends, unused credits become unavailable and can be forfeited. No conversion of old balances. Purchased Lyft Cash, gift cards and unrelated promotional credits don’t become usable on DoorDash. Business profile rides and shared rides don’t earn. Eligible bike and scooter rides do, but Boston and Washington, D.C. bike and scooter rides are excluded. Lyft includes Wait & Save in its announcement, although DoorDash’s launch FAQ contradicts that. DoorDash redemption has exclusions: non-DashPass-eligible orders, DoubleDash, prescriptions, gift cards and group orders. Then there’s the cancellation benefit: Lyft requires you to rebook within 15 minutes and complete the replacement ride. They charge the cancellation fee, then give it back as a ride credit. These aren’t three unconditional free cancellations. Pink All Access members can continue but that’s now closed to new members, you can only hold one membership at a time, and once you leave All Access, you can’t rejoin. Switching to Go requires contacting support. If there’s anyone with Chase DashPass actually paying separately for ordinary Pink that’s a win. So a frequent ordinary ride customer can gain – 8% back instead of 5% off, with earning continuing beyond four rides. A customer using the scheduled airport discount gets a lower percentage, has to spend the savings later, and loses the pickup upgrades. Here’s how the 8% works:

Business profile rides and shared rides don’t earn. Eligible bike and scooter rides do, but Boston and Washington, D.C. bike and scooter rides are excluded. Then there’s the cancellation benefit: Lyft requires you to rebook within 15 minutes and complete the replacement ride. They charge the cancellation fee, then give it back as a ride credit. These aren’t three unconditional free cancellations.

Interesting because Chase, Lyft, DoorDash, none of them sent us cardmembers and account holders any details on any of this. How Gary got advanced notice is cool, but, like, shouldn’t we, the actual users, get a heads-up, too? Sheesh.

Wonder how this impacts the Citibike benefits via Lyft. That free 45 minutes on non-ebikes can be useful.

(Ironically, got their email mere minutes after writing that comment… still…)

Losing priority pickup is going to hurt. On my last ride that saved me $17, though that was one of my most expensive rides. It seems to usually be around $9 which is still a large percentage add-on.

Yeah, what @nycityny said – the priority pickup made a real difference. These 8% credits are nice but don’t move the needle for me. Now it’s just a price war between Uber and Lyft whereas before Lyft had an edge with priority pickup.

Also Grubhub+ lost Amazon Prime today, and sent out an email extending GH+ membership through 12/2027. Amazon Prime now partners with Uber Eats and got an email about that today as well.

@Peter — All of these services are unnecessary. If Ben will publish it, time for the $3 MTA special!

This isn’t about Chase. T-Mobile also offers Dashpass for free, hence the Lyft benefit. Since T-Mobile offers it, it’s hardly an exclusive Chase benefit. Priority Pickup benefits will be missed, especially when taking a ride from an airport.

I’ve rarely found the scheduled fares to be reasonable (compared to booking on demand), but at least it was a savings if you felt obligated to book one in advance because few drivers may be available. Priority Pickup is a big loss. These would also often be an upgrade from a base vehicle.

#6129. Alaska Atmos Rewards Summit Card Bonus: 100K Points & 25K-Point Global Companion Award

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card is currently offering its best-ever publicly available welcome bonus, which can earn you 100,000 Atmos Rewards points plus a 25K-point Global Companion Award (which I consider to be worth face value).

We only saw this bonus return a couple of weeks ago, and I’d like to provide an update, as I’ve received word that this offer is ending soon (though I don’t have an exact date to share). Obviously this was a very short term limited time offer, so you’ll want to apply ASAP, if interested.

This is one of the most lucrative airline credit cards on the market — it’s a card that I have, and it’s also one that I spend a lot of money on. If you don’t yet have the card, you really can’t go wrong with this, and this is the time to apply.

Link: Learn about the Atmos Rewards Summit Card bonus offer

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome bonus that consists of 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award. To qualify, you need to spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.5 cents each. I consider the offer to be worth 125,000 points, putting the value of this at a staggering $1,875. Even if you’re not convinced on the long term value proposition of the card, I absolutely think it’s worth giving a try, given all the uses of Atmos Rewards points.

If you’re interested in applying for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, the good news is that the application restrictions are pretty limited. Specifically, you are eligible for this card if you have any of the other Atmos Rewards cards, whether personal or business. So you’re eligible for this card even if you have the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more) or Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card (learn more).

Personally, I find Bank of America to be one of the most straightforward and easier card issuers to get approvals from, though that’s anecdotal, and I’ve had good luck with these cards.

Read my guide to getting approved for Atmos Rewards cards.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card has a $395 annual fee, though it has to be one of the most interesting and rewarding airline credit cards we’ve ever seen. As I see it, here are the main reasons to consider getting this card, beyond the welcome bonus:

Read a detailed review of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is currently offering its best-ever publicly available welcome offer that can earn you 100,000 Atmos Rewards bonus points, and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award. It’s great to see a return of the best-ever offer on the card, so I absolutely think this is worth applying for, if eligible, and you’ll want to act fast, as the offer is ending soon.

This card is worth getting for the offer alone, given the huge value for travel on partner airlines, even if it’s “just” for domestic flights on American. But I think the card also offers good long term value, from the annual Global Companion Award, to all the other perks. For that matter, there’s an argument to be made for spending on the card to earn oneworld status.

This is a card that I and everyone else in my family have, so I would seriously recommend considering it, if you haven’t applied already.

Anyone plan to pick up the Atmos Rewards Summit Card with this great offer?

#6128. Former American Airlines CEO Explains How Carriers Use Wall Street Analysts To Pressure Rivals To Stop Growing

Doug Parker says airline executives don’t collude by signaling to competitors. However, the former American Airlines CEO explains how executives use Wall Street analysts to pressure other airlines over decisions they don’t like or to back off from competition. On this week’s Airlines Confidential, Parker rejects suggestions of signaling: it “absolutely, positively does not happen.” Yet earlier, describing how airlines enlist analysts, he says they’ll put it to an analyst: “ask them why they’re doing this.” Airlines don’t need a secret meeting where everyone agrees to raise fares. They have fare filings that competitors watch, earnings calls that competitors listen to, and analysts who cover several airlines and can make life uncomfortable for the one that’s adding seats. Whether it violates antitrust law depends on the particulars, but executives certainly do try to send signals to other airlines. American Paid $45 Million To Settle A Capacity Collusion Case While Parker was CEO, American agreed in 2018 to pay $45 million to settle a private antitrust class action. Passengers alleged that major airlines coordinated capacity restraint to increase fares. American also agreed to cooperate with plaintiffs pursuing the remaining defendants. American denied wrongdoing, but paid a very real amount to resolve exactly the sort of allegation he suggests is almost unimaginable. Parker Even Emailed Delta’s CEO Directly To Collude The Justice Department’s 2013 complaint challenging the American–US Airways merger described a 2010 email exchange about a Delta’s aggressive promotion and expansion. Parker, then running US Airways, complained internally about the effect on everyone’s profitability, portrayed Delta as foolish to Wall Street, and forwarded the chain to CEO Richard Anderson. Anderson sent it on to his general counsel. I’ve written about this before. It’s particularly striking because the old email chain and the new podcast describe the same intermediary: Wall Street. Airlines Can Send A Message Without Sending An Email Airlines publish fares through the Airline Tariff Publishing Company. That lets travel sellers distribute prices, and lets competing airlines see and respond to them. Matching a competitor’s fare isn’t, by itself, evidence of an agreement. But pricing departments know how to use the system to get each other’s attention. Fare basis codes. These combinations of letters and numbers identify fares and their rules. I’ve covered the less subtle examples, including discount fares in a competitor’s home market with codes ending in “FU.” That isn’t information a passenger needs to choose a ticket. Economist Severin Borenstein’s account of the government’s earlier fare-filing case explains how codes and footnotes could connect retaliatory fares across markets. Retaliation somewhere else. In the American–JetBlue litigation, the government’s trial filing described JetBlue responding to an American $139 Boston–Los Angeles fare with $139 fares on five routes involving American hubs. The matching amount helped make the connection obvious. Flash fares. The same filing, citing testimony and internal records, described JetBlue planning to flash American over $44 Boston–Philadelphia pricing in February 2020. A fare filing could be used to draw the other airline’s attention to a pricing dispute. Scott Kirby Has Been Doing This In Chicago I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive. The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened. An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers. Bob Crandall Was Less Subtle American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed: Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning. Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed. Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law). That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. Airlines publish fares through the Airline Tariff Publishing Company. That lets travel sellers distribute prices, and lets competing airlines see and respond to them. Matching a competitor’s fare isn’t, by itself, evidence of an agreement. But pricing departments know how to use the system to get each other’s attention.

Fare basis codes. These combinations of letters and numbers identify fares and their rules. I’ve covered the less subtle examples, including discount fares in a competitor’s home market with codes ending in “FU.” That isn’t information a passenger needs to choose a ticket. Economist Severin Borenstein’s account of the government’s earlier fare-filing case explains how codes and footnotes could connect retaliatory fares across markets.

Retaliation somewhere else. In the American–JetBlue litigation, the government’s trial filing described JetBlue responding to an American $139 Boston–Los Angeles fare with $139 fares on five routes involving American hubs. The matching amount helped make the connection obvious.

Flash fares. The same filing, citing testimony and internal records, described JetBlue planning to flash American over $44 Boston–Philadelphia pricing in February 2020. A fare filing could be used to draw the other airline’s attention to a pricing dispute.

I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive. The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened. An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers. Bob Crandall Was Less Subtle American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed: Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning. Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed. Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law). That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive.

The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened.

An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers.

American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed: Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning.

American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed:

Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning.

Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed.

Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law).

That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call.

#6127. Amex Platinum Card Review: Benefits & Credits That Easily Justify The Fee

While premium cards are incredibly popular nowadays, this is really a market that Amex started, with the American Express Platinum Card®. It takes some effort to maximize the card’s perks, but if you’re willing to put in the time, the value is potentially incredible.

This is my in-depth Amex Platinum Card review, so let me talk about the card’s value proposition, and the perks that make the Amex Platinum worthwhile. This is a card you should get for the rich benefits that it offers, including the lounge access, credits, and elite status, and not necessarily a card you should spend a lot of money on under normal circumstances, since there are more rewarding cards for that.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

Before I get into my full Amex Platinum Card review, I want to go over the card’s key details at a glance. The card has such a long list of statement credits that it’s impossible to cover those briefly, so keep reading below to see those, as they could be worth up to thousands of dollars annually. To keep the list to non-statement credit details, here’s what you can expect:

I also put together my pros and cons of the Amex Platinum Card:

The Amex Platinum Card potentially has a huge welcome offer, though the card also has a high annual fee. So let’s cover all those details first, including card eligibility, since these are major factors cardmembers consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Platinum Card currently has the following lucrative welcome bonus offer: You may be eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $12,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer, so you’ll want to start the application, and then you’ll see what kind of an offer is available to you.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, so depending on the offer you’re eligible for, this could be worth almost $3,000 in value. That’s pretty stellar, especially for a card that offers so much ongoing value after your first year.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card in the past (so the card has a “once in a lifetime” rule). If you’ve had the card in the past you’re still eligible to be approved, you just won’t get the bonus.

Note that this is a hybrid card and not a credit card, meaning that having this card won’t count toward Amex’s limit of five credit cards per person. Make sure you consider all of Amex’s standard application restrictions before applying.

Eligibility for this card is otherwise unrelated to having any other type of card that’s not an Amex Platinum, so lots of people should be eligible for the offer.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee. Even among premium cards, this is among the highest annual fees out there, though for many people, the perks will more than offset the fee.

If you want to add authorized users to the card, you’ll pay $195 each (Rates & Fees). Fortunately there are some solid perks for authorized users, including lounge access, so some people might find that adding them is worthwhile.

As you’d expect of a premium travel card, the Amex Platinum has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees). This means you can use it abroad without racking up fees, though it’s not usually the best card for maximizing everyday spending on categories like dining.

Personally, I think the Amex Platinum Card is worth having for the benefits it offers, though it’s not a card that I think is worth spending much money on, with limited exceptions.

Some other Amex cards offer big bonus categories. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x Membership Rewards points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 of spending per calendar year, and then 1x points), which is extremely lucrative.

Unfortunately, the Amex Platinum Card isn’t as generous in that regard. However, there are still some useful bonus categories…

The best bonus category on the Amex Platinum Card is 5x points on airfare purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of flight purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points). This is spectacular, and it makes it the best card for airfare purchases, in my opinion.

Officially booking through online travel agencies (except amextravel.com) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice it may still sometimes code for 5x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them.

I value Membership Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, so to me, that’s the equivalent of an 8.5% return on airfare spending, which is incredible.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

The exception is Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, where prepaid reservations earn 5x points. That can be a good deal because of the perks you get, and also because you still earn points with your preferred hotel loyalty program. You can also combine this with the card’s annual hotel credit to really maximize value. I’ll talk more about that in a bit.

The above are the only bonus categories — otherwise, the Amex Platinum Card offers 1x points per dollar spent, which isn’t especially good. There are other cards offering 1.5x-2x points per dollar spent, so I would much rather put my spending on those cards, or on another card that’s best for everyday spending.

The Amex Platinum Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many. While I love Membership Rewards, I’d say that not everyone should be earning these points.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to the below airline partners and hotel partners.

The reason this represents such a good option is that you can get outsized value toward premium airfare, especially for travel in first and business class. These tickets are often super expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal with points.

For example, I frequently transfer my Amex Membership Rewards points to Air France-KLM, and then redeem 60,000 points for business class across the Atlantic. Best of all, there are sometimes transfer bonuses of up to 25-30%, which lowers my real “out of pocket” in terms of Amex points even further.

I’d note that while you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than one cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Platinum Card really shines when it comes to its credits, as the card potentially offers thousands of dollars in annual credits. As you can imagine, for some people this alone will more than justify the annual fee. The catch is that there are some hurdles to using all of these, so don’t consider most of these credits to be worth face value.

However, I’d argue that it’s quite easy to recoup your entire annual fee on these credits alone. So let’s take a look at what you need to know about these credits, and how you can maximize them. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits. This is a semi-annual credit, so you get a $300 credit in January through June, and a $300 credit in July through December.

This is actually a pretty easy perk to use — just book a prepaid hotel through Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® (no minimum stay) or The Hotel Collection (two night minimum stay) through American Express Travel®, and you can receive up to a $300 credit semi-annually. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

If you ask me, this perk alone can help recoup most of the card’s annual fee. So a major point in deciding whether this card makes sense is crunching the numbers as to whether you can get full value from this.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $400 per year in Resy credits, and enrollment is required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $100 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward dining at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants.

There are no hoops you have to jump through, so as long as you dine at an eligible Resy restaurant and pay with your card, you can receive the statement credit. Personally, I’d consider this benefit to be worth close to face value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in digital entertainment credits, with enrollment being required. This comes in the form of a $25 monthly statement credit on eligible purchases or subscriptions with any of the following:

I’d consider this to be quite valuable, since there’s an impressive variety of partners with which you can maximize this perk.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Lululemon credits, with enrollment being required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $75 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward purchases at Lululemon stores in the U.S. If you’re in the market for some athleisure wear, this is a great option.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Equinox credits, and enrollment is required. This comes in the form of up to $300 in statement credits each year on a digital or club membership at Equinox. If you’d otherwise pay for an Equinox membership, this is a great perk, while otherwise, it’s probably of limited value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a $300 credit when purchasing a SoulCycle bike. This credit can be used toward the purchase of a SoulCycle at-home bike, and it can be used for the purchase of up to 15 bikes per year.

You need to make the entire purchase of a bike in one transaction on your Amex Platinum Card in order to qualify for these savings. Suffice to say that this will be of limited value to most cardmembers.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $219 per year in CLEAR credits. When using your card to pay for a CLEAR membership, you’ll receive statement credits of up to $219 per calendar year. For those not familiar with CLEAR, this company can save you time at security, by allowing you to use your biometric data to skip the ID check.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in airline fee credits, which can be used toward airline incidentals and fees. The credit is offered every calendar year, so it follows a strict January 1 through December 31 calendar.

Every year you can designate on which airline you want to receive the credit, of the following:

You can change your airline selection in January of each year. If you don’t change your selection, then you automatically keep the same airline choice as the previous year.

Unfortunately, you can’t use your credit toward the following:

Airline tickets, upgrades, mileage points purchases, mileage points transfer fees, gift cards, duty free purchases, and award tickets are not deemed to be incidental fees.

This is particularly useful for airline ticket change fees (of which there are few nowadays), baggage fees, and other costs you may incur with an airline. Personally, this is something I have no trouble maxing out.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Oura Ring credits. This is valid if you use your card to purchase an Oura Ring through ouraring.com, and enrollment is required. I’d say this is very niche, but if you’re in the market for this product, it has the potential to be valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Uber credits. The way this is broken up, you get a $15 credit per month, and then in December, you get a total of $35 in credits. You can use this either for rides with Uber in the US, or for food with Uber Eats in the US.

To activate this benefit, you need to enter your Amex Platinum Card card number on your Uber account, and then you should see the benefit unlocked. You’ll see an amount added to your Uber Cash balance every month, and the discount will automatically be applied to the first eligible ride or food delivery.

An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $120 in statement credits each calendar year after purchasing an auto-renewing Uber One membership with the card. This is separate from the card’s $200 annual Uber Cash benefit.

An Uber One membership offers all kinds of benefits for rides with Uber and deliveries with Uber Eats, so if you use the platform with any frequency, this is pretty valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $12.95 per month in credits toward a Walmart+ membership, which covers the full membership cost. Enrollment is required. (Up to $12.95 plus applicable local sales tax. Plus Ups not eligible.) With Walmart+, you can receive free deliveries on groceries or get savings at gas stations or on video streaming.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck statement credit every four years. Simply charge the membership fee to your card, and it will be automatically reimbursed. It’s worth getting Global Entry, which has a $120 application fee compared to PreCheck’s $85, because it includes TSA PreCheck membership too.

It doesn’t matter who the fee is being paid for, as long as you charge it to your eligible card.

The Amex Platinum Card offers one of the most comprehensive lounge access benefits of any card. This is called the Global Lounge Collection, and it offers access to over 1,550 airport lounges across 140 countries for eligible cardmembers. This includes proprietary Amex lounges, as well as access to lounges run by other airlines and companies.

Before I go through the details, let me mention that Lufthansa lounge access has been cut as of October 1, 2026, which is why I’m not including it in the list, though that used to be a benefit.

Amex is well known for its Centurion Lounges, and the Amex Platinum Card can get you into these lounges. These are significantly better than what you’ll find in most U.S. airline lounges, with a solid selection of hot food and cocktails.

Currently, U.S. locations include Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York JFK, New York LaGuardia, Philadelphia, Phoenix, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, with more to come. There are also Centurion Lounges in Amsterdam, Hong Kong, London, and Tokyo, among other international destinations.

You can access these lounges up to three hours before your flight’s departure (if you’re connecting, then the three-hour limit doesn’t apply). Please note that you’re only eligible to bring in guests on a complimentary basis if you spend at least $75,000 per calendar year on the card.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers access to the Delta Sky Club, with some limitations. Card members can receive access within three hours of a departing or arriving flight, and must present their card, a boarding pass showing a confirmed reservation for an eligible Delta flight, and a government-issued ID.

Eligible cards issued in the United States receive 10 visits to the Delta Sky Club each year, to be used from February 1 until January 31 of the next calendar year, with all visits within a 24-hour period counting as a single visit. It’s also possible to earn an unlimited number of visits by spending $75,000 in eligible purchases on a card account in a calendar year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Priority Pass™ membership, which gives you access to lounges around the world. You can bring up to two guests into these lounges. While these aren’t the most exciting and high quality lounges, there’s no denying that this gives you access to a comprehensive collection of lounges.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to Plaza Premium Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card, and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring one guest with you at no additional cost. This is hugely valuable, as Plaza Premium has dozens of lounges around the world, which are among the highest quality contract lounges you’ll find.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to the growing network of Escape Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring in guests.

Beyond the annual credits that potentially more than justify the annual fee, as well as an incredible lounge access program, the Amex Platinum Card also offers status with three hotel loyalty programs, status with three rental car loyalty programs, access to a program that gets you valuable hotel perks, and discounts on many premium cabin airline tickets. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Hilton Gold elite status for as long as they have the card. This status is useful, and offers the following perks:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Marriott Gold status for as long as they have the card, which offers the following perks, among other things:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World. Leading Hotels of the World is a collection of independent, luxury properties, so this offers perks at some properties that don’t otherwise participate in major global hotel groups.

This status typically requires $5,000 in annual spending at these hotels and offers perks such as five pre-arrival upgrades per year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Your status is valid as long as you remain a cardmember; you just need to enroll. This should take the pain out of renting cars and offers the following perks:

The Amex Platinum Card offers National Emerald Club Executive status. You have to enroll to take advantage of this, and it’s valid for as long as you have your card. National is my favorite rental car company, and Executive status lets you pick out your car from the lot, and skip the counter altogether.

The Amex Platinum also offers Avis Preferred Plus status. Once you enroll, you’ll get this mid-tier status level with the rental car company and qualify for complimentary upgrades when available, a 25% points bonus, and a dedicated reservation and customer service line. You also get access to a discount code that can save you up to 25% off qualifying rentals.

With the Platinum Member Airfares program (formerly known as the International Airline Program), you can save on the cost of international first class, business class, and premium economy airfare, on around two dozen airlines. This typically provides discounts even on already discounted tickets, so is a spectacular value.

If you book paid international premium cabin travel with any frequency, this could cover the card’s annual fee over and over.

With the Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® program, you can receive extra perks for stays at over 1,900 luxury hotels around the world. These benefits include the following:

Best of all, the rate is typically in line with the best available rate. Having the Amex Platinum Card gets you access to this, and if you prepay your reservation, you even earn 5x points. You can even stack this with the card’s up to $600 annual hotel credit.

The Amex Platinum Card offers several travel insurance benefits that can add extra peace of mind. You’ll want to consult the card’s benefits guide for the exact terms and any caps and exclusions, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The card also offers an extended warranty protection benefit as well as purchase, return, and cell phone protection.

Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

What benefits do authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card get? They receive most of the same perks as primary cardmembers.

This includes all the lounge access perks, access to Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, Hilton and Marriott Gold status, Leading Hotels of the World Sterling status, access to the Amex International Airline Program, additional Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credits, and more.

The main thing that authorized users aren’t getting is incremental credits, so they’re not receiving extra airline fee credits, digital entertainment credits, Uber credits, etc.

Of course there’s never going to be any “one size fits all” answer as to whether a card makes sense, since we all value perks differently. However, speaking only for myself, I’d argue that the Amex Platinum Card is rather easy to justify.

To start, let’s just take a look at the credits. Personally, I’m able to get full value out of the $600 annual hotel credit, $400 annual Resy credit, $300 annual digital entertainment credit, $200 annual airline fee credit, and $200 annual Uber credit. That’s $1,700 in value right there, and it actually doesn’t take much effort for me to maximize that.

That also says nothing of all the other perks offered by the card, from the bonus points on airfare, to the lounge access, and more. So yeah, I’m really finding this card to be pretty great. Let me emphasize that in 2027 the hotel credit will be harder to maximize, so I’ll need to assess how much value I get out of that. But even if you drop that benefit entirely, I’m still getting $1,100 in value from the other credits.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves, but I think the math works out very nicely on this product. But that’s not the case for everyone. So who should skip the Amex Platinum Card?

If it won’t be easy for you to get full value out of the card’s many travel and statement credits — or even if you just don’t want to be troubled with keeping track of so many credits to prevent leaving value on the table — the Amex Platinum may not be the card for you. Credit card fatigue is a real problem!

It’s also not a great card for everyday spending, since it doesn’t earn bonus rewards on categories like dining. I’ve written a more detailed post specifically addressing the question of whether the Amex Platinum is worth it, so I recommend checking that out.

This also brings me to the next section, which is the best Amex Platinum alternatives.

There are several premium cards to choose from nowadays, so it always makes sense to look at what the competition is offering. Let’s look at a few popular alternatives to the Amex Platinum.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) is the other premium card heavy hitter, with a slightly lower annual fee of $795. I have a full post comparing the Amex Platinum and Chase Sapphire Reserve — my verdict is that both cards are worth having, but if you can only pick one, the Sapphire Reserve is better for lazy optimizers while the Amex Platinum is better for those willing to put some real work into optimizing all the card’s benefits.

Here’s an overview of the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s standout features. It’s no slouch when it comes to perks, but its list of benefits and statement credits is considerably shorter than the Amex Platinum Card’s. Specifically:

If you take full advantage of the Amex Platinum’s main statement credits for travel and dining, it has the potential to offer more value than the Chase Sapphire Reserve. But the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s earning rates are better for maximizing everyday purchases, and you might prefer having fewer “coupon book” style benefits to keep track of.

In my opinion, the Amex Gold Card (learn more) is one of the most rewarding cards out there. At $325 (Rates & Fees), its annual fee is significantly lower than the Amex Platinum Card’s, and while it doesn’t have as many benefits, it’s a better choice for everyday spending, especially if you eat out frequently.

Here are the highlights of the Amex Gold:

The Amex Gold Card can’t beat the Platinum when it comes to travel perks, but if your main goal is earning as many Amex points as possible on your spending, it could be a more useful everyday pick.

The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another premium card with an annual fee that’s one step down from the Amex Platinum — in this case, it’s $395. I find this card to offer strong value, and it’s much simpler than the Amex Platinum Card:

The travel credit and anniversary bonus miles help justify the annual fee, and while 2x miles isn’t the highest everyday spending rate, it’s a better base than 1x points with the Amex Platinum. It’s also worth comparing Amex points with Capital One miles to see which currency you prefer before making a final decision.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee and a much longer list of credits than it used to. This isn’t a card that you should get for the return on spending it offers, but instead, it’s a card to get for all of the perks and credits that it offers.

While the $895 annual fee is obviously steep, personally I’m able to get outsized value thanks to all the credits offered, which offer significant value. And that says nothing of the bonus points on airfare, the lounge access, and more.

So even if you haven’t been able to make the math on this card work in the past, it might be time to give it another look.
