#6114. New Jersey mayor who charged at resident during council meeting concedes election loss

Video captures Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a heated council meeting before being restrained by others in attendance (Credit: Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful).

The Republican New Jersey mayor who was physically restrained while charging toward a resident during a Pemberton Township council meeting last month has conceded the mayoral race to his Democratic opponent.

Mayor Matthew Bianchini congratulated Belinda Fontanez in a Facebook post Wednesday.

"The voters of Pemberton Township have spoken, and the results are clear. I offer Belinda Fontanez my sincere congratulations on her victory. As she prepares to take on the responsibility of leading our community, she has my full support for a smooth transition," Bianchini wrote.

"I care deeply about the future of this township, and its success matters far more than any single election," he added.

Bianchini was decisively defeated, earning just over 30% of the vote, according to unofficial results.

'I BASICALLY SNAPPED': NEW JERSEY MAYOR CHARGES AT RESIDENT DURING CHAOTIC COUNCIL MEETING

Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini charged toward a resident during a heated council meeting in New Jersey before being restrained by others in attendance. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)

Bianchini, who was tapped to serve as mayor following the resignation of his predecessor, will remain in the role until the end of this year.

Video footage from an October Pemberton Township council meeting captured the mayor being restrained as he sought to advance toward resident Michael Sawka after Sawka appeared to give the middle-finger gesture at the mayor.

"I am f---in' gettin' you!" Bianchini can be heard declaring as another individual intervening in the tense situation pushed the mayor back.

"I should not have said that," Bianchini told WPVI, adding that it "was wrong" and that he is "not gonna get anybody."

NEW JERSEY PRE-K AIDE FACES 61 CHARGES, ACCUSED OF FILMING HIMSELF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING STUDENTS AT SCHOOL

"I will not apologize for my actions last night. If you attack my family, as that resident did last night, I will act," the mayor wrote on Facebook, according to the New York Post.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported the mayor's wife, who was in the audience during the meeting, noted in a Facebook comment on a Pine Barrens Tribune post, "I am not condoning my husbands [sic] actions but I will say as a parent and a spouse, I get his protection mode."

"He was saying verbally abusive comments about my wife and my daughter," Matthew Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune. "And then he did a hand gesture and looked at my daughter. To me, it appeared like he gave her the finger and that is when I stood up. He looked at me, smiled and gave me the finger and that is when I went out after him."

Bianchini and Sawka have a history of bad blood between them.

The mayor told WPVI, "I just basically snapped," noting, "I hate to put it this way, but ... it's a long time coming."

"Was it wrong? Absolutely. Was it justified? Absolutely. And I would do it again if I had to," the mayor told the outlet.

TRUMP BEDMINSTER GOLF COURSE FALLS TO DEMS AS REPUBLICANS LOSE KEY HOUSE SEAT

Video shows Pemberton Township Mayor Matthew Bianchini rushing toward a resident during a council meeting before several people intervened. (Ryan Elmore/Pine Barrens Tribune via Storyful)

Sawka, who according to WPVI denied making comments towards Bianchini's family, told the station, "All I've ever been trying to do is show that we're wasting money."

"His family, his stepdaughter, his stepson, his daughter, they all attack me online, and they just come after me just with personal attacks," Sawka told WPVI.

Bianchini alleged to the Pine Barrens Tribune that Sawka has been harassing his family "for a long time."

"Mr. Sawka has been a thorn in this township's side for a number of years," Bianchini told WPVI.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

#6112. American Airlines Adds New App Option When Flights Go Wrong—Try For An Earlier Flight Without Giving Up Your Confirmed Seat

American Airlines is making it easier to try for an earlier flight when your travel falls apart. Its app and website will now offer standby options when you’re dealing with a travel disruption while keeping your new confirmed flight. You don’t need an agent for this – it’s part of their self-service tool. The change to list yourself for free standby on an earlier flight went into effect this week. During a disruption, the flight you can confirm may be hours later than one you could actually get on if a seat opens up. You no longer need to deal with customer service to get on the standby list. . How The New Standby Option Works American calls its tool Dynamic Rebooking. Here’s the sequence described in an internal company memo: Open your disrupted trip on aa.com or in the American Airlines app. Start with Flight Options or Rebook Trip in the disruption banner. If your flight was canceled and you don’t have a replacement, confirm one first. Choose a flight with availability, then return to Flight Options to look for standby. Look for earlier nonstop flights. Up to three standby options may appear when American can’t confirm the earlier rebooking. Pick one. You can join one standby list at a time through this tool. You can remove yourself or switch to another option without contacting an employee. Keep your confirmed flight while you wait. Your itinerary changes only if you clear onto the standby flight. If you’re confirmed for an 8 p.m. flight and the app can’t confirm you on the 5 p.m., you can standby for it while remaining confirmed on that 8 p.m.. If you don’t clear, your confirmed itinerary remains intact. Employees are told, Do not cancel the customer’s confirmed flight because the customer joined standby If you do clear standby you lose the confirmation on your original flight so if you can’t make it you need to remove yourself from standby. What American Is Actually Adding For Passengers American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process. Here’s one example of where this matters: an Executive Platinum member facing a seven hour Dallas–Charlotte delay could see confirmed alternatives in the disruption tool, but couldn’t find a way to request earlier standby. Even accepting a later confirmed flight didn’t solve it. An agent eventually added them to standby and they cleared. I covered American’s new disruption banners in January, alongside rebooking, baggage tracking, and digital hotel and meal vouchers. Standby was one of the additions they said was coming. American also described the feature in its October 26 iPhone app release notes. American is trying to offer more tools for managing disruptions. That’s both a cost savings and also empowering to the passenger. A customer who feels in control of their options is going to have a better view of the airline than one who feels at the mercy of broader forces. It’s about raising net promoter scores when things go wrong, which is part of customers being willing to be repeat purchasers, purchasers of premium products, and passengers willing to pay more to fly American. That’s the strategy anyway. In contrast, in 2024, American restricted most passengers to digital standby even when its systems couldn’t handle their requests. They restored agent assistance in July 2025. Improving digital tools and offering agent help is ultimately the right direction to be moving. The Limits Customers Should Know Nothing is being taken away here, but the new tool has limits: Three displayed choices means one standby request. You aren’t joining three lists at once, and the memo only describes nonstop options. That’s not every possible way to get where you’re going. This doesn’t fix ordinary same day confirmed changes. I’ve written about American’s restrictive availability and routing rules. This update is an improvement for recovery from disruptions, but ordinary standby and confirmed flight changes are still broken at American. United introduced a broader version of this in September: disrupted customers can select up to three eligible earlier flights, and United monitors for seats and texts when one opens. Customers choose whether to switch while retaining their confirmed reservation until they decide. American’s memo allows one standby listing and says the confirmed itinerary changes when standby clears. This isn’t going to change the need for me to work with an agent, but it’s going to be helpful to a lot of people. Plus, American’s Executive Platinum members and higher can have more than one flight in their itinerary confirmed at a time during irregular operations (for instance, I book a backup in case I misconnect when my first segment is delayed – rather than having to make the call early to make the switch and give up my shot at making it, I can lock in the option of flying later while still running for my connection). And bear in mind that you can still ask for a partner flight (such as on Alaska Airlines) if your confirmed option is the next day as well. The Limits Customers Should Know Nothing is being taken away here, but the new tool has limits: Three displayed choices means one standby request. You aren’t joining three lists at once, and the memo only describes nonstop options. That’s not every possible way to get where you’re going. This doesn’t fix ordinary same day confirmed changes. I’ve written about American’s restrictive availability and routing rules. This update is an improvement for recovery from disruptions, but ordinary standby and confirmed flight changes are still broken at American. United introduced a broader version of this in September: disrupted customers can select up to three eligible earlier flights, and United monitors for seats and texts when one opens. Customers choose whether to switch while retaining their confirmed reservation until they decide. American’s memo allows one standby listing and says the confirmed itinerary changes when standby clears. This isn’t going to change the need for me to work with an agent, but it’s going to be helpful to a lot of people. Plus, American’s Executive Platinum members and higher can have more than one flight in their itinerary confirmed at a time during irregular operations (for instance, I book a backup in case I misconnect when my first segment is delayed – rather than having to make the call early to make the switch and give up my shot at making it, I can lock in the option of flying later while still running for my connection). And bear in mind that you can still ask for a partner flight (such as on Alaska Airlines) if your confirmed option is the next day as well. American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process.

Here’s one example of where this matters: an Executive Platinum member facing a seven hour Dallas–Charlotte delay could see confirmed alternatives in the disruption tool, but couldn’t find a way to request earlier standby. Even accepting a later confirmed flight didn’t solve it. An agent eventually added them to standby and they cleared.

I covered American’s new disruption banners in January, alongside rebooking, baggage tracking, and digital hotel and meal vouchers. Standby was one of the additions they said was coming. American also described the feature in its October 26 iPhone app release notes.

American is trying to offer more tools for managing disruptions. That’s both a cost savings and also empowering to the passenger. A customer who feels in control of their options is going to have a better view of the airline than one who feels at the mercy of broader forces. It’s about raising net promoter scores when things go wrong, which is part of customers being willing to be repeat purchasers, purchasers of premium products, and passengers willing to pay more to fly American. I get asked some version of the same question all the time: what’s the best travel credit card to actually keep in your wallet?

For me, the answer has changed over time. As my travel habits have evolved, so has the mix of cards I rely on. Some help me earn points quickly, others offset travel costs with built-in credits, and a few simply make traveling more comfortable.

While getting outsize value from a travel credit card often means paying an annual fee, I've found that the right perks can more than justify the cost. And one of the cards I'm looking to add to my wallet next doesn't charge an annual fee at all.

These are the travel credit cards I keep coming back to — and in some cases, the ones I'm planning to add next — based on their earning potential, flexibility and benefits I actually find useful.

I chose these cards based on the value they can provide travelers. In particular, I considered:

I've also included cards for different types of travelers, from beginners and those seeking premium perks to airline and hotel loyalists and travelers who don't want to pay an annual fee.

Purchases that qualify for the $300 annual travel credit will not earn points.

*Welcome offer value is an estimated value based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by the issuer.

The newest premium travel card in my wallet is the Chase Sapphire Reserve, and after just a few months, it's already become one of my favorites.

While the $795 annual fee is steep, I've been getting plenty of use out of the card's travel perks. One of my favorite benefits so far has been the up to $500 in annual credits for The Edit, Chase’s curated hotel booking platform (issued as two credits of up to $250 per calendar year for stays of two nights or more).

I recently used one of those credits for a luxury stay at At Six in Stockholm, where I also enjoyed some of the other perks when you book with The Edit, such as complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit. The hotel's impressive breakfast spread was a particular highlight, and I was able to use the property credit to cover a couple of dine-in meals.

Lounge access has also been a major benefit. I frequently fly through Dulles International Airport (IAD) when visiting family on the East Coast, and the Etihad Lounge, which is part of the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, has become one of my go-to spots to relax before a flight.

I've also booked other hotel stays through Chase Travel, where the card earns 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. Between the hotel benefits, lounge access and $300 annual travel credit, I've found plenty of ways to put the Reserve to work in a short period of time.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 valuable points

The Sapphire Preferred was the first travel card in my wallet — and that goes for a lot of us here at TPG. It’s also the card I recommend most often to beginners or casual travelers who want flexible points without a sky-high annual fee.

With beginner-friendly perks like a $100 annual hotel credit and strong travel protections, it delivers real value without overwhelming complexity.

The card also makes it easy to get quick, upfront value. After earning the welcome offer and maximizing bonus categories — like 3 points per dollar spent on dining and 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchased outside the Chase Travel portal — I was able to build a sizable stash of points within a few months.

I ultimately redeemed those points for a trip through four European countries, which felt like a pretty great return for my first year with the card.

I'm also particularly excited about the card's newer earning category for vacation rentals. As someone who's stayed in more than 60 Airbnbs, I love that I can now earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation home rentals, including Airbnb bookings.

It’s the travel card I recommend over and over again to friends and family because of its ease of use, strong earning potential and outsize value relative to its modest $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred.

Related: 6 ways to maximize the Chase Sapphire Preferred as a beginner

Best for: Straightforward premium rewards

Another top contender in the premium space — and one that’s firmly earned a place in my wallet — is the Capital One Venture X Rewards Card. For me, its biggest selling point is how easy it is to get value from the card without having to overthink my spending.

Part of the reason I added the card was to diversify my points and miles beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards. Up until recently, I’d been almost exclusively earning Chase points, but as I’ve gotten deeper into the points and miles world, I’ve realized how valuable it is to have access to multiple transferable currencies and transfer partners.

At the same time, the Venture X fits naturally into my everyday spending habits. Cardholders earn a flat 2 miles per dollar on nearly every purchase, which removes the need to track bonus categories or optimize every swipe. It’s become my go-to catch-all card and the one I reach for whenever a purchase doesn’t neatly fit into a bonus category on another card.

I've also gotten great use out of its travel benefits. I recently used the card's $300 annual Capital One Travel credit toward a three-night stay at the DoubleTree by Hilton London Marble Arch, bringing the cost down from $1,096 to $796. I also appreciate being able to relax in Capital One Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges when I travel.

For me, the Venture X works because it combines straightforward everyday earning with travel benefits I actually use, making its $395 annual fee easier to justify.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Related: 5 reasons why I’m applying for the Capital One Venture X

For travelers who regularly fly a single airline — especially those based near one of that carrier’s hubs — a cobranded airline card can make a lot of sense.

That’s been true for me with United, but I think the same general strategy applies to frequent Delta and American Airlines flyers as well. If you consistently fly one carrier, the right airline card can make your travel experience cheaper, smoother and more comfortable through perks like travel credits, free checked bags and priority boarding.

Despite its $350 annual fee, the United Quest offers several easy-to-use benefits that help offset the cost. The $200 annual United travel credit, for instance, has helped offset flights home to visit family. And the two free checked bags for me and a travel companion have already saved me a significant amount in baggage fees.

The card also offers award flight discounts, anniversary bonus miles, priority boarding and improved award availability, which make the card feel like a keeper for the long term.

That said, I do wish it included lounge access — especially at this price point.

Still, the Quest has made flying United more affordable and convenient for me, which is exactly what I want from an airline credit card.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

Not every worthwhile travel rewards card needs to charge an annual fee. The Freedom Unlimited is one I'm interested in adding to my wallet because it could fill an important gap in my Chase strategy without adding another annual fee.

On its own, the Freedom Unlimited earns cash-back rewards. But when you pair it with an eligible Ultimate Rewards-earning card like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you can combine your rewards and potentially get more value by redeeming them for travel or transferring them to Chase's airline and hotel partners.

That's particularly appealing to me because I'm working toward building the Chase Trifecta, a strategy that combines multiple Chase cards to maximize earnings across different types of purchases.

With no annual fee, the Freedom Unlimited could give me another way to earn rewards on everyday spending while letting my Sapphire cards handle travel purchases and unlock more valuable redemption options.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Related: The best beginner Chase card combo for travel rewards

Best for: Hilton perks without the premium price tag

The Hilton Surpass is the newest addition to my wallet — and my first hotel credit card.

For years, I've prioritized flexible rewards over hotel-specific points because I didn't want to commit to a single hotel program. But as I've started traveling more and spending more nights in hotels, I realized I was leaving some valuable perks on the table.

After comparing several hotel cards, I ultimately chose the Hilton Surpass because it struck the right balance between cost and benefits. One of the biggest draws for me is automatic Hilton Honors Gold status, which gives me meaningful hotel perks without requiring me to earn status through stays.

I'm also a fan of the card's up to $200 in Hilton statement credits each calendar year, issued as up to $50 each quarter. And Hilton's large footprint means I'm much more likely to find a property where I can actually put those benefits to use when I travel.

For me, the Surpass is a relatively approachable way to test-drive hotel loyalty while getting useful benefits from the start. As I spend more nights with Hilton, I'll be able to see whether a hotel card deserves a permanent place in my travel strategy.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass.

Related: How I chose my first hotel credit card — and the 4 cards I considered

Choosing the right travel credit card ultimately comes down to how you travel, where you spend your money and which perks you'll actually use.

For beginners, the Chase Sapphire Preferred remains one of the strongest entry points thanks to its balance of value, flexibility and simplicity. Frequent travelers looking for a more premium experience — especially when it comes to lounge access and travel perks — may get more value from the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Meanwhile, the Capital One Venture X is a great fit for travelers who want premium benefits without overcomplicating their rewards strategy, and the United Quest offers a strong value proposition for frequent United flyers who prioritize convenience and United-specific perks.

For travelers who don't want to add another annual fee, the Chase Freedom Unlimited can be a useful complement to a Sapphire card, particularly if you're building a Chase trifecta. And for travelers who want hotel-specific perks, the Hilton Surpass offers a relatively accessible entry point to hotel loyalty with automatic Hilton Gold status and useful Hilton credits.

You certainly don't need all six cards on this list to get good value from travel rewards. But whether you're looking for your first travel card or considering adding another to your wallet, I'd start by thinking about which benefits you'd use most often — and whether they're worth the annual fee.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

Minor Hotels has opened the first urban location of its Life Longevity wellness brand inside The St. Regis Bangkok — a hotel Minor owns but Marriott operates under its own brand. The move follows Layan Life by Anantara at Anantara Layan Phuket Resort, which Minor spent more than $11 million developing, and replaces the property's former Longevity Hub by Clinique La Prairie. Minor Chief Commercial Officer Ian Di Tullio said the brand was designed from the start to work independently of Anantara, giving Minor the freedom to place it in its own luxury properties or someone else's. Minor still owns or leases almost 70% of its portfolio under what it calls an asset-right strategy, and Di Tullio said that lets the company fund a concept itself, test the economics, and then approach third-party owners. He named three formats for the brand: a resort retreat, an urban hub, and eventually a residence. Di Tullio declined to say whether Marriott approved the concept under its brand standards or shares in revenue, citing confidentiality. Marriott did not immediately respond to Skift's request for comment.

Photo Credit: A KLM Boeing 737 at Amsterdam Schiphol Airport. KLM/Capital Photo

Despite improving profits, the Dutch airline says its future is far from guaranteed, with big changes needed to bring costs under control and restore competitiveness.

KLM is preparing to shrink its workforce by almost 15% as part of a major restructuring aimed at cutting costs and improving its long-term competitiveness.

The Dutch flag carrier announced the measures on Thursday alongside parent company Air France-KLM's third-quarter earnings. Around 5,000 positions have already been or will be affected, with jobs eliminated, outsourced or transferred within the wider airline group.

The overhaul aims to deliver an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, bringing the total targeted improvement to €1.4 billion.

Speaking on Thursday, Marjan Rintel, KLM's CEO, delivered a stark message about the need for change: "KLM's future is not guaranteed… That's why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we're taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute."

KLM will cut, outsource, or transfer about 5,000 positions — close to 15% of its workforce — in a restructuring announced Thursday alongside Air France-KLM's third-quarter results. The plan targets an additional €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in annual earnings improvements, lifting the total goal to €1.4 billion. Roughly 1,250 catering jobs have already moved to Gategroup, 800 ground services roles are expected to go to third-party providers at Schiphol and for KLM Cityhopper, and 2,000 positions, including 1,500 at contact center Cygnific, will transfer to parent Air France-KLM. Another 1,000 reductions are planned through productivity gains, and KLM is seeking union agreements covering at least an 8% productivity improvement by 2028 and restrained wage growth. The fleet is being resized too: A321neos stay, Embraer E195-E2s replace previously planned A320s, and older 737s and E190s will be phased out, giving Cityhopper a bigger role in Europe. The cuts come despite improving numbers — KLM's third-quarter operating profit rose €106 million to €458 million, and group operating profit hit €1.35 billion, sending shares up about 12% — with CEO Marjan Rintel saying the cost base remains too high and that "KLM's future is not guaranteed."

Passenger traffic dropped 22% to 21.8 million, capacity fell 17%, and seat factor slipped to 72% from 79.5%, as connecting traffic moved to Istanbul, Singapore, and other hubs. Pre-hedge fuel costs rose 60% year over year; hedging cut the net increase to 13%, with fuel still 34% of operating cost. Cargo was the bright spot: tonnage fell 1% but revenue rose 52% as conflict squeezed airfreight capacity and shipping disruption pushed volume to air. Emirates kept spending through the downturn, taking nine A350s, refitting 12 aircraft under a $7 billion-plus retrofit program, and adding Starlink to 36 more aircraft. Linus Benjamin Bauer of BAA & Partners said the core flying business was likely loss-making on an unhedged basis and that the second half will show whether the operating model has recovered. Emirates has not disclosed its hedging position for the fiscal second half.

#6085. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

The European Commission released its EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy on Wednesday, setting out a vision to spread visitors across lesser-known destinations and across the full year — without new funding, binding mandates, or numerical targets. The Commission said 42% of nights spent in a destination fall, on average, in its three busiest months, and the strategy arrives after a summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and continued overtourism backlash. Its sustainability pillar rests on three voluntary instruments: the EU Model for Tourism Management, a proposed Council Recommendation for Balanced Tourism, and an EU Toolbox for Balanced Tourism that will include shared approaches to short-term rentals. A Cruise Cooperation Dialogue was also proposed. The Commission said €18 billion in EU support is expected to have benefited tourism from 2021 to 2027 but committed no fresh money, pointing instead to the 2028–2034 budget still under negotiation and to combining private investment with financial instruments. Industry voices quoted by Skift welcomed the volume-to-value direction while pressing for measurable targets, simpler funding access, and practical fixes such as interoperable transport ticketing, which the Commission said it would only "explore" by 2028. The strategy also flags that AI trip-planning tools could reinforce existing tourism hubs if destinations stay passive.

Nonetheless, Boratâs relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant â except for when he revealshis subjectsâ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Boratâs stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in âSubsequent Moviefilm.â Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctorâs office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohenâs infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama âwith the Wuhan flu.â

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business donât tell us anything we donât already know. Instead, itâs what the context implies about Americaâs psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isnât merely in the pastorâs misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutarâs stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutarâs father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesnât disturb the status quo.

Thereâs the Texas baker who uses icing toÂ pipe the wordsÂ âJews Will Not Replace Usâ on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. Thereâs theÂ shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the âno means yesâ dress section. Thereâs the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, âWhat color is best for racist family?â says without pause or reaction, âI wouldnât go any darker than a six or a seven.â

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; sheâs also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first âBoratâ and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, sheâs a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of âSubsequent Moviefilmâ relative to the first âBoratâ sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has arenât deadly, although itâs plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the filmâs ending in ways that donât feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the âBoratâ of 2006 and the 2020 âSubsequent Moviefilmâ is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trumpâs election in 2016, to say nothing of howÂ decline and fall of basic critical thoughtÂ has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, thereâs simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If thereâs a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called âlesserâ nations.

Now it doesnât allow the audience to be so sure of itself,Â implying in the final sceneÂ that we arenât merely ugly Americans. Weâre a once glorious nationÂ being led by goons who areÂ sliding us backwardÂ into diminishment, and dangerously so. ThatÂ is nothing to laugh about.Â

âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ is currently streaming on Amazon.

Tripadvisor is cutting jobs in its legacy hotel metasearch business under a global restructuring, and both CEO Matt Goldberg and CFO Michael Noonan are leaving. Goldberg said the decision to combine the Viator and Tripadvisor experiences teams "hasn't proved out as we expected," a judgment backed by the numbers: third-quarter experiences revenue fell 3% and adjusted EBITDA in the segment fell 27%. The restructuring shifts product engineering and data analytics roles into experiences and is expected to deliver $40 million in gross annualized savings. Tripadvisor said it will keep investigating strategic alternatives and will use the $685 million from the sale of TheFork to American Express to pay down debt. Goldberg leaves February 16, 2027; Noonan departs December 31, with Chief Strategy and Operations Officer Kristen Dalton stepping in as interim CFO.

#6077. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

At least 27 flights across Europe were disrupted Thursday by bomb threats, the second wave in a week, and no explosives were found in any case. French fighter jets intercepted an Aer Lingus Dublin–Rome flight carrying more than 150 passengers and escorted it to an air base in Normandy, Bulgaria's air force escorted three airliners to the ground, and Madrid authorities searched Air Europa and Iberia aircraft after receiving three emailed threats in under 20 minutes. Earlier threats on Monday and Tuesday hit flights operated by Wizz Air, Ryanair, LOT, and Scandinavian Airlines, plus a cruise ship in Greece. No government has said who is responsible, and Bloomberg reported no pattern in the carriers or routes targeted. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions told the AP the threats could be copycats, a single person or group, or "hybrid warfare" by state actors, and pointed to a possible Russian link; Moscow has denied European accusations of sabotage this year. The operational math is the problem: each threat an airline acts on means a diversion or stopped departure, a full search, often a replacement aircraft, crews timing out, and passengers rebooked — and Skift has reported that insurance typically doesn't cover those commercial losses. The hoaxes arrive while European carriers are already absorbing jet fuel prices that have more than doubled year over year, Middle East airspace closures that lengthen Asia routes, and drone incursions at airports.

#6071. Schumer faces mutiny from newly elected Senate Dems as party prepares to seize power

Several newly elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

Senate Democrats will soon decide who will lead them with their newly acquired grip on power in the upper chamber, and while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., appears to be the favorite, some in the caucus aren’t eager to back him.

Schumer has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, helming the caucus as both majority and minority leader since 2017. But many of the fresh crop of Democratic senators-elect, which spans the ideological gamut from moderate to progressive, are tepid, at best, in backing him for another term.

And some said throughout their campaigns that they wouldn’t support him at all.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL REJECTS SCHUMER BUT BENEFITS FROM MILLIONS IN SPENDING BY HIS ALLIES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is confident he will continue to lead Senate Democrats, but newcomers to the caucus aren't on board with him at the helm.  (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer, but we need new leadership," Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton told CNN in September. "We need new younger leadership, young blood."

Hamilton is the moderate megachurch pastor who toppled Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., on Election Night, flipping the Sunflower State for the first time in nearly a century. He, like others this cycle, argued that Democrats needed "fresh ideas and fresh leadership."

"In Kansas, Chuck Schumer is a liability for Democrats, and we've got to have leaders that can unite us, bring us together, not just Democrats, but bring together Democrats and Republicans to solve real problems," he said. "And I think people are frustrated with the gridlock in the sense that people are not working together to solve problems."

Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections later this year, and Schumer will have to shore up support within his newly expanded caucus to stay at the top. But he will only need a majority of Senate Democrats to back him.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM

So far, Democrats’ majority in the upper chamber is at 54 seats and could further expand depending on the results in Mississippi and Alaska, which as of Thursday were leaning in their favor.

Schumer believed that he would still be the one to lead Democrats and contended to reporters on Wednesday that issues that incoming senators and their voters may have had with the direction of the Democratic Party in recent years were not about him.

"The issue is not me," Schumer said. "I'll be re-elected as majority leader, but the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want."

Still, there is a faction of newcomers, including senators-elect Troy Jackson in Maine, Julianna Stratton in Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, who aren’t all in for Schumer.

THUNE GOES ALL-IN ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS SCHUMER STAYS ON BENCH, FACES REJECTION FROM FELLOW DEMS

Former state Sen. Troy Jackson, a Democrat from Maine and then-gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a Fighting Oligarchy event. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Jackson, speaking to reporters just before Election Day, said his position hadn’t changed on Schumer.

"I told Schumer that I’m going to, you know, support somebody else," Jackson said. "So it’s no different now."

That somebody else could be Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who has been proposed as an alternative by progressives, like El-Sayed, to lead Senate Democrats instead of Schumer. Van Hollen may have his eyes elsewhere — he has said that he’s "kicking the tires" on a 2028 run.

A Democratic aide familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking told Fox News Digital that before selecting a new leader, the lawmaker believed "the caucus needs to have an honest and open conversation about how we move an agenda forward that reflects the will of the American people."

"He’s made it clear that the new Democratic majorities need to use their power to push a proactive, economic agenda," they said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6069. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”

In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.
